items.descriptionOriginal: Imagine walking into a house and finding a stream flowing beneath your feet. Not outside the entrance or in a garden designed to resemble a natural waterbody, but directly beneath a transparent glass floor. Look up, and there is a tree framed by glass walls and a glass roof. Walk a little further, and the architecture opens towards a valley, allowing the surrounding landscape to become part of the experience. This is Whispers of the Wild, a residential project by MAWI Design, led by Chennai-based architect Malli Saravanan , in Yercaud, Tamil Nadu. But the most interesting thing about this house is not what its architects added to the landscape. It is what they chose not to take away. Spread across a 10,000-square-foot plot in the eco-sensitive Shervaroy Hills, the 2,400-square-foot residence was designed for a family of six. Completed in 2024, it occupies two levels and sits within Wild Orchid, a 100-acre residential community that follows an eco-sensitive development approach. "We wanted the terrain to flow naturally over here and then bring the entire thing out," Saravanan tells The Better India . "I wanted much of it to remain tucked into the landscape, with its built form designed to sit beneath the surrounding tree canopy." The tree that became the centre of the design When the MAWI Design team first visited the property, they found a sloping site with a valley opening up on one side. A mature tree occupied a prominent position on the land, its canopy extending across the site. Instead of treating it as an obstacle around which the building had to be designed, the architects decided to make it the focal point. The team first conducted a total-station survey and mapped the trees across the property. This helped them understand where the existing vegetation stood and how the proposed structure could be positioned without cutting them down. "We made sure that we didn't want to cut any of the trees, and we tried to work around them without cutting the tree," Saravanan explains. The design was subsequently broken into three architectural fragments, allowing the tree to remain at the centre of the composition. "As visitors enter the house, their first visual connection is with this tree. The private and communal spaces open towards an L-shaped deck that wraps around it, creating a shared outdoor space overlooking the valley." "The tree is not retained as a decorative feature. We tried to retain this tree as the hero of the site and started building a story around this tree," he says. The same idea extends to the interiors. Instead of treating it as an obstacle around which the building had to be designed, the architects decided to make it the focal point. Photograph: (mawidesign.india) The living, dining and kitchen areas follow an open-plan arrangement , while the communal deck creates a transition between the house and the outdoors. The master bedroom, meanwhile, projects outwards in a cantilevered form. Its glass frame opens towards a panoramic view of the valley. Saravanan points out that the corners have been kept free of columns to preserve the expansive views. "We don't have any TV walls and stuff, so the bedrooms are designed to open towards nature, too," he says, describing the decision to make the surrounding landscape the primary visual experience. A stream that disappeared, and an attempt to bring back its memory One of the most distinctive features of Whispers of the Wild is its entrance foyer. Here, the team separated two building blocks to create a transition space that feels open rather than enclosed. They also introduced a cascading water feature beneath a glass floor. There is a story behind this intervention. The living, dining and kitchen areas follow an open-plan arrangement, while the communal deck creates a transition between the house and the outdoors. Photograph: (mawidesign.india) "We tried to pull out the rocks that were there at the site. And then we set up a water feature so that when one comes into this foyer space, the flooring is completely glass, so the water will be flowing underneath," Saravanan says. The experience is deliberately immersive. The glass floor reveals the water below, while glass on the opposite side reflects the trees. A glass roof completes the visual connection with the surroundings. What happens during heavy rainfall? The team incorporated rainwater harvesting and constructed a storage tank to collect water from the roof and other catchment areas for use within the house. "Since it is a slope side, we have made sure that when there is heavy rain, the water gets collected and then it is harvested inside the ground, and the overflow gets down to the valley," Saravanan says. There is, however, an important distinction in the project's assessment of water systems. Saravanan confirms that the team conducted a soil test and a general site survey, but did not undertake a separate hydrological assessment . What happens when the house borrows from the landscape? The walls of the house incorporate locally available random rubble stones, many sourced from within the property or nearby areas. Saravanan explains that construction activity in and around Yercaud often brings up large boulders when soil is excavated. Some of these were already available on the property, while smaller stones were sourced from nearby community areas. "We use this material as a kind of expression of the context. We use the same material in the exterior and also in the interior, so that we create a very timeless kind of palette inside the house," he says. The rubble stone is used as an exterior-facing element over brick construction, rather than as the primary structural wall. According to Saravanan, the thickness and overall mass of the wall contribute to thermal comfort within the house. The flooring uses leathered Kota stone. Saravanan wanted the sensation of walking indoors to resemble the experience of walking outdoors. The stone's natural texture and coolness were important considerations. View this post on Instagram A post shared by Mawi Design (@mawidesign.india) "For us, the first thing is experiential. The second is the sustainable aspect of it, and third is the aesthetics," he explains. Oxide finishes and other natural materials complete the palette. The intention was not to create a polished, artificial version of nature, but to let the materials sit comfortably within the surrounding landscape. The team also retained the site's existing vegetation, including fruit-bearing plants and a fig tree. Saravanan says they avoided introducing non-native plants. The one notable addition was bamboo, planted along the property boundary. It serves two purposes. The community has a pathway running along the edge of the property, and the bamboo provides visual privacy for the residents . It also contributes to the sensory experience of the house. "We love the rustling sounds. So whenever there is wind, you listen to the rustling sounds, and it adds to the overall experience of the space," he says. Does wildlife find a place here, too? A house in a hillside landscape cannot be understood only through its architecture. The Shervaroy Hills have their own distinctive vegetation, including shrubs and fruit-bearing plants. Saravanan says the team tried to retain the existing flora and make the new landscape blend with the region. He has also noticed changes in the presence of birds and other smaller wildlife around the property. "Butterflies, birds, and peacocks started coming after this," he says, adding that peacocks are frequently seen around the house. A home that changes how its residents experience nature Interestingly, Whispers of the Wild was not originally conceived as a permanent retirement home. The client, 67-year-old Chandrapratapan from Salem, purchased the property. "One of our favourite things about living here is never knowing what we might see in the morning. Peacocks often wander by in the garden, squirrels move between the trees, and occasionally we spot a mongoose passing through. We've started recognising different birds by their calls. The old tree is probably the busiest spot on the property, with birds and insects constantly moving through it," he shares with The Better India . "This has made us much more aware of all the life we share this place with. We love that we've been able to preserve much of what was already here — the trees, the slope and the natural landscape," Chandrapratap adds. Saravanan also believes this reflects a shift in how people think about their homes. "We are in a very rushed world, with all these tensions and pressure, running here and there. At the end of it, people want to spend time for themselves," he says. He has noticed more people looking beyond metropolitan neighbourhoods for homes that offer a connection with nature and a sense of calm. For him, this is not simply about having a second home or spending money on elaborate interiors. It is about the relationship between people, their surroundings and the communities they live in. Can building with nature also make financial sense? There is another question worth asking. Is this approach financially viable, or is it an architectural luxury accessible only to people who can afford expensive homes in the hills? Saravanan puts the construction cost of Whispers of the Wild at approximately Rs 1.3-1.4 crore. He considers this reasonable for a project of its scale and location, particularly because transporting materials to a hill station and arranging labour can increase construction costs. View this post on Instagram A post shared by Mawi Design (@mawidesign.india) "We had all those good elements around the site. We wanted the site not to be manicured. We wanted things to be imperfect and just flow seamlessly," he says. "We don't know where that new landscape starts or where the new construction starts. It should feel like it's very well lived in, especially the exterior parts." The project does not establish that this approach is cheaper in every situation. Its costs depend on the terrain, construction requirements, materials and site conditions. But it offers an example of how existing natural features can become part of the architectural experience rather than being removed and recreated. Before building on a hillside, what should architects reconsider? For Saravanan, the first step is to understand the site before drawing up the building. "First, we need to understand the existing terrain, the flora, the fauna, and the existing site conditions. Making less impact on nature is the first fundamental thing they need to consider," he says. He believes the value of a mature tree, for instance, cannot be measured simply in terms of the money required to plant another one. "Today, we can buy anything, but a well-grown tree like this, with whatever money they want, they can't buy it." He also emphasises the importance of keeping the building footprint small. At Whispers of the Wild, the architects used cantilevered sections and elevated portions to reduce the amount of building mass touching the ground. The intention was to allow the landscape to continue around the structure. "If the footprint is very small, it is always better. It is the idea that a building does not always need to begin with a cleared, levelled piece of land," he adds. All pictures: mawidesign.india

items.descriptionOriginal: Advanced computing models can reconstruct complex molecular structures with high accuracy, but predicting how potential drug compounds behave remains a challenge, according to a new medicinal chemistry benchmark introduced by OpenAI. Called MedChemBench, the evaluation tests whether models can connect molecular structures with experimental evidence to explain research findings, compare compounds, and predict their properties. The benchmark draws on 117 published papers and patents and includes 761 distinct molecular structures across 99 problems. At the xhigh reasoning setting, GPT-6 Astra earned 95.4 percent of the available credit for reconstructing molecular structures. However, the model earned only about half the available credit for selecting compounds and predicting their numerical properties. The findings highlight a gap between identifying chemical structures correctly and understanding how changes to those structures influence a potential drug’s behavior. Testing complex chemical trade-offs Medicinal chemists routinely balance competing properties when developing drug candidates. A compound may effectively block a disease-related protein but perform poorly when absorbed by the body or break down too quickly. Improving one characteristic can also weaken another, making it difficult to identify compounds that meet several requirements simultaneously. MedChemBench evaluates four capabilities: molecular structure reconstruction, scientific reasoning, compound ranking and selection, and numerical property prediction. One of its problems draws on research into inhibitors of PRMT5, a protein studied in cancer drug discovery. Models receive molecular structures and experimental results from earlier stages of the research. They must predict how three related compounds will perform in terms of PRMT5 inhibition in cells, permeability across a cell barrier, and breakdown by liver enzymes. Later experimental results, withheld from the models, revealed competing advantages. Compound 23 inhibited PRMT5 at a lower concentration, while compound 24 crossed the cell barrier more readily and degraded more slowly in the laboratory assay. The task tests whether models can recognize that stronger activity against a biological target does not necessarily translate into better absorption or metabolic stability. Molecular accuracy remains crucial The benchmark also examines whether models can reconstruct molecules accurately from chemical drawings, including their atom connections, ring structures and stereochemistry. In one example, models were asked to assemble a compound while preserving an 18-atom ring. GPT-6 Astra reconstructed the structure correctly in all 10 responses at the highest reasoning setting shared by the evaluated models. In contrast, GPT-5.6 Sol produced a smaller, 15-atom ring, while GPT-5.6 Luna generated disconnected molecular fragments. Such errors can change the identity of the compound being analyzed, undermining subsequent predictions about its properties. Despite its strong structural performance, the model struggled more with compound selection and numerical predictions. These tasks require connecting molecular changes with several experimental measurements rather than simply reproducing a chemical structure. The researchers evaluated 11 models across different reasoning settings. Higher reasoning effort generally improved performance, although substantial differences remained between models. The team cautioned that the results do not establish whether models can discover new drugs or improve laboratory decisions. The benchmark relies on historical research, and prior exposure to published sources cannot be ruled out. Models also completed the tasks without tools, feedback, or new experiments. MedChemBench therefore offers a way to identify progress and remaining weaknesses in computational reasoning for medicinal chemistry, rather than demonstrating that these systems are ready to replace drug discovery research.

Η Neuralink μοιράστηκε ένα δίλεπτο βίντεο στις 20 Νοεμβρίου, που δείχνει τον συμμετέχοντα να παίζει τον τελευταίο τίτλο της Rockstar Games, ο οποίος κυκλοφόρησε παγκοσμίως στο N…
items.descriptionOriginal: A Neuralink clinical trial participant has played Grand Theft Auto VI (GTA VI) using a brain implant, demonstrating how the company’s technology can translate neural signals into inputs for digital devices. Neuralink shared a two-minute video on November 20, showing the participant playing Rockstar Games’ latest title, which launched worldwide on November 19 for PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X|S. In the clip, the player steers a speedboat beneath a bridge and into a narrow, tree-lined channel while following an in-game instruction to collect a package. A small video feed shows the participant alongside a live neural-decoding dashboard and a graphic of a game controller. The controller’s inputs light up as commands are registered. Neuralink did not identify the participant or confirm which console was used for the demonstration. The company captioned its post on X simply: “Playing GTA VI with a Neuralink.” Brain signals control devices The demonstration uses Neuralink’s brain-computer interface (BCI) technology, which is designed to translate neural activity associated with intended movements into commands that a computer can understand. Its Telepathy system listens to activity in the brain region responsible for controlling hand movements. Participants learn to move a computer cursor by imagining moving their hand, with the system translating those signals into mouse actions such as clicking and navigating. Playing GTA VI with a Neuralink pic.twitter.com/ViFjXK9OSV — Neuralink (@neuralink) November 20, 2026 Neuralink says some clinical trial participants are also testing experimental features that extend control to gaming consoles, keyboards, wheelchairs and robotic arms. However, these capabilities are not available to everyone enrolled in its studies. The company is investigating the technology primarily to restore digital independence for people living with paralysis. Its device-control trials include people with quadriplegia resulting from spinal cord injuries, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) and brain stem strokes. This is not Neuralink’s first gaming demonstration. In 2024, the company shared an update on its first PRIME study participant, Noland Arbaugh, who used the implant to play Civilization VI and Mario Kart. Arbaugh, who has quadriplegia, also demonstrated how the implant allowed him to control a computer cursor and interact with digital applications using intended movements. Neuralink’s latest demonstration extends that work into a newly released game, although it does not establish that all participants can independently control commercial gaming systems. Blindsight awaits approval The GTA VI demonstration comes as Neuralink prepares another experimental technology, called Blindsight, designed to help people with severe vision loss regain visual perception. Elon Musk said on October 30 that the company’s second product was ready from an engineering standpoint and was waiting for regulatory approval. Blindsight is intended to bypass damaged eyes or optic nerves by stimulating the brain’s visual cortex directly. The technology aims to translate visual information into electrical signals that the brain can interpret. Musk has said the system could eventually help people who are completely blind, including those who have never had sight. However, the technology has not yet demonstrated that it can restore useful vision in human participants. The US Food and Drug Administration granted Blindsight Breakthrough Device Designation in 2024. The designation is intended to speed up the development and review of promising medical technologies, but it does not constitute regulatory approval. Neuralink’s brain implants remain investigational and have not been approved by the FDA or other regulatory authorities.

items.descriptionOriginal: In 1973, American brothers Michael and Brian McCormack mailed 1,360 letters in seven languages to government leaders across the globe, encouraging them to participate in the inaugural World Hello Day. “We wanted to do something to celebrate the importance of personal communication to preserving peace,” Michael, a senior at Harvard at the time, previously told the university paper, The Crimson . He and Brian had pooled their money to pay for the postage, with the goal of getting their recipients to agree to, quite literally, spread the word. The idea behind the holiday, observed every Nov. 21, is that differences should be addressed through peaceful conversation rather than conflict. To participate, all you have to do is say “hello” to 10 people. Fifteen countries pledged their support the first year; today, individuals in 180 have joined in — including 31 Nobel Peace Prize winners who sent the brothers letters championing World Hello Day. “It’s something people can do on their own in widely different places,” Michael explained to the Associated Press back in 1991. “It gives people a chance to do something about the world; it empowers them.” Ready to get started? Before you do, consider broadening your reach by learning how to say hello in a few different languages — below are 25 translations (plus two bonus ones, just for fun). Portuguese – olá Hindi – namaste Dutch – hallo Filipino – kumusta Ukrainian – pryvit Arabic – marhaban Polish – witam Greek – geiá sou Hebrew – shalom Mandarin – nǐ hǎo Spanish – hola Esperanto – saluton Yoruba – pẹlẹ o Hawaiian – aloha Japanese – kon’nichiwa Icelandic – halló Swahili – habari French – bonjour Zulu – sawubona Korean – annyeonghaseyo Persian – salām Turkish – merhaba Swedish – hej Samoan – talofa Italian – ciao Klingon (from Star Trek ) – nuqneH Dothraki (from Game of Thrones ) – m’athchomaroon

items.titleOriginal: If you struggle with changing people’s minds, it probably says something positive about you
items.description: Αν δυσκολευτήκατε ποτέ να πείσετε κάποιον να αλλάξει γνώμη, είτε πρόκειται για επαγγελματική απόφαση, για διαφωνία με ένα παιδί ή προσπαθείτε να κάνετε τη γιαγιά να αλλάξει τη συνδρομή του καλωδίου, μπορεί να είναι απογοητευτικό. items.descriptionOriginal: If you ever had a hard time persuading someone to change their mind , whether it’s a work decision, a disagreement with a child, or trying to get grandma to change her cable subscription, it can be frustrating. It can even make you doubt your knowledge on a subject—even if you know it well—because you couldn’t explain it to someone else. The funny thing is that if you can’t explain something you are well-versed in to someone with half the understanding, it’s probably because you’re highly intelligent. Research has found repeatedly that experts in a subject are often pretty bad at explaining it to others because they can’t bridge the gap between their knowledge and the other person’s. The curse of knowledge The problem is that if you have a hard time persuading people to change their minds, you may think you aren’t the expert that you thought you were. However, psychology experts say the exact opposite, and they have a dramatic name for the problem: the curse of knowledge. A frustrated teacher. Credit: Canva “Lots of us have expertise in particular areas. Becoming an expert in something means that we become more and more fascinated by nuance and complexity,” Chip and Dan Heath write in Stick: Why Some Ideas Survive and Others Die. “That’s when the curse of knowledge kicks in, and we start to forget what it’s like not to know what we know.” The curse of knowledge stems from people’s natural inclination to forget what they knew before they became experts. That’s why it can be hard for a parent in their 40s to explain basic math to a 9-year-old. “That is the curse of knowledge,” Miro Kazakoff, a senior lecturer in managerial communication at MIT Sloan, told the university’s publication . “We have to work really hard when we are communicating information to people who don’t have the same level of expertise that we have.” “When we see a pattern or recognize something or know something, we forget what it was like before we knew that thing. We can’t unsee [it],” he continued . “This is why experts struggle to communicate about their own domain to nonexperts. There is a tremendous amount of context and knowledge that makes it hard to recognize what it was like before we knew what we now know.” the curse of knowledge pic.twitter.com/8ytwFMuuez — ọrẹ (@orethebrave) March 12, 2023 The Dunning-Kruger effect The curse of knowledge is similar to the Dunning-Kruger effect , which states that experts often undervalue their knowledge because they know that there are gaps in their understanding. But those who know very little about a subject overestimate their knowledge. Couple having a disagreement. Credit: Canva If you suffer from the curse of knowledge, the best way to overcome it is to empathize with your audience to gauge how much they know. It’s also important to simplify your message to make it more accessible and to determine the audience’s knowledge base by practicing active listening and asking questions. In the end, if you underestimated your intelligence because you had a hard time being persuasive, the problem is probably the other way around. The curse of knowledge may be a communication problem, but it’s also a sign that you know so much, you’ve forgotten what it’s like to know so little. The post If you struggle with changing people’s minds, it probably says something positive about you appeared first on Upworthy .

items.title: Ένας ήχος τυμπάνου στο «Stayin’ Alive» επαναλαμβάνεται για έναν λόγο που μπορείτε να ακούσετε σε μια άλλη επιτυχία των Bee Gees
items.titleOriginal: A drum sound on ‘Stayin’ Alive’ repeats for a reason you can hear in another Bee Gees hit
items.description: Από το πρώτο beat, η επιτυχία των Bee Gees του 1977 «Stayin’ Alive» έχει έναν από τους πιο αναγνωρίσιμους ήχους στην ιστορία της ντίσκο. Αλλά το μυστικό πίσω από τον σταθερό ρυθμό του βρίσκεται σε μια άλλη από τις επιτυχίες τους, το "Night Fever". Όταν ο ντράμερ του συγκροτήματος χρειάστηκε να φύγει από μια ηχογράφηση, οι μουσικοί βρήκαν μια δημιουργική λύση που βοήθησε να δώσει στο τραγούδι τα διακριτικά του…
items.descriptionOriginal: From the opening beat, the Bee Gees’ 1977 hit “Stayin’ Alive” has one of the most recognizable sounds in disco history. But the secret behind its steady rhythm lies in another of their hits, “Night Fever.” When the band’s drummer had to leave a recording session, the musicians came up with a creative solution that helped give the song its distinctive sound . What began as a quick fix became the signature beat of “ Stayin’ Alive .” And it all happened long before musicians could copy and repeat a recording on a computer. The Bee Gees needed a drummer. They found another solution. The Bee Gees were working on songs for the soundtrack to Saturday Night Fever , the film starring John Travolta. Recording sessions were underway at Le Château Studios, about an hour north of Paris, France, when their drummer, Dennis Bryon, had to return to England for a family matter. The filmmakers were waiting to hear “Stayin’ Alive,” and finding a replacement drummer on short notice wasn’t easy. Recording engineer Karl Richardson described the problem in a 2000 interview with Mix . The group first tried using an electric organ’s built-in drum machine, but the results were disappointing. “It sounded terrible,” Richardson said. Producer Albhy Galuten had an idea, which he described in a 2002 interview with Berklee College of Music . “Back then, drum machines were really primitive, not even close to what they are today. I had a brainstorm and told Karl we should take a bar from ‘Night Fever,’ which we had already recorded, and make a drum loop,” said Galuten. Two bars of music become a disco classic Galuten and Barry Gibb listened through the drums on “Night Fever,” searching for a section with the right feel. They eventually settled on two bars of music. “We chose a bar that felt so good,” recalled Galuten. The next step was figuring out how to repeat those few seconds throughout the song. Richardson copied the drum section onto a separate piece of magnetic tape and joined the ends together to make a continuous loop. The final tape was too long to fit around the recording machine alone, so he stretched it around microphone stands and other equipment in the studio. As the tape passed through the recording machine, the same few seconds of drumming played over and over. The loop provided a steady beat without losing the natural sound of Bryon’s original performance. By the time Bryon returned to the studio, the group liked the result too much to replace it. He added additional drum parts, but the loop remained the foundation of the song. The mysterious drummer named Bernard Lupé The recording technique led to a joke involving a drummer who didn’t exist. The Bee Gees credited the drum performance to Bernard Lupé, a fictional musician whose name was a playful reference to legendary session drummer Bernard Purdie . Of course, there was no Bernard Lupé. The performance was Dennis Bryon’s drumming, repeated over and over on a loop of magnetic tape. The trick proved useful beyond “Stayin’ Alive.” The same drum loop was also used on the Bee Gees’ “More Than a Woman” and later on Barbra Streisand’s 1980 hit “Woman in Love.” According to recording engineer Karl Richardson, who recalled the joke in an interview with Sound on Sound , the fictional drummer attracted inquiries from people hoping to hire him. The post A drum sound on ‘Stayin’ Alive’ repeats for a reason you can hear in another Bee Gees hit appeared first on Upworthy .

items.title: Οι Beatles έκαναν πάρτι στους Monkees. Ο Micky Dolenz έκρυψε τους καλεσμένους σε ένα τραγούδι.
items.titleOriginal: The Beatles threw the Monkees a party. Micky Dolenz hid the guests in a song.
items.description: Ο τραγουδιστής των Monkees, Micky Dolenz, βρισκόταν στο Λονδίνο το 1967 όταν το συγκρότημα βρέθηκε σε ένα πάρτι που θα μπορούσε να είχε συμβεί μόνο στη δεκαετία του Swinging Sixties. Ως αποχαιρετιστήρια γιορτή μετά τις παραστάσεις του γκρουπ στο Λονδίνο, πραγματοποιήθηκε μια ιδιωτική συγκέντρωση στο Speakeasy. Αυτό το ήδη διάσημο κλαμπ ήταν ένα δημοφιλές στέκι εκτός ωραρίου για τη μουσική βιομηχανία του Λονδίνου…
items.descriptionOriginal: Monkees vocalist Micky Dolenz was in London in 1967 when the band found themselves at the kind of party that could only have happened in the Swinging Sixties. As a farewell celebration following the group’s London shows, a private gathering was held at the Speakeasy. This already famous club was a popular after-hours haunt for London’s music-industry crowd. Music manager Vic Lewis organized the July 3 party, and John Lennon, Paul McCartney and George Harrison were among the guests , along with Eric Clapton, The Who, Manfred Mann and Dusty Springfield. Dolenz would later reveal the experience inspired a song he wrote afterward, which became his first commercially released composition for The Monkees. Some accounts place the songwriting during an earlier part of the London visit. So the precise chronology is a bit murkier than the legend makes it sound. But what isn’t murky is what Dolenz did with those wild experiences and larger-than-life characters he encountered, which went on to shape a tune named “Randy Scouse Git.” The Beatles are hiding in the lyrics The song’s most conspicuous clue is the line about “the four kings of E.M.I.” Those four kings were, of course, The Beatles, who were signed to EMI. Dolenz later explained that the line referred to the band and their recently released Sgt. Pepper’s Lonely Hearts Club Band . This album arrived just weeks before his London adventures. The lyrics contain a few more clues about the people around Dolenz at the time. “The being known as Wonder Girl” referred to Samantha Juste, whom Dolenz had fallen for and would eventually marry. And the “girl in yellow dress” has traditionally been identified as Mama Cass Elliot of The Mamas & the Papas, although Dolenz did not specifically confirm that identification himself. There was also the waiter who brought breakfast, plus, as is fitting for a rockstar lifestyle, the girls screaming outside. View this post on Instagram From there, the song gets even more abstract. There are birds on the sidewalk, a valet at the door, a dude compared to a penguin, talcum powder on a letter, and a “birthday boy” who may or may not need to “cut his hair.” Rather than forming a carefully constructed narrative, the images tumble into one another the way memories sometimes do. That was essentially the point. Dolenz described the process as “ word association ,” more or less turning his London experience into a musical diary. No deep hidden meanings lurked behind the lyrics. Just a musical collage of intertwined moments. Then the title became a problem As for the song’s title, Dolenz had heard “ randy scouse git ” on the BBC sitcom Till Death Us Do Part , thought it sounded funny, and wrote it down without knowing its risqué connotations. Unfortunately, the record company preparing to release the song as a single wasn’t as entertained. Considering the title (which basically translates to “sex-crazed Liverpudlian jerk” or “fool”) too crude for the British market, executives told Dolenz to come up with an “alternate title.” Dolenz took the suggestion literally. The song became “Alternate Title” in Britain and reached No. 2 on the U.K. chart , just behind The Beatles’ “All You Need Is Love.” Fitting that a song born from Dolenz’s Beatles-filled London adventure wound up competing with The Beatles on their own home turf. Apparently, the Monkees are still making history The Monkees’ history is getting another timely footnote this week. Andrew Sandoval, the band’s longtime manager and historian, has been nominated for a 2027 Grammy for Best Album Notes for his work on Pisces, Aquarius, Capricorn & Jones Ltd. (Super Deluxe Edition) . View this post on Instagram Sandoval’s nomination is recognition for preserving the story behind the band’s legendary music. In his own way, Dolenz did something similar almost six decades earlier, without really knowing it. The post The Beatles threw the Monkees a party. Micky Dolenz hid the guests in a song. appeared first on Upworthy .

items.titleOriginal: A crash closed the highway an hour before their wedding. An elk hunter saved the day with his dirt bike.
items.description: Ο Erich Thalacker και η Kyla Dickey ήθελαν οι φωτογραφίες του γάμου τους να είναι μεγάλες. Έτσι, την ημέρα του γάμου τους, οδήγησαν στα βουνά Sawtooth του Αϊντάχο με το κοστούμι και το φόρεμά τους για μια φωτογράφηση πριν επιστρέψουν στην τελετή στο South Fork Lodge στο Lowman. «Θέλαμε να το συλλάβουμε και θέλαμε να νιώσουμε άγριοι και περιπετειώδεις και οτιδήποτε άλλο», Thalacker…
items.descriptionOriginal: Erich Thalacker and Kyla Dickey wanted their wedding photos to feel big. So on their wedding day , they drove up into Idaho’s Sawtooth Mountains in their suit and dress for a photo shoot before heading back to the ceremony at South Fork Lodge in Lowman . “We wanted to capture that, and we wanted to feel wild and adventurous and whatnot,” Thalacker told KTVB, according to Yahoo! . On the way back, they got more adventure than they’d planned. A fatal crash had closed Highway 21, cutting them off from the lodge, 16 miles away. The estimated wait was four hours, which was bad since the ceremony was in one. “My jaw dropped a little bit,” Dickey said. “Like, oh my, I don’t even know what we can do to get around this.” Also stuck in the backup was Garrett Kerr, who was heading home to Eagle after 10 days elk hunting, with a large elk in the back of his pickup. He’d seen helicopters overhead and guessed the road was in trouble. Then a man in a three-piece suit walked up to his truck and asked how long the closure would last, explaining he had to get to his wedding in an hour. “I’m going to get you to your wedding,” Kerr told him. Kerr had a small electric pit bike he’d used to haul the elk out of the woods. He also found a woman named Jessica who had an ATV. So Dickey climbed onto the ATV, Thalacker got on the back of the pit bike, a vehicle he’d never ridden before and that wasn’t built for two, and the little convoy worked its way around the crash and down the 16 miles to the lodge. Representative image of a bride in her wedding dress walking toward a man on a dirt bike. Photo credit: Andriyko Podilnyk via Unsplash . They made it. The guests figured out pretty quickly that something had happened along the way. “They also saw my hair all messed up and knew, like, ‘Oh, yeah, this was not probably planned,’” Dickey said. The two met 12 or 13 years ago in a high school composition class. Kerr thinks the day was good practice for the marriage. “They’ll take those bumps in the road, and they’ll put a smile on their face, and they’ll get through it together,” he said. Thalacker remembers getting to the altar and looking at his bride with the mountains behind her. “This is awesome!” he recalled thinking. “Like, this is my wife. We’re going to live a long, awesome life together.” The post A crash closed the highway an hour before their wedding. An elk hunter saved the day with his dirt bike. appeared first on Upworthy .

items.description: Τόσο συχνά, όταν ανοίγουμε τα τηλέφωνα ή τους φορητούς μας υπολογιστές, βομβαρδιζόμαστε από περιεχόμενο από πλατφόρμες στις οποίες δεν είχαμε καν εγγραφεί. Ο θεραπευτής Kier Gaines συζητά αυτήν την ιδέα σε ένα πρόσφατο επεισόδιο o…
items.descriptionOriginal: So often when we open our phones or laptops, we are bombarded by content from platforms to which we didn’t even subscribe. For some, it’s becoming more and more difficult to weed out all the “noise.” And yet, now more than ever, we need to find ways to do that in order to de-stress . Therapist Kier Gaines discusses this notion on a recent episode of the Mel Robbins Podcast . With a chyron reading “This is why you feel drained all the time,” he explains how the world seems to operate, at least in terms of getting people hooked on social media/television. He shares, “The world isn’t really designed to support your peace and happiness.” View this post on Instagram How the world is designed Instead, Gaines shares, “The world is designed for your productivity and for your attention. And that’s it. If you just take a look at where we spend the majority of our time…social media, watching the news, being subject to marketing.” He then asks how that makes us feel. “What are they designed to do? Social media is designed to make you feel like you’re behind. Marketing is designed to make you feel like you’re being left out. The news is designed…I don’t know what the news was originally designed for, but now it’s designed to scare the hell out of you.” He explains just how pervasive it is. “When you open up your social media feed, you are being subjected to tens of millions of bad takes and half-chewed ideas, unsolicited and without your consent. And it’s like you’re drinking from a fire hose. If you drink from a water fountain, it quenches your thirst. If you drink from a fire hose, it breaks your teeth.” Take a pause He and Robbins have a quick laugh as the realization sinks in. Gaines continues, “And every single day, we’re getting our teeth broken by opinions and views that we don’t necessarily care for or jive with. And I realize that there’s a gap where people don’t have that.” The good news is there are ways to combat this “new normal” of fire hoses. Later in the podcast, another clip is captioned “The first thing to do when you’re overwhelmed.” Gaines gets right to the point. “The first thing that you need to do is you need to pause. Just pause. I know, overwhelm creates this profound sense of urgency. But when everything is urgent, nothing is urgent. Let’s just pause.” He continues to the next step. “Second, I want you to call it out by name. Because that’s an uncomfortable truth that I talk about. ‘I’m overwhelmed.’ We are afraid to admit it, because we think it speaks to our incapability. Not necessarily true. It just speaks to your circumstances.” He reiterates the idea of pausing. “So you pause and you name it. Call it out! Call it what it is. Let it exist outside of just your mind. ‘I’m overwhelmed right now.’ Localize it. Sometimes overwhelm is a failure of systems that are supposed to be designed to hold you up. And you can’t fix systems in a moment’s notice. So you don’t have to fix it all. You don’t have to have all the answers. You just need to slow it down.” Slow down He shares a metaphor from the NFL. “It makes me think of this running back, his name was Brandon Jacobs. He used to run for the New York Giants back in the day. Man, this dude was like 6 foot four. He had a neck the size of a torso and he was 264 pounds. Most running backs are like 200, 210. This man was 264 pounds. And his job was to run through your face and astral project your soul into oblivion. That man was terrifying and he was a running back! And I remember a coach was asked one time, ‘How do you stop Brandon Jacobs?’ The coach laughs and answers, ‘You don’t stop Brandon Jacobs. You slow him down enough for the defense to catch its breath.’ You don’t always have to stop overwhelm when you’re already in it. You slow it down enough for you to catch your breath.” Upworthy spoke with Beth Sonnenberg , LCSW, who has been in practice as a psychotherapist for 28 years. She offers excellent solutions for finding comfort in the chaotic world in which many find themselves. Ways to handle chaos “-Watch the news or social media content for only 10–15-minute increments at a scheduled time of day, preferably later in the day. -Take breaks by stretching your legs or going on a 10-minute walk outside. -Call a friend when you have a break or even while the news or social media is on so it’s just background noise. -Shut down the scrolling or news watching and pick up a book afterward. If you are engaged in a story, it is a much better way to relax or fall asleep than being on your phone because it won’t exacerbate your anxiety. -Focus on gratitude and what is good in your life when you start being upset by the news and social media posts or first thing in the morning or last thing at night.” The post Therapist explains why so many of us always feel ‘drained’ using a powerful ‘fire hose’ metaphor appeared first on Upworthy .

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News 5 Ways Healthcare SaaS Software Supports More Sustainable Business Practices Reading Time: 8 minutes 5 Ways Healthcare SaaS Software Supports More Sustainable Business Practices Health care produced roughly 8.5 percent of all US greenhouse gas emissions in 2018 , according to a 2020 analysis in Health Affairs that put the sector’s total at about 553 million metric tons of CO2 equivalent. My argument here is simple: healthcare SaaS, the software a clinic rents over the internet instead of running on its own machines, is one of the cheapest ways for a practice to shrink its share of that number, and most of the savings show up in the budget too. Now picture one family clinic. Behind the front desk sits a back room lined with manila folders, a shredding bin and a fax machine that still rattles every afternoon. Across the hall, a server closet hums all night with its door propped open because the room runs hot. That clinic is not a villain. It is just carrying what I call everyday carbon : the emissions that come from paper, idle servers, car trips and supplies that expire on a shelf. None of it is dramatic. All of it adds up, and almost all of it can be trimmed without touching a single clinical decision. I have spent years building and fixing software for clinics and hospitals, from appointment tools for two-doctor practices to records systems for regional hospital groups. The five changes below are the ones I have seen stick. 1. Paperless records and e-prescribing empty the archive room Before the switch, a typical small practice runs on paper that moves. Charts travel from the shelf to the exam room and back. Prescriptions get printed, signed, handed over, and sometimes lost in a coat pocket, which means a second trip for the patient. Old files go to an off-site storage unit, and someone drives there whenever a records request comes in. After the switch, the chart lives in a cloud-based electronic health record. A prescription goes straight from the doctor’s screen to the pharmacy, so there is no paper slip and no handwriting for the pharmacist to call about. Intake forms get filled out on a phone the night before instead of on a clipboard in the waiting room. What surprised me the first time I watched a practice go through this was where the real savings hid. The paper itself mattered less than the trips around it: courier runs to the storage unit, patients coming back for a forgotten form, staff driving boxes to a shredding service. One practice I worked with turned its old archive room into a third exam room within a year, which was the moment the owner stopped calling the project “the IT thing.” Nobody misses the fax machine. (Well, one office manager did, for about a week.) 2. A slice of a big data center beats a humming server closet The on-premise server is the quiet energy hog of small health care. It runs around the clock, needs its own cooling, gets replaced every few years, and in most clinics I have visited it sits mostly idle outside office hours. Backups often mean a second machine, or a drive someone takes home on Fridays. Large cloud data centers do the same work far more efficiently, and the numbers on this are striking. A Berkeley Lab analysis published in Science found that from 2010 to 2018, global data center computing output rose 550 percent while energy use rose only 6 percent , with most of the gains coming from big operators running highly efficient facilities. When a clinic moves its records, billing and scheduling to a SaaS product, it trades a single half-used box for a tiny, well-managed slice of one of those buildings. Off-the-shelf products cover most of what a typical clinic needs, but not everything. A fertility center with an unusual lab workflow, or a rural health network that wants its own patient app tied to existing systems, often ends up working with a partner that offers healthcare software development services to build the missing piece. My advice to anyone in that position is to make the green choices at the design stage: pick a cloud region on a cleaner power grid, decide how long logs and imaging files stay in fast storage before they move to cheaper cold storage, and stop the system from keeping five copies of the same scan. Building those rules in from day one costs very little. Retrofitting them into a live system full of patient data means migrations, compliance reviews and weekend downtime, and in my experience that costs far more. One pushback comes up in nearly every conversation I have about this. Skeptics raise a fair objection: the cloud does not cut emissions, it just moves them into giant data centers, and with AI pushing demand up, those buildings are only getting hungrier. Part of that is true. AI is driving a wave of new data center construction, and it deserves close scrutiny. But a clinic is not choosing between the cloud and zero emissions. It is choosing between the cloud and a lone server in a closet with a window air conditioner, and the Berkeley Lab work shows that the efficiency gains landed at the large operators. A clinic can also ask its vendor which region hosts its data and pick one on a cleaner grid, which is a settings change, not a construction project. 3. Telehealth takes car trips off the road without anyone noticing The most visible change is also the easiest to measure. Every follow-up visit that happens over video is a round trip that never happens, and for patients in rural areas that round trip can eat half a day. A national study published in The American Journal of Managed Care in 2025 looked at claims for 44.7 million insured US adults from April to June 2023. Scaled to the whole insured adult population, the researchers estimated that telemedicine averts between 21.4 million and 47.6 million kilograms of CO2 every month , roughly the monthly emissions of 61,000 to 130,000 gasoline cars. The authors call the effect modest relative to all of health care, and they are right to. Still, that is a cut that came almost entirely from visits people preferred anyway. In the practices I have worked with, the clinics that get the most from telehealth are the ones that decide on purpose which visits belong on video. Medication check-ins, test result reviews and most mental health sessions move online well. A sprained ankle does not. There is a second, smaller commute hiding in the same change. Once records, billing and scheduling live in the cloud, the people who handle them no longer have to sit next to the server. I have seen coding and billing teams move to two office days a week, which takes a few more cars off the road and frees up desk space the clinic was paying to heat and cool. The patient keeps the afternoon. The planet keeps the gas. 4. Smarter scheduling and inventory keep vials out of the trash Waste in a clinic is rarely one big mistake. It is a slow trickle of small ones: a box of supplies ordered twice because nobody checked the cabinet, a vaccine lot that expired behind a newer one, a refrigerator that failed on Saturday night and was found on Monday morning. Before SaaS, inventory usually lives in a spreadsheet or a clipboard that one person understands. Orders go out “just in case,” because running short feels worse than overbuying. After the switch, stock levels connect to the appointment calendar, so the system knows that next week has twelve flu shot appointments and only ten doses on hand. It flags lots that are close to expiring so staff use them first, and a cheap temperature sensor in the vaccine fridge sends an alert to a phone the minute something goes wrong. I once watched a pediatric practice lose a full fridge of vaccines to a weekend power fault. After they added a connected sensor, the next fault triggered a text at 2 a.m., a staff member drove in, and the doses moved to a backup unit before any of them warmed up. Nobody wrote a sustainability report about it. It was simply less waste. Scheduling tools help in a quieter way. Automated text reminders cut no-shows, which means fewer wasted slots and fewer rebooked trips. For home health teams, route planning groups nearby visits together, so nurses drive less and see more patients in a day. The software does not care about carbon at all. It cares about minutes and miles, and the carbon follows. 5. Remote monitoring keeps patients home and out of the ambulance The last change reaches past the clinic walls. Patients with heart failure, high blood pressure or diabetes can now send daily readings from a connected scale, blood pressure cuff or glucose meter, and a nurse sees a warning sign days before it becomes an emergency. Evidence from the research side is encouraging, though not unanimous. A 2025 meta-analysis in Cureus pooled 15 studies, nine of them randomized trials, and found that remote patient monitoring reduced heart failure hospitalizations , with the strongest effect from implanted monitors and a smaller one from simpler home devices. The authors rated their confidence in the hospitalization result as moderate, which is an honest grade for a field that is still maturing. Here is where I go a step further. Every avoided hospital stay also means an ambulance ride that did not happen, a bed that did not need heating and cooling for four days, and a stack of single-use supplies that never got opened. The meta-analysis did not count any of that, so this is my own extrapolation. But anyone who has seen how much material a single admission consumes will find it hard to argue the other way. For patients, the benefit is simpler. They sleep in their own beds. What changes when a clinic makes all five moves? Put side by side, the before and after look like this. Practice Before After with SaaS Records and prescriptions Paper charts, printed scripts, fax, off-site storage runs Cloud health record, e-prescriptions sent straight to the pharmacy IT infrastructure Server closet running around the clock with its own cooling Hosted in large data centers, where Berkeley Lab found compute grew 550 percent on 6 percent more energy (2010 to 2018) Routine visits Every follow-up means a car trip Suitable follow-ups on video, an estimated 21.4 to 47.6 million kg of CO2 averted each month across insured US adults (2023 data) Supplies and scheduling Overordering, expired stock, missed fridge failures, no-shows Stock tied to the calendar, expiry alerts, fridge sensors, automated reminders Chronic care Problems surface in the emergency room Daily readings from home, fewer heart failure hospitalizations in pooled studies None of these rows asks a clinic to become a climate organization. Each one is a normal operations upgrade that happens to shrink everyday carbon along the way. Where can a clinic start this quarter? You do not need a sustainability officer to begin. Most everyday carbon sits inside decisions a practice manager already makes, so the steps below fit into budgets and meetings that exist today. Count the paper before you cut it. Spend one week tracking what gets printed, faxed, couriered or driven anywhere. The list is usually shorter than people fear and points to two or three workflows worth moving online first. Start with whatever generates car trips, because those carry the biggest footprint. Ask every software vendor where your data lives. A good SaaS provider can tell you which cloud region hosts your records and whether that region runs on a cleaner grid. If your vendor cannot answer, that tells you something about how closely they watch their own infrastructure. The same question belongs in every new contract. Make video the default for follow-ups that do not need hands. Sit down with your clinicians and agree on a short list of visit types that start as virtual unless the patient prefers otherwise. Patients in rural areas will thank you first. Review the list every six months, since comfort with video tends to grow. Connect the supply room to the calendar. Even a basic inventory module that knows upcoming appointments will stop most double orders. Add a connected temperature sensor to any fridge that holds vaccines or biologics. It is one of the cheapest insurance policies a clinic can buy. Write a retention rule for data, not just for paper. Federal and state law set how long medical records must be kept, so start there, then decide what happens to everything else: old logs, duplicate image files, test exports. Data that nobody needs still sits on powered drives somewhere, and a clear rule keeps your cloud bill and your footprint from creeping upward. A greener clinic in 2030 might look like this What follows is a picture of what is possible, not a forecast. It is a Tuesday morning in 2030. The front desk has no printer. The room that once held folders is an exam room with a window, and the old server closet stores yoga mats for the staff wellness class. Half of today’s follow-ups happen on video, so the parking lot has empty spaces. A home nurse’s route was planned overnight, with four visits on the same side of town. In the vaccine fridge, every vial is in date, because the system flagged the oldest lot last week and the team used it first. Three heart failure patients sent their morning weights before breakfast, and one of them got a phone call and a medication adjustment instead of an ambulance ride. Nothing in that scene requires a breakthrough. Every piece of it exists today. The greenest clinic of 2030 will not look heroic, just quietly well organized. I can only imagine how life-changing a device like this is that’s kind of subtle and elegant and simple and has a really big impact on just the mental and physical space that suppressing tics has, and also just having to go through the world with people staring at you, not really understanding what’s going on. The source for this article came from the BBC, and I actually took a minute to watch their video on this, and I highly recommend watching the video so that you can kind of get a better sense for how much impact this small device has on people. Karissa: Yeah. And how exactly does it work? Arielle: So how it works is kind of wild. There’s rhythmic pulses to the median nerve cha- which changes activity in the parts of the brain that control movement. In a trial of 121 people, tics dropped by about 25% on average, and it even works for people who don’t have Tourette’s. There was another teenager named Ollie, and he has a functional neurological disorder which makes his neck move constantly without him having any control over it. And when he tried the device, it also just completely stopped the neck movements. There’s a lot of potential for this wearable neurotech to positively affect the lives of people with Parkinson’s tremors or anxiety or even OCD. “Animal welfare ballot measures had a strong night in the 2026 midterms” Arielle: The next solution is titled “Animal welfare ballot measures had a strong night in the 2026 midterms.” Okay, so we’ve already talked about the midterms, but we haven’t talked about this specific area of it. I think most people have never eaten foie gras in their lives, and yet it produced some of the most lopsided votes of election night. Animals came out of these midterms surprisingly well, and there’s a pattern in what passed and what didn’t that I found quite interesting. First of all, do you know how foie gras is made? Have you ever eaten it, Karissa? Karissa: Never eaten it, and I didn’t really know much about it until this article actually. Arielle: Yeah. I, I wanna say I have never tried it, but I can’t be for certain. I, I- worked a lot in the hospitality industry and, uh, tried a lot of different things, but it makes me feel a bit bad if I, if I had, because they basically, like, force feed ducks. Karissa: Yeah. Arielle: Um, or is it geese? But they- I think it’s geese, yeah … force feed them, and it produces this pâté-like, um I’m not describing this well, but people who know foie gras, you know what I’m talking about. Yeah. And those of you who don’t, look it up ’cause it is a l- well, it’s kinda disturbing. Um, so DC voted 73% and Denver 66% to ban foie gras sales, and a DC chef has been hosting foie gras tasting dinners to fund a lawsuit against the ban. So, yeah. Oh. There’s a, a little bit of tension there. Karissa: Yeah. Arielle: Colorado rejected a constitutional right to hunt and fish, and the fight came down to two words: traditional methods, which critics said could have brought back leg-hold traps and poison as, um, as hunting strategies. Denver voters said no to banning fur and slaughterhouses in 2024, but yes to banning foie gras now. So it seems like narrow bans on one practice seem to have a much easier time going through than ones that take on a whole industry for, of course, concerns about employment and yeah, having to restructure or get rid of a whole industry. Um- so more people are actually paying attention to how their food is produced, even when they’re not really changing their diet. Like, they’re not going vegan, they’re not going vegetarian, but they are concerned about how their food is produced and where it comes from. “The Greek coastline cleanup that turned trash into a pollution map” Arielle: The next solution is titled “The Greek coastline cleanup that turned trash into a pollution map.” The team that’s doing the cleanup isn’t just picking up trash. They’re noting down every single piece of it. This project consists of one ship, 20 people, five inflatable boats, and 1,140 tons of trash pulled off remote shores since 2019. For a visual, that’s 22 Olympic swimming pools’ worth of pollution. They’ve built what they say is the largest marine pollution database in the Mediterranean, and university researchers are using it to map plastic on the seabed. The data led them somewhere they didn’t necessarily expect. A lot of the trash came from inland, from rivers and illegal dumps, so they also started a second program on land. Beach cleanups are pretty popular, but there’s growing frustration that cleaning up the beach doesn’t necessarily stop the flow, or it doesn’t nip the issue in the bud. But it’s nice to see that citizen science and cleanup data are increasingly shaping policy on plastics. “April Surac built NeuraSensa so art adapts to the people using it” Arielle: The last solution that I’m going to share with you before I hand it over to Karissa is a Local Changemaker. This one’s titled “April Surac built NeuraSensa so art adapts to the people using it.” This week’s Local Changemaker is April Surac, a Florida teenager who grew up in her family’s furniture workshop and has a younger sister who has autism. Her installations are made of fabric with sensors built in, so the surfaces shift under your hand and the light and sound change as you move through the room. They’re designed for people with autism and people with sensory or cognitive differences, including dementia. More than 15,000 people have experienced the installations, and she sent over 250 sensory kits to families, schools, and hospitals. And she funds a lot of it with her own savings. I think she started this when she was only 16 or 17, which is so impressive. She’s also a 2025 Barron Prize winner, and she’s now working on gallery commissions in New York, LA, and London. Plus, she is developing a wearable sensory tool, and she’s moving towards patents for that. I think it’s really encouraging that a lot of people are growing in their awareness and compassion for diverse bodies and experiences. Sensory-friendly hours are popping up at museums, grocery stores, and movie theaters, which comes from people just realizing how much public spaces assume about our bodies. It’s wonderful to see the shift from accessibility compliance to designing for everyone from the very beginning of a project. Karissa: Yeah, exactly. And I really loved that she had a line that said, “Design should adapt to people, not the other way around.” And that’s something we don’t see enough of in our world. So I think this is just such a fascinating, uh, story, what she’s doing, and I feel so honored to be able to share her story here on The Optimist Daily as one of our local changemakers this year. “US homelessness decline hits its steepest one-year drop in a decade” Karissa: “US homelessness decline hits its steepest one-year drop in a decade.” So homelessness in the US dropped more than 6% last year. That’s about 49,000 fewer people without housing, and the biggest one-year drop in over a decade. One of the biggest points here in this article is that veteran homelessness is down nearly 60% since 2010, and advocates say it’s proof that putting people in housing first with no strings attached actually works. On the other hand, the Trump administration credits immigration enforcement and encampment crackdowns to this decline, but advocates say their data shows cities with camping bans did worse than average. It’s important to note, too, that not everyone saw a drop because people who’ve been homeless for a long time increased slightly, and that’s the group that both sides are fighting over the best way to help them. But yeah, I mean, in a time where housing affordability is one of the biggest issues in the country right now, this is encouraging news nonetheless. “Dreading plans you made yourself? There’s a name for that feeling” Karissa: The next solution is another lifestyle one, and it’s “Dreading plans you made yourself? There’s a name for that feeling.” So you know when you’re the one who made the plans, and then an hour before you’re supposed to leave, you’re on the couch drafting a text reading, “I’m so sorry, something came up,” or, “I feel sick.” There’s actually a name for this experience, and there’s a surprisingly simple trick for getting out the door anyway. Arielle, have you had this feeling before? Arielle: Oh my gosh, this is so relatable. I do find myself kind of dreading plans, and I try not to cancel. I try to push myself through it, but there are some days where I’m just like, “Ooh, I don’t wanna hop on my bike and go through the rain,” and- you know, I don’t wanna see anyone. I don’t wanna talk to anyone. I’m so tired. So yeah, this solution definitely spoke to me. Karissa: And I’m sure probably all of us have been there at some point or another. But this feeling is called anticipatory anxiety. 55% of Gen Z say they feel relief when plans get canceled, and a UK survey found that 68% of under 34s have flaked. But there’s a simple therapist-approved trick to get over this anxiety. Set an alarm for when you need to start getting ready, and when it goes off, shower and get dressed without debating it. So kind of just going forward with it without overthinking it. I think flaking has become so normal now that some people kind of dread planning anything, including their own birthdays and events. And in a time where loneliness is being talked about as a public health issue, canceling plans is a small part of this bigger picture. I feel like it’s kind of a lot easier to cancel plans, too, especially ’cause you don’t even have to call someone to cancel. You just send a text. But usually it’s better for all of us to push through and go forward with that connection anyways. Arielle: I like how this article said that part of the strategy is to imagine a moment when you did push through and you did go to whatever event or whatever gathering or, or meetup that you were once dreading. And chances are you ended up enjoying yourself, and you forgot all about that dread that you had before you actually stepped out the door. And there’s a lot of discussion around protecting our own peace, which I think is valid, but it can make it a lot easier to cop out. We have to be really careful about whether or not we are protecting our peace and we do need that break, because sometimes we definitely do need to take a moment for ourselves, or if we’re just letting the anxiety take over. “Bans cut two forever chemicals by 30 percent in England’s rivers” Karissa: Well, moving on to the next solution, “Bans cut two forever chemicals by 30 percent in England’s rivers.” Two of the most toxic forever chemicals have dropped by almost a third in England’s rivers over the last 10 years, and in fish by about half. The UK basically banned PFOS in 2010 and PFOA in 2020, and the river data now shows the effect, that 30% and 29% drops. But the catch is the chemicals didn’t actually disappear. The total amount is probably the same, but it’s just been diluted and washed out to sea. So it’s still out there, but there’s not as much, you know, going in. There are about 15,000 types of PFAS, and England has just two facilities that can destroy them for good, so not a lot, uh, out there that can get them out of here. PFAS are in the news constantly. They’re in our drinking water, in non-stick pans, rain jackets, and people are increasingly worried about them in their own homes, with good reason of course, because they don’t go away. And the UK government just announced it will start measuring forever chemicals in people’s bodies, so we should have more data on, you know, how exactly forever these chemicals are, and hopefully that will inform more policy in the future. “CAR-T therapy helps stiff person syndrome patients walk and work again” Karissa: The next solution is “CAR-T therapy helps stiff person syndrome patients walk and work again.” Stiff person syndrome is a rare condition that Céline Dion lives with, and until now, there’s been no real treatment for it. Doctors at the Mayo Clinic tried a therapy that’s normally used for cancer, and some patients who needed help walking are now miraculously back at work. CAR-T therapy is something that takes your own immune cells, reprograms them in a lab, and puts them back to wipe out the cells causing the disease. Patients in this one got a single treatment, and one patient, Jonathan, went from needing his family’s help with basic tasks to returning to his favorite hobbies like hunting and fishing again, and he says he hasn’t had a single episode since. This condition, like I mentioned at the beginning, was, you know, kind of brought into the spotlight by Céline Dion’s diagnosis in 2022. She was part of a documentary that brought this condition to the fore. So yeah, CAR-T therapies are one of the biggest stories in medicine right now, and researchers are also trying it out on lupus, MS, and other autoimmune diseases. But as of now, these therapies are incredibly expensive, so it raises the questions about who will have access to them. But hopefully with all medical breakthroughs and advancements, it will become more accessible to more people who need it. “6 hosting habits that leave holiday guests feeling uneasy (and how to avoid them)” Karissa: The last solution I have to share is also a lifestyle-oriented one, and has to do kind of with Thanksgiving and the holidays coming up. “6 hosting habits that leave holiday guests feeling uneasy (and how to avoid them).” So yeah, this holiday party season is about to start, and this one’s all about the stuff your guests notice but would never mention. This goes over a lot of great, uh, you know, pointers about hosting. One prominent one is the parking and coats problem. A party can be beautifully decorated and still feel chaotic if peoples have to circle the block searching for parking, or if they have to hold their jackets for 30 minutes without somewhere to put them. Arielle: The tip that spoke to me was about letting yourself as a host enjoy the gathering as well, instead of always being concerned with, like, cleaning up or prepping things or grabbing whatever, because the people who are there, the people you invited, are there to presumably spend time with you and each other. And it can put people on edge if you’re just constantly, like, fluttering around and, you know, making sure that everything is running perfectly without actually taking the time to settle in. And that, that is kind of challenging for me. Um, especially because I enjoy cleaning. But that’s definitely something that I’m going to be taking to heart this holiday season. And yeah, there’s a lot of other really great tips here as well. But yeah, exciting to get into the festive spirit. Karissa: That’s all the solutions we had this week on The Optimist Daily. Closing quote Arielle: Before we wrap up this episode, we have an inspiring quote, as usual. Karissa: Yes. The quote is, “My turn shall also come: I sense the spreading of a wing.” And that’s from Osip Mandelstam. Very poetic. Yeah, a poetic end to this edition of the weekly roundup. Thanksgiving sign-off Arielle: Yes. We will be back… Oh, we won’t actually be back next week with a full episode, but we will have a special Thanksgiving greeting from The Optimist Daily team to all of you. But in the meantime, Karissa and I wish you all a very, very happy, restful weekend.
