items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Singapore’s Southern Islands and the Strait of Sicily and Tunisian Plateau Named Mission Blue Hope Spots® Reading Time: 5 minutes From one of the world’s busiest ports to a Mediterranean crossroads, two new Hope Spots show that ocean protection can thrive wherever communities choose to work together. Mission Blue has designated Singapore’s Southern Islands as a new Hope Spot, championed by Friends of Marine Park, recognising an extraordinary tropical marine ecosystem where marine life, science, culture, and one of the world’s busiest waterways converge. The Hope Spot designation celebrates decades of work by Singapore’s marine community, alongside government agencies, scientists, educators, and other partners, to better understand and conserve the country’s marine heritage. One example is the establishment of Sisters’ Islands Marine Park, Singapore’s first marine park, which helps safeguard the rich marine biodiversity and ecosystems of the Southern Islands. More than 250 species of hard coral have been recorded around the Southern Islands, alongside seagrass meadows, mangroves, rocky shores, reef fish, seahorses, giant clams, sharks, sponges, and critically endangered hawksbill turtles. Among them are remarkable stories of resilience: the rare Neptune’s Cup sponge, once thought globally extinct, has been rediscovered in Singapore’s waters, while Small Sister’s Island is home to Singapore’s first and only turtle hatchery, where hawksbill turtle nests are relocated to for protected incubation and hatching. The Southern Islands are especially significant not only for the diversity within the Hope Spot, but also for their location. Just minutes from downtown Singapore, these reefs persist alongside shipping lanes, coastal infrastructure, and heavily used marine spaces. Research shows the reefs around Sisters’ Islands function as important source reefs, releasing coral larvae that may help replenish connected habitats elsewhere in the Singapore Strait. The Southern Islands offer a compelling model for how growing coastal cities can make space for biodiversity and build resilience into the future. The Hope Spot is championed by Friends of Marine Park (FMP), a multi-stakeholder network that brings together more than 60 representatives and organisations from civil society, academia, government, industry, education, and the wider community. FMP co-chairs Sam Shu Qin, a marine conservationist and educator focused on coral reef restoration and ocean literacy, and Dr. Jani Tanzil, a marine ecologist and Facility Director of the St. John’s Island National Marine Laboratory, lead the Hope Spot. The nomination itself grew from that community. In March 2025, 42 stakeholders representing 16 organisations gathered at a Friends of Marine Park meeting where the proposal to pursue Hope Spot recognition received strong support. Emeritus Professor Chou Loke Ming, a pioneer of coral reef research and conservation in Singapore, captured the determination behind that work, stating: “Our reefs have not given up; why should we?” The Southern Islands already benefit from legal protection through Sisters’ Islands Marine Park, which is managed by Singapore’s National Parks Board. While Hope Spot recognition does not create additional regulations or legal protections, it provides greater international visibility and a platform to build momentum around Singapore’s marine community aspirations. Friends of Marine Park has developed a three-year vision centred on strengthening community participation, expanding education and citizen science, developing youth leadership, supporting research and reef restoration, securing sustainable funding, and building support for stronger and expanded marine protection in Singapore. Work is already underway. Annual coral monitoring, community clean-ups, research programmes, and educational initiatives continue across the marine park. Singapore’s largest artificial reef garden has been installed at Sisters’ Islands Marine Park under the Grow-a-Reef Garden Initiative, and is expected to contribute approximately 1000 square metres of additional reef habitat by 2030. In one of the world’s most densely populated and busiest coastal environments, the Southern Islands Hope Spot carries a simple but powerful message: there is still space for nature, and communities can choose to protect it together. Thousands of kilometres away, another of the world’s busiest maritime crossroads has also earned Hope Spot recognition, this time one that stretches across national borders. Mission Blue has designated the Strait of Sicily and Tunisian Plateau as a new Hope Spot, championed by WWF Mediterranean Marine Initiative, bringing global recognition to a marine ecosystem where extraordinary biodiversity, cultures, economies and nations converge. Positioned between the eastern and western Mediterranean basins, the Strait is a vital ecological corridor and one of the region’s most important biodiversity hotspots. It is also a strategic maritime crossroads connecting Europe and North Africa, shaped by fisheries, shipping, energy infrastructure, trade, culture, and human movement. “The ocean does not recognise the lines we draw on maps. Whales, sharks, turtles and tuna move through these waters as one connected system. The Strait of Sicily and Tunisian Plateau Hope Spot reminds us that protecting the ocean requires us to work the same way: together, across boundaries. This new Hope Spot is a source of hope for the Mediterranean and a call to turn knowledge into action.” — Dr. Sylvia Earle, CEO & Founder of Mission Blue The Strait of Sicily and Tunisian Plateau, newly named a Hope Spot championed by WWF Mediterranean Marine Initiative, spans just over 114,000 square kilometers of seagrass meadows, coralligenous reefs, and deep-sea coral supporting fin whales, loggerhead turtles, bluefin tuna, and 32 species of sharks and rays. Photo by Simone Niedermueller, courtesy of Mission Blue . Covering just over 114,000 square kilometers, the Hope Spot encompasses a remarkable range of habitats. Important oceanographic processes, including upwelling, create nutrient-rich waters that support Posidonia oceanica seagrass meadows, coralligenous reefs, maërl beds and deep-sea coral ecosystems. These habitats provide critical feeding, breeding, nursery, and migratory grounds for a wide variety of marine life, including fin whales, sperm whales, bottlenose dolphins, loggerhead sea turtles, bluefin tuna, and seabirds. The Strait is especially important for sharks and rays, supporting 32 species and earning recognition as an Important Shark and Ray Area for its exceptional elasmobranch diversity. Marine ecosystems do not recognise political borders. The Strait connects waters associated with Italy, Malta, and Tunisia, while wildlife, currents and ecological processes move freely between jurisdictions. That makes cooperation essential to its long-term protection and sustainable management. Giuseppe Di Carlo, Director of the WWF Mediterranean Marine Initiative, described the Strait as one of the clearest expressions of a shared Mediterranean future, where marine wildlife, trade routes, energy corridors and cultures converge. He said the designation offers Italy, Malta, and Tunisia a chance to show how countries can work together to safeguard a shared natural heritage, making the Strait a symbol of regional cooperation, resilience and hope. The designation builds on years of scientific research and conservation work already underway across the region. Since 2023, WWF Marine Mediterranean and its partners have brought together science, policy, and stakeholder engagement to identify conservation priorities and lay the foundations for a more coordinated approach across the Strait. The need for that cooperation is growing. The Strait faces mounting pressures from intensive fishing, maritime traffic, pollution, offshore development, habitat degradation, and climate change. These pressures do not stop at national borders, yet existing protections remain fragmented across jurisdictions and sectors. Hope Spot recognition does not create new regulations or legal protections. Instead, it adds visibility, momentum, and a shared platform for the work already underway: helping make connections around a common vision for the Strait. The next chapter moves from recognition to coordinated protection and management. One pathway being advanced is a proposed Specially Protected Area of Mediterranean Importance (SPAMI) under the Barcelona Convention, which could provide a framework for countries to work together at the ecosystem scale. The Strait of Sicily and Tunisian Plateau Hope Spot is a beacon of hope for the Mediterranean: a place of exceptional biodiversity, shared stewardship and international cooperation, where protecting one sea can benefit nature, people and generations to come. The post Singapore’s Southern Islands and the Strait of Sicily and Tunisian Plateau Named Mission Blue Hope Spots® appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: The shame belongs to stigma, not to the person asking for help. “Just eat less.” “Move more.” “You need more discipline.” Is weight mainly the result of personal choices? Not quite. Choices matter, but they operate within biology, genetics, appetite, environment, health conditions and access to support. Why does that distinction matter? Because blame can delay care. Obesity is recognised as a chronic, complex and relapsing disease. A better conversation doesn’t ask, “Why can’t you control your weight?” It asks how weight may be affecting health, and what realistic, evidence-led management support is available. So keep building habits that support you: balanced meals, regular movement, strength activity and good sleep. And speak to a qualified doctor about what support is appropriate for you. Asking for medical help is responsible care, not weakness, failure or cheating. Talk to a qualified doctor about your weight-management needs. This is general information, not a diagnosis or medical advice. #CountWhatMatters #WeightStigma #Obesity #WeightManagement #HealthNotJudgement [weight is not a character test, weight stigma, obesity is a chronic disease, willpower and weight, weight management support India]

items.descriptionOriginal: P arc des Madelinots, a humble wedge of green space in the Verdun borough of Montreal, is not in the most tranquil of settings. The 6,500-square-foot pocket park sits beside a busy junction and is flanked on two sides by roads often filled with cars. For years, locals in the historically working-class neighborhood had to deal with the noise of constant passing vehicle traffic while trying to relax, meet with friends, play with their kids or, indeed, do anything else in this outdoor community space. But today, Parc des Madelinots is bathed in a very different kind of sound: the lap of ocean waves, dulcet bird calls and the crunch of sand underfoot. Reasons to Be Cheerful · Parc des Madelinots Soundscape It’s not because a beach has suddenly arrived in Verdun. The sounds are recordings being broadcast in an attempt to reshape urban noise, fighting sound with sound in a constructive way to reduce noise-induced disturbance, reinvigorate the use of the public space and even preserve cultural memory for displaced communities. “Sound is more than just noise, it can be a powerful resource,” says Catherine Guastavino, a professor at McGill University and principal investigator of Sounds in the City , a research team that is one of the collaborators on Les Madelinéennes , the sonic project in Parc des Madelinots. “We can use sounds to improve people’s experience of places.” A field recording session at the Parc des Madelinots. Credit: Paysages During the course of the 20th century, many inhabitants of the Magdalen Islands, a remote archipelago in eastern Canada, were forced to relocate to Montreal, largely in search of work. Many of them ended up in the Verdun district, which today has the largest community of madelinots outside of the islands. Yet this highly urbanized area has a problem: It’s noisy and a far cry from the islanders’ former home. So Guastavino’s team joined forces with France’s Ircam , the Institute for Research and Coordination in Acoustics/Music — one of the world’s largest public research centers dedicated to both musical expression and scientific research — and Paysages , a Montreal-based studio specializing in immersive installations, to create a more agreeable and “soothing” atmosphere in the Parc des Madelinots. This was done while at the same time paying homage to and evoking the cultural heritage of the Magdalen Islands’ diaspora. Weighed down by negative news? Enter your email below to receive our smart, uplifting newsletters. Or click here to choose exactly which ones you want [contact-form-7] The installation consists of four minimalist, mounted speakers, set up in 2023, that play field recordings taken on the Magdalen Islands by Canadian sound artist Charles Montambault. The idea is that playing these natural sounds in urban areas can make them more relaxing, particularly when the sounds are familiar to residents. This method — actively cultivating the balance of sounds that are heard in any given space — is known as soundscaping. “We wanted to investigate how these coastal sounds could change the mood of the park, which had been mostly used as a place of transit,” says Valérian Fraisse, a soundscape researcher who helped prototype the installation. Urban areas are often noisy due to road traffic, construction, large cultural events and other factors. The impact of chronic noise exposure on human health is well-documented , from sleep disruption to reduced concentration and even cardiovascular disease, and cities have belatedly begun to take action. The Montreal project is part of a new wave of experiments looking to harness the power of sound rather than simply blot it out. “Sound is typically underused, it’s often considered as noise pollution,” says Guastavino. “There are detrimental impacts of noise exposure and I’m not playing that down. But sound can enhance the quality of urban experience.” A speaker (center) in Parc des Madelinots as part of the Les Madelinéennes sonic project. Credit: Paysages While the field of urban soundscaping is still emerging, similar yet simpler methods have long been used in public and private spaces, such as positioning park benches far from roads or playing music in elevators. But a growing number of innovative projects are sprouting up across the world. In Antwerp, Belgium, for example, “noise-canceling” fountains have been deployed to replace unwanted background noise like traffic. In Warsaw’s main train station, a set of stairs has been turned into giant interactive piano keys , creating a playful public space. Dating back further, Japan’s metro stations have long played out Hassha-merodii chimes to induce calm and prevent rushing, among other functions. For soundscaping to be effective it must take into account the specific contexts of each site, according to André Fiebig, a researcher and head of the working group on Psychoacoustics and Noise Effects at the Technical University of Berlin. “The solution can’t be to play sounds everywhere,” he says. “It needs to be adequate, appropriate and fit to the place.” The impact of a soundscape depends a lot on what Fiebig calls “psychoacoustic” qualities, such as how people perceive the source of noise. “People will complain about sightseeing buses, but almost never public buses,” he says. Ocean waves are usually considered relaxing, elaborates Fiebig, but if they are played everywhere then their impact lessens. And there are plenty of varieties of sound, not only loud and quiet, but sharp and subtle, strange, exciting and surprising, he adds. Soundscaper Fraisse agrees: “I don’t think there’s a universal approach we can apply to every space.” In the case of Les Madelinéennes , collaboration with residents in the development phase was important, though those involved admit it could have been more integrated. The process involved plenty of trial and error, says Fraisse, and for the first few weeks many residents didn’t even realize the installation was there. Indeed, the project was notably challenging since the park is at the intersection of roads. “An interesting result was the potential confusion,” he says. “The sound of waves could be mixed up with traffic noise.” But Fraisse, who is currently developing a methodology for creating effective sound installations, including acoustic measurement and user feedback surveys , helped adapt the sound frequency ranges so that it wasn’t mistaken for traffic, and toned down the use of boat horns, which while authentic weren’t perceived as relaxing. Reasons to Be Cheerful · Parc des Madelinots Soundscape with Horn Meanwhile, the seagull squawks weren’t quite as evocative of home as hoped — there’s plenty of them in Montreal already, and they can often be a nuisance. “That’s why it’s so important to get feedback, to design site-specific interventions with people from the place itself,” says Fraisse. Reasons to Be Cheerful · Parc des Madelinots Soundscape with Seagulls Emilie Bourgey, a resident of Verdun who was not involved in the survey, says that in the past she would not regularly go to the Parc des Madelinots due to the noise of the vehicle traffic. At times, she might briefly sit on a bench and look at the trees. But she discovered the sound installation in the summer of 2025 when walking near the kids’ play area, and that transformed her experience of the space. “I love the installation, the sound of waves, the birds, it’s very rejuvenating,” says Bourgey. “I come here specifically for the boost it gives me afterwards.” Wait, you're not a member yet? Join the Reasons to be Cheerful community by supporting our nonprofit publication and giving what you can. Join Cancel anytime A growing body of research is echoing the benefits of soundscapes. A review of 22 academic studies, published in 2026, found that natural soundscapes in urban areas “were consistently associated with improved mental health outcomes.” In 2024, a study of 2,000 passengers by British train operator South Western Railway found that natural sounds such as birdsong, rivers and rainfall reduced passenger stress levels by 35 percent. The Montreal installation, initially a pilot, has since become permanent. And the team wants to take the collaborative aspect to the next level. Instead of simply asking residents to evaluate sounds, it plans to involve them in the creation and selection of sounds next year as part of a third iteration of the project. “We have to try to understand their logic, what they prefer, and then try to find solutions,” says Fiebig. “It shouldn’t be decided from the top, it should be about co-creation, close cooperation between the locals and those running the project.” The post Montreal Is Harnessing Soothing Ocean Sounds to Combat Traffic Noise appeared first on Reasons to be Cheerful .

Μέσα ήταν 20.000 δολάρια σε μετρητά, αρκετά για να κροταλίσουν τους περισσότερους, αλλά η Λάου και οι συνάδελφοί της «δεν τόλμησαν να το αγγίξουν», μια λεπτομέρεια που λέει…
items.descriptionOriginal: At the height of a Saturday dinner rush in Singapore, a coffee shop server named Lau Guat Toh spotted an unattended bag and did what came naturally to her - she protected it, placed it under a security camera, and waited. Inside was $20,000 in cash, enough to rattle most people, but Lau and her colleagues "did not dare touch" it, a detail that says more about their character than any declaration of honesty could. The bag's owner, a noodle manufacturer who had rushed off to a friend's wake, returned at 11pm simply trying his luck, and found everything intact. What lingers in the story is the quiet ecosystem of goodness surrounding the moment: a boss who had spent his evening delivering donated soup to elderly residents, a customer whose first response to losing a fortune was not panic but acceptance, and a server who plans to keep her $200 reward as a souvenir rather than spend it. "If something is meant to come, it will come," said the man who lost the money - and somehow, in this small coffee shop in Bedok, it did.

items.descriptionOriginal: Early each morning in the month of Margazhi , a statistics professor would set out on his motorbike to watch women at work on their doorsteps. Gift Siromoney admired the kolams , but he was chasing a different question. How did women, many of them nonliterate, loop a line around a grid of dots, close it without error and repeat the feat from memory the next day? Working with his wife and fellow academic Rani Siromoney at Madras Christian College in Tambaram during the early 1970s, he concluded that the drawing follows rules precise enough to be written down as a formal grammar that a computer can run. A tradition older than the textbooks Every morning, women across Tamil Nadu sweep their thresholds, sprinkle them with water and cow dung, and trickle powder between their fingers to build symmetrical patterns, as the mathematician Marcia Ascher described in American Scientist in 2002. A kolam begins with a grid of dots called pulli , and tradition holds that the rice flour feeds ants and insects, so the day opens with an act of kindness. In the early 1970s, mathematician Gift Siromoney observed these drawings, curious about the rules guiding their creation. Siromoney traced the earliest mentions of kolam in Tamil literature to the 16th-century Madurai Meenakshiammai Kuram , followed by the 17th-century Thiru Kutraala Kuravanji . He also noted that older Tamil word lists, ancient paintings and travellers' accounts say nothing about the art, so its documented literary history begins only in the 16th century. A red pen and seven sheets of carbon paper To see how a kolam grows, Siromoney devised a trick. He stacked seven sheets of paper, interleaved them with carbon paper, and asked practitioners to draw with a red ballpoint pen, removing the top sheet and its carbon at the end of each stage. Every sheet then showed earlier strokes in black and the newest stage in red, which gave him a frame-by-frame record of the drawing. Skilled practitioners always drew the pulli first and then built the pattern stage by stage in its natural segments, which suggested that they remembered kolams as chains of smaller units rather than as whole pictures. Practitioners and novices differed in how well they copied unfamiliar kolam patterns, so Siromoney treated kolam drawing as a learned skill. T Robinson of the college's mathematics department adds that the women drew almost like the turtle moves of a programming language, with instructions such as go forward, turn left, and make a loop. How a folk art became a picture language With the computer scientist Kamala Krithivasan, the Siromoneys published 'Picture languages with array rewriting rules' in 1973 and 'Array grammars and kolam ' in 1974. Using seven sheets of paper and carbon copies, Siromoney documented how women built kolams, one stroke at a time. Their idea treated each kolam as a sentence in a pictorial language , where rules rewrite a small array of symbols into a larger one, much as grammar rules grow a sentence. Computer programs could then generate kolam patterns of a given type mechanically. Later researchers use these models, which they call Siromoney array grammars. The team also asked whether a pattern is made of one strand or several. For interlaced sikku kolam , Siromoney introduced operations called cut and join, which turn a single-strand pattern into a multi-strand one and back. Rani Siromoney and colleagues later noted that the same operations appear in the theory of circular DNA splicing. Why the discovery still matters For computer scientists, kolams supplied ready-made examples of existing picture languages and inspired new types, so a doorstep craft helped shape how machines draw and recognise images. None of this required the women to know any grammar. R Narasimhan, who worked alongside Siromoney, observed that a large share of practitioners were nonliterate and unaware that their designs have grammatical properties. The couple's school of formal language theory at Madras Christian College, he wrote, became one of the best and most active in the field. The research continues. A 2018 paper by K G Subramanian, T Robinson and colleagues generated kolams using membrane computing, a model inspired by living cells, and showed that it can produce designs that earlier array grammars could not handle. Subramanian did that work in the college's Department of Mathematics, so the research still runs from Tambaram. Kolams were one strand of a restless career. Siromoney also used computing to date medieval Tamil inscriptions, applied cluster analysis to sculptures at Mamallapuram and built what South First describes as the first teleprinter keyboard for Tamil. He died on 21 March, 1988, aged 56. Yet every Margazhi morning, the women whose hands inspired his grammar keep drawing, and the rules he glimpsed keep running quietly beneath their fingers. Sources ' Gift Siromoney, polymath who used AI concepts in the 80s to solve historical mysteries ': by Poorani Balendra for South First, Published on 21 March, 2023 ' KOLAM ': by T. Robinson for Chennai Mathematical Institute (Gift Siromoney memorial pages) ' The Kolam Tradition ': by Marcia Ascher for American Scientist, Published in January-February 2002 (Volume 90, Number 1) ' Generation of Kolam-Designs Based on Contextual Array P Systems ': by Ibrahim Venkat, T. Robinson, K. G. Subramanian and Philippe de Wilde for Springer (Diagrams 2018), Published in 2018

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Rangers Gain New Tools for Protecting Whale Sharks in the Maldives Reading Time: 3 minutes Rangers protecting whale sharks in the Maldives now have new tools to help manage heavy tourism and boat traffic in the South Ari Marine Protected Area. Protecting whale sharks in the Maldives has a new set of tools. In August 2026, rangers at the South Ari Marine Protected Area (SAMPA) received new equipment. Thermal cameras, body cameras, and a vessel-tracking device now help them enforce rules in busy waters. Tech4Nature , a partnership between the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) and Huawei, provided the tools. The program, part of Huawei’s Tech4All initiative, helps protected areas use technology to meet global management standards. Designated in 2009, South Ari is the Maldives’ largest marine protected area. It covers about 5,600 hectares, nearly the size of Manhattan. Whale sharks gather there all year, making it a site of global importance for the species. Researchers have identified more than 910 whale sharks in the Maldives since 2006, mostly in South Ari. Most are young males that use the area to feed and grow. Whale sharks are the largest fish in the ocean and are listed as Endangered on the IUCN Red List. These sharks draw more than 65,000 visitors a year, or about 180 every day. A 2014 study valued South Ari’s whale shark tourism at USD 9.4 million in 2013 alone. The same boats that bring that income also pose a serious threat. Whale sharks feed on plankton near the surface, where visitors can easily see them. That same habit puts them in the path of passing boats. A 2021 study in Scientific Reports found that 61% of South Ari’s whale sharks suffered major boat-strike injuries. Injured sharks tended to stay in the area longer, likely to heal in warm, food-rich water. However, staying put may mean fewer trips to breeding grounds. The researchers also pointed to a gap in protecting whale sharks in the Maldives. At the time, the area’s boating rules were suggestions, with little enforcement. SAMPA ranger Ali Gasim lists speeding vessels, crowding, and light pollution among the main problems. Speeding boats are the same risk the 2021 study linked to injuries. With limited resources, his team struggles to monitor such a large stretch of ocean. Protecting whale sharks in the Maldives remains difficult because boating rules in the area were once only suggestions with little enforcement, and SAMPA rangers, working with limited resources, struggle to monitor a large stretch of ocean while speeding vessels, crowding, and light pollution persist. Photo by Derek Keats on Pexels. Tech4Nature began by measuring those gaps. In April 2026, the team ran a baseline review with the IUCN Green List Self-Assessment Tool. The IUCN Green List is a global standard for well-managed protected areas. That review confirmed two needs: more operational capacity and stronger day-to-day enforcement. Each piece of new equipment was chosen to meet them. A vessel-mounted thermal camera detects heat, so rangers can spot boats after dark. A vessel tracking device helps them follow boat movements across the protected area. Together, these tools extend patrols into hours and places that were hard to watch before. Body cameras let rangers record encounters and collect evidence of violations. A telephoto lens lets rangers document sharks and vessels from a distance. Clear records make it much easier to take action against boats that speed or crowd an animal. Rangers completed introductory training and field tests in August 2026. The sessions covered camera use and maintenance, and how to fit the tools into existing patrol routines. Protecting whale sharks in the Maldives also depends on partners who can act on rangers’ records. The project works with the Maldives Ministry of Climate Change, Environment and Energy and the Maldives Police Service. Maldives Whale Shark Research and the Big Fish Network also contribute. Founded in 2013, Maldives Whale Shark Research tracks individual sharks over time. Each whale shark has a unique pattern of spots behind its gills that photos can identify. Divers and tourists can add their own photos to Wildbook for Whale Sharks, a global online database. That long-term record is key to measuring progress in protecting whale sharks in the Maldives. It can show whether new injuries become less common as enforcement improves. Muhusina Abdul Rahman, director of the Protected Areas Section, says innovation is essential where marine park resources are limited. Najfa Shaheem Razee, who manages the Maldives Country Program, says the project links real management needs with targeted support. The project will continue to support monitoring and data collection in South Ari. The 2014 economic study had already called for licensed operators, a code of conduct, and GPS logbooks for boats. The new tools bring several of those ideas within reach. Protecting whale sharks in the Maldives has always meant managing boats and people, not just sharks. With better tools , a small ranger team can now see more and act faster. If injuries fall, South Ari could become a model for other whale shark sites. The post Rangers Gain New Tools for Protecting Whale Sharks in the Maldives appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: Even in the emergency room, Sapna Singh asked a nurse for a pen and paper. She wanted to draw. In the middle of a frightening medical emergency , art offered the 44-year-old something familiar to hold on to. Until then, she had been pursuing a PhD in the UK, building on years of work as an artist and teacher. Now, she was trying to make sense of a diagnosis that would change almost every part of her life. In February 2025, she began experiencing weakness in her left hand and leg. An MRI revealed a cancerous brain tumour, and a seizure soon left the left side of her body paralysed. She had moved to the UK with her 13-year-old son, Kabir, only a few months earlier. Her research was underway, and she had cleared her PhD proposal. Her attention shifted from her research and future plans to treatment and the demands of everyday life. After returning to India in April, she underwent brain tumour surgery. She had to relearn everyday movements and depend on others for tasks she had once managed without a second thought. Walking became a goal in itself, and even the easiest routines required patience. Through the uncertainty, however, she kept returning to her art. "Cancer made me a patient, but art reminded me that I was still Sapna," she says. From failing an entrance exam twice to earning a PhD scholarship Her relationship with art began long before she imagined it would help her through an illness. Growing up in a joint family in Delhi, she spent much of her childhood drawing. By Class 9, she was making portraits, and when it came time to choose a subject in Class 11, she opted for painting. In September 2022, she enrolled in a master's in design at Leeds Arts University in the UK, specialising in world-building and creature design. Turning that interest into a career took determination. She failed the entrance examination for Delhi's College of Art twice, in 1999 and 2000. She tried again, secured admission in 2002, and went on to graduate in 2006, ranking second in her final year. She later completed a diploma in 3D animation and multimedia and began working in exhibition and stall design. Around 2008, she married Akshay Singh, an entrepreneur from Meerut. Over the following years, she continued to build her career while making room for family life. The family moved to Dubai in 2016, where she found new ways to work with art. She began teaching and taking private classes in 2017. Later, she joined Manipal Academy of Higher Education in Dubai, teaching animation, media, and communication. Teaching kept her connected to the creative world, but Sapna was not finished learning herself. In September 2022, she enrolled in a master's in design at Leeds Arts University in the UK, specialising in world-building and creature design. She completed the course in a year, opening the door to another ambition. In 2024, she received a vice-chancellor's scholarship to pursue a PhD at the University for the Creative Arts. Her proposed research focused on the impact of artificial intelligence on creative education and hiring in the industry. "Returning to education after so many years helped me rediscover my confidence and gave me a fresh motivation to keep learning," she says. "I wanted to show myself that it is never too late to learn something new or chase a dream. For me, it was about much more than earning another degree. It was about giving myself the chance to begin again." In October 2024, she moved to the UK with her son, while Akshay remained in Dubai for work and visited them frequently. She settled into her new life and began working towards her research. After years of studying, teaching, and finding her way into new areas of art, she was ready for the next chapter. A few months into her PhD, everything took an unexpected turn Around 10 February 2025, she noticed that her left hand and leg were becoming weak. Kabir was the first to pick up on the change. At the time, neither of them realised how serious it would turn out to be. "I thought it was something temporary and that she would soon be back to normal. I never imagined things would get this serious," he says. She visited her general practitioner after a few weeks and was referred to Frimley Park Hospital. An MRI scan revealed a cancerous brain tumour. She was alone when she received the news. Her blood pressure rose, and she later suffered a seizure that left the left side of her body completely paralysed. The change was devastating. A woman who had spent years studying, teaching, travelling and managing her own life now faced the possibility of losing much of that independence. An MRI scan revealed a cancerous brain tumour. Soon, the family had to return to India for her treatment. She underwent brain tumour surgery at Fortis Hospital in Noida in April 2025, followed by chemotherapy, radiation, physiotherapy, rehabilitation, and anti-angiogenesis therapy. As treatment progressed, she had to adjust to a very different daily routine. Moving from her bed to a wheelchair, bathing, dressing, and using the toilet all required help. She also experienced fatigue and vertigo, while problems with her vision made some activities more difficult. For a period, her right eyelid remained closed. Although it has gradually opened, medication can still leave her vision blurred . The physical challenges were difficult, but losing the freedom to manage her own life took an emotional toll, too. "The hardest part was losing my independence. I went from managing my own life to needing help with basic everyday tasks. That change affected not only my body, but also the way I saw myself," she tells The Better India . Akshay had to adjust, too. Before her illness, his wife was fiercely independent. She travelled on her own, pursued her studies, taught, and managed family responsibilities. Now, he was helping her through the most basic parts of the day while also caring for Kabir and keeping up with work. He cooked fresh meals to take to the hospital and spent as much time as he could with Sapna. Leaving her alone in the ward at night was especially hard. "There were moments when I would look at her and think, 'How did our life change so much, so quickly?'" he says. He wanted to make things easier for her, but he also understood that help could not replace what she had lost. For her, being able to do things for herself had always been important. "You want to help, but you also know that the thing she wants most is not help. She wants her independence back," he adds. Regaining that freedom has been a slow but consistent process. At first, she needed four people to help her walk. Over time, that number came down to three, then two, and eventually one. She has recently managed a few steps without support. She has also progressed from using a bedpan to a portable commode and later to using the toilet with assistance. These changes have taken time, and recovery has come with its share of complexities. Still, each improvement has given her something concrete to work towards. "I coped by focusing on very small improvements rather than thinking too far ahead," she explains. When an MRI scan became a painting of a lotus Even before she knew what her recovery would look like, Sapna had found a way to cope with the uncertainty. During the medical emergency, she continued sketching, keeping her materials close by. She represented the tumour as a lotus, a flower she associated with wisdom and awakening. "In the emergency room, I asked a nurse for a pen and paper to draw. It was just my coping mechanism to take my thoughts away from the uncertainty and chaos," she says. Her right hand, the one she used for painting and writing, remained functional. That gave her a way to return to a familiar part of herself, even as other parts of her life felt unfamiliar. Drawing also allowed her to express feelings that were difficult to put into words, from fear and frustration to loneliness, hope, and gratitude. One painting was based on her own brain MRI. She represented the tumour as a lotus, a flower she associated with wisdom and awakening. The scan that had delivered frightening news became the subject of a work she could interpret in her own way. Painting was not always easy . Her vision problems made it harder to work with fine details, which had been an important part of her practice. Rather than stop, she began adapting her approach, experimenting with patterns and finding different ways to create. Akshay has watched her work around these limitations. For him, seeing her paint is a reminder that her identity extends beyond her illness. "When she paints, I see her reconnecting with the person she has always been, not just the patient she has become," he says. He has seen how difficult it can be for her to work when her vision is affected, but also how determined she is to find another way. "For an artist, whose work depends so much on observation, detail, colour, and visual control, this could have easily become another reason to stop. But she did not stop. Instead, she adapted," he says. Art has not removed the challenges of recovery, but it has given Sapna a way to keep expressing herself while she works through them. She has continued painting and has also started writing about the turning points in her life, including the difficult moments she has experienced during treatment. Her son has seen how much effort this takes. Kabir, now in Class 8, notices the small changes in her recovery as well as her strength to keep working. "Nowadays, she can open her right eyelid and manages to eat by herself," he says. For her son, these changes are part of seeing his mother gradually regain some of the abilities she had lost. He has also watched her continue to work towards her goals, even when recovery has made everyday life harder. "Art has become a kind of therapy for my mother during her recovery. Even with all the challenges she faces, she continues to paint, write her autobiography, and plan exhibitions. She is determined to see her dreams through, and watching her keep going has been inspiring for all of us," he says. That aspiration has already taken her back to an exhibition. In March 2026, she participated in a four-day College Mate exhibition at a gallery near Parliament House in Delhi. After months of treatment and rehabilitation, it gave her the chance to share her work with an audience again. Art has not removed the challenges of recovery, but it has given Sapna a way to keep expressing herself. She is now planning a solo exhibition and hopes to publish an autobiographical book. Alongside these projects, she wants to return to her research and complete the PhD she began in the UK. Learning to measure progress differently Sapna's recovery is still underway. She continues to need help with everyday activities, and walking independently remains a goal. Fatigue and vision problems can also limit what she is able to do on some days. Her life is not the one she imagined when she moved to the UK in 2024. But she is finding ways to make space for the things that matter to her, even as she learns to live with the changes brought on by her illness. Her husband says her ambitions have not disappeared with the changes to her physical abilities. "Her body has gone through a huge change, but her dreams, inquisitiveness, and zeal are still very much alive," he says. "Her circumstances have changed, but she has not lost herself." For her, moving forward does not mean pretending that the past year has been easy or expecting herself to return to the person she was before her diagnosis. It means allowing recovery to take the time it takes, while continuing to work towards the things she still hopes to do. She wants to regain more independence, return to research, and keep creating. Some days are spent focusing on her health; on others, she paints or writes. The progress may be slower than she once expected, but she is learning to recognise it on its own terms. "This experience has taught me that starting over does not always mean beginning from zero. Sometimes it means continuing from a completely different place, with a different body, different circumstances, and a different understanding of life," she says. She knows that recovery cannot be rushed and that the plans she once made may take longer to realise. For now, she is learning to measure progress on her own terms. "Your timeline may change, but that does not mean you have to abandon your dreams. Give yourself permission to move slowly and redefine what progress looks like," she says. Sapna still has a long way to go in her recovery, and the PhD remains a goal she hopes to return to. There is no definite timeline for what comes next. Sapna still has a long way to go in her recovery, and the PhD remains a goal she hopes to return to . Right now, she is taking things one step at a time, making art when she can and putting her experiences into words. "I am still learning, creating, and hoping. For me, that itself is a form of moving forward," she says. All pictures courtesy Sapna Singh.

items.descriptionOriginal: Many of us are fortunate to have a wildlife preserve right in our backyards, or just outside of our windows. City, rural, suburban—almost anyone can look outside and find a squirrel, a chipmunk, or even a strange insect we’ve never seen before. Perhaps the most common animal most humans see on an everyday basis is also the most fascinating: Your ordinary backyard birds . While not as intelligent and mysterious as the crow or raven, these birds are surprisingly adept at forming bonds with humans nonetheless. More than backyard birds than meets the eye Robins, house finches, and sparrows are wildly common in most parts of America. More regional, but still extremely common, are cardinals, blue jays, chickadees, and even magpies. Many of these songbirds are so commonplace, in fact, that we barely notice them. We’re more interested in rarer finds like the fox, deer, coyote, or hawk. But more rewarding than getting a passing glance at a fox might be making friends with the birds who visit, and live in, our yards every single day. These friendships can be wildly rewarding. Literally, some of these backyard songbirds will perch on you once you gain their trust. Some of them may even start to bring you gifts. Why birds give gifts to humans Again, crows get most of the good press when it comes to human-animal friendships. They’re incredibly smart and good at remembering faces. They’re also famous for giving presents to people they trust. For people who feed them, crows have been known to leave behind shiny things like tinsel, foil, or found jewelry. They might leave a pebble or a nice twig, or even a feather. Some people swear the crows have “made” them unique presents. The National Audubon Society writes of a person who, after feeding crows, found a “short pine sprig with a soda tab threaded through the end” several times in the same feeding spot. Not many people know that “regular” backyard birds can do this, as well. It’s particularly common in bird species that are related to crows like fellow corvids magpies and jays. Gift giving in birds is a deeply instinctual behavior. They use it in their courtship rituals, to reinforce social bird-to-bird bonds, and even sometimes just for fun. Chirp writes, “Play-based gifting is another way birds connect and collaborate with each other. Young birds pass pinecones, twigs, and other on-hand objects in playful exchanges, even engaging in tug-of-war and ‘keep away’ games. These activities help birds develop dexterity, explore their environment, and connect with other birds.” It’s hard to know exactly why birds seem to give gifts to humans who feed them. It could be a token of appreciation, or it could be because they accidentally dropped something and then food showed up—and they want to see if it will happen again. But we can all agree that, no matter what the intent, it’s still pretty flattering. Other benefits of befriending backyard birds Not everyone who feeds and makes friends with their local magpies, blue jays, sparrows, or robins will start receiving presents. It’s an unpredictable behavior, at best, and even more rare in the non-corvids (like sparrows and robins). But there are still tons of amazing benefits to interacting with the birds outside your window. Scientific studies have shown that watching, feeding, and interacting with birds has an incredible effect on overall well-being A study from Virginia Tech found that “People described feeling joy, gratitude, hope, and calm when they fed birds. Some said watching birds helped reduce stress or gave them something positive to focus on during difficult periods, such as illness or experiencing a death in the family.” Plus, responsibly feeding and caring for birds gives a major boost to your immediate ecosystem. Having more birds around helps control pests and even improves biodiversity when they spread seeds as they fly and eat. Everybody wins. 4 easy steps to make bird friends By now you’ve probably realized that the best way to make friend with birds is to feed them. But the real key is patience and consistency. 1. Experts advise putting out fresh food and water in feeders on a set schedule—the same time every day. Even wearing the same outfit and standing or sitting in the same spot can help the birds get used to your presence. 2. Use yummy, nutritious foods like bird seed and not processed human food. Never feed birds bread or crackers. 3. Over a period of time, you can start to gently move closer to the birds as they eat. Once they’re used to you and understand you mean no harm, they may allow you to come closer and closer. 4. Eventually, you can try putting some seed in your hand and leaving it extended. Once the birds like and trust you, they may perch and eat right from your hand. Finally, do yourself and the birds a favor and keep your cats inside. Domestic and feral cats kill over two billion birds a year , and they’re much less likely to become your friends if they’re terrified to set foot in your yard. It’s good for you and it’s good for the birds when you take the time to become friends. At the very least, it’s well worth your while to pause for a second the next time you look out the window and take these beautiful and fascinating creatures in. items.descriptionOriginal: Actress Audrey Hepburn was known for her classic beauty. From her full brows to her signature bangs, Hepburn’s stunning appearance always stood out on the silver screen. And Hepburn embraced aging gracefully . She famously rejected any plastic surgery or enhancements, and was proud of her wrinkles . Family members and others close to her have shared stories on her beauty philosophy over the years. And one story in particular is a stand out—with Hepburn refusing to have her wrinkles erased from one of her favorite photos of herself during her devoted work for UNICEF. Audrey Hepburn accepted her wrinkles Later in her life, Hepburn became a UNICEF Goodwill Ambassador in 1988, and was devoted to helping people in need around the world. For her advocacy work, she earned the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 1992. Hepburn’s granddaughter, Emma Ferrer, told PEOPLE in 2017 a story about her grandmother that “truly embodies her concept of beauty”, on how Hepburn refused to have her wrinkles removed from one of her most beloved UNICEF photos taken by John Isaacs, a photographer for the United Nations and National Geographic . American Photo magazine asked Hepburn to choose the photo she loved most, and it was one where her smile revealed wrinkles. “John called and asked her if she wanted him to do some Photoshop, because you could see her wrinkles. She told him, ‘Don’t you dare touch any one of those wrinkles, I earned every single one of them.'” Ferrer added, “She never once thought of getting plastic surgery. For her, wrinkles were symbols of age, experience and wisdom.” Audrey Hepburn’s thoughts on plastic surgery Pamela Keogh, author of Audrey Style , also told PEOPLE more about Hepburn’s beauty philosophy and her thoughts on plastic surgery. “Audrey never touched her face. In those days, there was no Botox. She would have had to have a facelift. Audrey never, ever did a thing,” she said. And Hepburn’s two sons, Sean Hepburn Ferrer and Luca Dotti, also shared more on their mother’s beauty philosophy with the publication. That said, she didn’t judge other women who chose plastic surgery, Dotti explained that while his mother didn’t opt for plastic surgery herself, she believed other women should have the choice and not be judged. “She wasn’t against plastic surgery,” he told PEOPLE. “She said, ‘If you really are unhappy about a feature about yourself that really depresses you… A woman should be free to indulge in whatever she pleases.’ She didn’t have a mantra that was for anybody else.” Ferrer added more on her thoughts of aging gracefully as an actress, sharing, “She always used to say, ‘I’m too old to be the love interest and too young to be the grandmother.’ She felt that in Hollywood. That’s ingrained in the 40s and 50s.” And in the book titled Intimate Audrey: An Authorized Biography , co-written by Ferrer and Wendy Holden, they also noted , “Any suggestion of plastic surgery was anathema to her, as she honored the history of every line on her face.” The post Audrey Hepburn gave a beautifully defiant response when a photographer offered to erase her wrinkles appeared first on Upworthy .

Μια εκδήλωση καραόκε πραγματοποιήθηκε μια ζεστή Κυριακή μετά…
items.descriptionOriginal: Carole Wade has been singing her whole life. Her velvety voice and deep connection to the lyrics she belts are not lost on listeners. At 86 , she continues to let that voice soar. She became known to Upworthy readers last year when I met her by chance at my mother’s senior living facility in Dallas. A karaoke event took place on a warm Sunday afternoon in July. Wade sang Fleetwood Mac’s “Landslide,” bringing the room to tears. We shared that clip, and millions of people heard and shared it too. View this post on Instagram But there’s even more to unveil about Wade’s fascinatingly brilliant life. Before she wowed audiences at senior karaoke and before she was in her local Dallas band, she sang backup for not one, not two, but three Elvis impersonators. I had a second chance to interview her and find out more. How it all began How did you land the job originally singing backup for Elvis impersonators? “I had a guy friend that I had known that was into music. And he knew the first (Elvis impersonator) that I worked with. His name was Steve West. I ended up knowing him over 20 years. So, we got together with him, and got to working, and did quite a bit of stuff. He thought he was Elvis, I think, really. And when he wasn’t performing, he was wearing clothes like Elvis, you know, the big sleeves and all that. But bless his heart. Now he died a couple of years ago. He had heart problems. His family is still good friends of mine. And so that’s how I got to start. He was the first one.” So he was doing these shows in Dallas and asked you to come sing backup? “Yes, and we did clubs and restaurants and, oh, anything he could, you know, on the holidays. We did the state fair. We did that. It was fun. It really was. He was easy to work with because I’d worked with him for so long.” Were you already an Elvis fan? “I was, but I wasn’t a maniac fan. You know. I didn’t go crazy. And I never did see one of his shows live, which I wish I had. Yeah, I liked Elvis. I really did. And I loved his songs. In fact, right now, in karaoke, I do ‘Burning Love.’” I love “Suspicious Minds.” “Oh, that’s my favorite. I didn’t think about that. I may do that one too, then. Oh, that’s nice. You reminded me about that one. Oh, that’d be a good one to do at karaoke.” When you were singing backup, did your appreciation for Elvis’s music grow? “Yeah, it did. It sure did. It definitely made me appreciate it more and note the songs and be familiar with them.” She couldn’t help falling in love Were there any songs that stood out as the toughest to sing, as far as range? “Well, yeah, um, oh, gosh, the last one of the night, he always sang, ‘Can’t Help Falling in Love.’ That had some highs in it. But we managed. It wasn’t bad at all. I don’t think I really ever had a problem harmonizing with that.” What about outfits, hair and makeup? Did you have to match his energy? “Yeah, well, this depended [on] where we were working. If we were doing something that required an evening gown or whatever like that, I would do that. And then the rest of the time, it was just normal. We tried to kind of duplicate what Elvis did, and what his backup singer did.” How many backup singers were there? “I worked with Steve longer than any of them, and some of them would come and go, and there usually would be about three of us. And sometimes four. But it just depended on who was working with us at the time.” You worked with other Elvis tribute artists as well, not just Steve. Was that before your band (Psychedelic Oatmeal) formed? “Yeah, it was. It was before my band all started.” Was Steve the best impersonator or was there another one that stood out? “Steve was really good. But we worked with a young guy that just popped up. And he was like, oh, my gosh, he must have been 18, 19 years old when he started. His name was Johnny Lovett. And, believe it or not, he has passed away too. He turned out to be really, really good. And, on top of that, he was real funny. He was kind of a comedian. And he would, you know, do things like that on the stage.” They were all fabulous Who else did you work with? “And then I worked also with George Campisi.” (The Campisi family had quite the legacy in Dallas, ultimately running one of the most popular Italian restaurants, Campisi’s, often frequented by Jack Ruby). “Now, we, we traveled a little bit with him. That was after Steve, I was kind of going back and forth with him. And, so when George would call, you know, we’d go do a job with him, because, you know, the music so well, you don’t have to rehearse that much. George was very good, and he looked Italian. He was a very, very nice guy. They all were. Every one of them I worked with. And I do miss working with them, it was fun.” How were the crowds? Did they draw in real big Elvis fans? Did they go crazy like it was actually Elvis? “Yeah, they sure did. They loved Elvis so much. And the majority were women.” That must have been interesting to be on stage from your point of view and to watch these women get so excited. “Yeah, it was! Johnny, now he was young when he passed away too. He was really good looking, good. Steve, of course, was an older guy. Not old, but older. And, when Johnny started singing, he sang with us. We kind of got him started on stuff. And then he went on his own and did real well.” ‘Don’t put it off’ Looking back at all your decades of singing and performing, if you had a piece of advice to give to another aspiring entertainer, what would it be? “I think what they should do is start when they’re young. And don’t put it off. And just push yourself as much as possible. You get to meet people, get to know them, and that’s how you get in with someone. And go to jam sessions and sing, and they see you there. That would be my advice on it.” The post Before 86-year-old went viral for singing ‘Landslide,’ she had a job in Dallas that few karaoke singers can claim appeared first on Upworthy .

Όταν κάτι δεν είναι ελαφρώς, όμως, το αισθάνονται πολύ πριν το πουν δυνατά. Ένας καλεσμένος που γ…
items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM The best holiday parties tend to be the ones where nobody thinks about the hosting at all. Guests walk in, find a spot for their coat, settle in with a plate and a drink, and the evening carries them along. When something’s slightly off, though, they feel it long before they’d ever say it out loud. A guest who can’t hear the person next to them, or who’s stuck eating bread rolls all night because everything else has nuts in it, probably won’t complain. They’ll just leave a little earlier than they planned. The good news is that most of these little snags are easy to catch if you picture the evening from your guests’ side of the door. So let’s walk through it the way they will, from the moment they pull up to the moment they say goodbye. Before holiday guests arrive A clean home where it counts First impressions start at the entryway. Clutter underfoot or a sink full of dishes can make guests more focused on where to step than on catching up with each other. You don’t need a spotless house, though. Rooms that will stay closed can wait. Put your energy into the spaces people will use, like the bathroom, kitchen, and living room, plus the guest room if anyone’s staying over. Spreading the cleaning across a few days instead of saving it all for the night before keeps you from running on fumes when the doorbell rings. Parking, coats and the weather Even a beautifully decorated party can feel disorganized if guests circle the block looking for a parking spot or end up holding their coats for the first half hour. A short message a few days ahead covering where to park and what to expect when they arrive takes the guesswork out of it. If you live somewhere with snow or ice, it helps to have a backup plan ready in case the weather turns on the day. Food everyone can eat Nobody wants to be the guest pushing food around a plate because of an allergy the host didn’t know about. Before you settle on a menu, send a quick note asking whether anyone has dietary needs. Even if no one replies with anything, having a few dishes that happen to be gluten-free, vegan, or nut-free is an easy way to make sure no one goes hungry. Making holiday guests comfortable once the party starts Room to move around Every home has its own quirks, and the layout shapes how comfortable people feel once they’re inside. Before the party, take a slow lap through your space as if you’d never seen it. Where will people gather? Is the buffet in a spot that blocks the hallway? Is there somewhere to sit near the food? Shumaila Panhwar , a hosting professional, recommends exactly that kind of walkthrough. “When you walk through the space from the perspective of the guests and their experience, it makes it easier to determine placement of items and what makes sense best for flow,” she advises. Music that stays in the background A festive playlist does wonders for the mood, right up until people have to lean in and shout to hear each other. Keep the volume low enough that conversation comes first. Your neighbors will appreciate it too, and nothing ends a party faster than a noise complaint. Being a present host Let yourself enjoy it Here’s the one that catches even the most organized hosts. It’s easy to spend the whole evening refilling bowls and checking the oven, but your guests came to see you. Your presence matters most when people are meeting for the first time and could use an introduction to get a conversation going. Making a plan the night before and running through it once can help a lot. When you know everything is ready, it gets easier to set down the serving spoon, pour yourself a glass of something, and join the people you invited, which, when you think about it, is what made you want to host in the first place. items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM A cell therapy built to fight cancer is helping people with stiff person syndrome get back on their feet. In an early trial led by neurologists at Mayo Clinic, patients who had needed family members to help them walk and handle daily tasks regained enough function to return to work, exercise, and hobbies after a single round of CAR-T cell therapy. The results, published in JAMA Neurology , point to a treatment that targets the root of the disease instead of only easing its symptoms. A rare disease with no cure What stiff person syndrome does to the body Stiff person syndrome (SPS) is a rare autoimmune condition in which the immune system attacks the central nervous system. The result can be severe rigidity throughout the body, painful muscle spasms, and frequent falls. Decades of research have produced treatments that can soften symptoms, but none that cure it. The condition drew global attention in December 2022, when singer Céline Dion revealed her diagnosis . In an Instagram video, she said it affected “every aspect of my daily life,” including her ability to sing. How CAR-T works against stiff person syndrome CAR-T therapy is already an established treatment for some blood cancers. Doctors extract a patient’s T cells, a type of immune cell, and engineer them in a lab to seek out and destroy specific targets. For this trial, the cells were redesigned to eliminate the immune cells that drive SPS, using a CD19-targeted therapy called mivocabtagene autoleucel. Each participant received a single treatment, and the study ran across three sites, Mayo Clinic among them. Dr. Anastasia Zekeridou , a neurologist and researcher at Mayo Clinic in Rochester, Minnesota, said the scale of the response stood out. “What was most striking was the degree of improvement we saw in some patients,” she said. “With existing treatments, we may be able to improve symptoms but we very rarely see patients return to their previous level of function.” Patients back at work and on the treadmill Jonathan Walden: hunting and fishing again Before the trial, Jonathan Walden relied on his family for help with walking and basic daily tasks. He has since returned to his job. “I can go to work every single day. I can do everything I did before. I go hunting; I can go fishing,” he said. “I have not had one episode since receiving treatment.” Shari St. Germain: seven minutes on a treadmill Shari St. Germain’s illness progressed from severe leg cramps and trouble walking to rigid muscles and falls. After CAR-T, she said, each day has felt “better and better.” One morning she felt well enough to try the treadmill. “My husband comes running in because I’m crying and he’s like: ‘Are you OK?’ And I’m like: ‘I just walked for seven minutes on the treadmill,'” she said. Next questions for CAR-T in neurology Will the improvements last? The researchers are clear that this is early evidence from a small, nonrandomized trial, and that larger studies are needed. “These early results are very encouraging and the key question now is whether those improvements will be sustained over time,” Zekeridou said. Beyond blood cancer Dr. Sean Pittock, who chairs the department of neurology at Mayo Clinic, sees a wider opening. “CAR-T therapy has already transformed the treatment of some cancers, and we are now beginning to see its potential in autoimmune neurologic diseases,” he said, adding that the results offer hope for other immune-mediated neurologic conditions with few effective options. Yasmin Sheikh, head of policy and public affairs at the UK blood cancer charity Anthony Nolan, which was not involved in the trial, called the research “an exciting development” and more evidence that CAR-T could reach well beyond blood cancer. If the gains hold in larger trials, people with stiff person syndrome could have something they have never had before: a treatment aimed at giving them back the lives the disease took, not just making those lives easier to manage. Αρχικά προήλθε από απάντηση του Κ…
items.descriptionOriginal: “Run the dishwasher twice” might sound like strange mental health advice, but a viral post is proving that it’s actually quite helpful. Danielle Wunker, a licensed professional counselor and supervisor, shared a story on her Facebook page that is resonating with people who struggle with mental health issues. It originally came from an answer from Kate Scott on Quora to the question “Has a therapist ever told you something completely unexpected?” It reads: When I was at one of my lowest (mental) points in life, I couldn’t get out of bed some days . I had no energy or motivation and was barely getting by. I had therapy once per week, and on this particular week I didn’t have much to ‘bring’ to the session. He asked how my week was and I really had nothing to say. “What are you struggling with?” he asked. I gestured around me and said, “I dunno man. Life.” Not satisfied with my answer, he said, “No, what exactly are you worried about right now? What feels overwhelming? When you go home after this session, what issue will be staring at you?” A woman is unhappy at a party. Photo credit: Canva She almost didn’t say it out loud I knew the answer, but it was so ridiculous that I didn’t want to say it. I wanted to have something more substantial. Something more profound. But I didn’t. So I told him, ‘Honestly? The dishes. It’s stupid, I know, but the more I look at them the more I CAN’T do them because I’ll have to scrub them before I put them in the dishwasher, because the dishwasher sucks, and I just can’t stand and scrub the dishes.’ I felt like an idiot even saying it. What kind of grown ass woman is undone by a stack of dishes? There are people out there with *actual* problems, and I’m whining to my therapist about dishes? But he nodded in understanding and then said: “Run the dishwasher twice.” A woman loading the dishwasher. Photo credit: Canva I began to tell him that you’re not supposed to, but he stopped me. “Why the hell aren’t you supposed to? If you don’t want to scrub the dishes and your dishwasher sucks, run it twice. Run it three times, who cares?! Rules do not exist.” There are no rules It blew my mind in a way that I don’t think I can properly express. That day, I went home and tossed my smelly dishes haphazardly into the dishwasher and ran it three times. I felt like I had conquered a dragon. The next day, I took a shower lying down. A few days later, I folded my laundry and put them wherever the f**k they fit. There were no longer arbitrary rules I had to follow, and it gave me the freedom to make accomplishments again. Now that I’m in a healthier place, I rinse off my dishes and put them in the dishwasher properly. I shower standing up. I sort my laundry. But at a time when living was a struggle instead of a blessing, I learned an incredibly important lesson: There are no rules. Run the dishwasher twice. The comments took it even further “For me it is not exactly that there are no rules, but I ask myself ‘Whose rules are these?’ ‘Do I want them to be mine or can I come up with better ones?’ No rules might work for some folks, but I like a little structure, the structure I supply and can alter if it is not working,” Sam wrote in the comments. “That is brilliant! Thank you for sharing that profound story. Isn’t it amazing how often we miss the faulty assumption that is stymying us? I’m glad to hear you are in a much better place now,” Charlie added. Motivation often follows behavior The therapist’s advice to the woman follows a psychological principle : motivation often follows behavior . So, when you don’t feel motivated to scrub the dishes, by simply doing part of the act, putting them in the dishwasher, you are prompting your brain’s reward system to build momentum. Simply taking one step can make it easier to keep going or help you rebuild a healthy routine. Anyone who has been in a mental or emotional place where even the most basic, mundane tasks feel overwhelming understands the wisdom of this lesson. Dishes might seem like such a minor detail of life, but those kinds of minor details can be the straw that breaks the camel’s back mentally. If you’ve never stared at a basket of laundry that would take three minutes to fold and thought, “Nope, can’t do it. Not now. Maybe not ever…” then you may not need this lesson, but there are millions of people who appreciate the express permission to let go of the rules in our heads about how things have to be done. Adjusting expectations and arbitrary ideas about how something works is incredibly freeing and can provide a temporary fix for a seemingly insurmountable problem. Oddly enough, that temporary fix can be the bridge that moves someone from being unable to cope with daily life to functioning on a somewhat normal level. Why this advice works, according to psychology Mental health is such a tricky thing to manage, and many of the tools for managing it run counter to what we might expect. That’s what therapists are for: they help us step outside the box of our own brains, adjust our thoughts and behaviors to create greater possibilities for ourselves, and give us permission to reject the negative voices in our heads that try to keep us locked in unhelpful or unhealthy patterns. Even when that unhelpful pattern is as simple as letting the dishes pile up instead of running the dishwasher twice. This article originally appeared five years ago. It has been updated. The post Woman shares her therapist’s life-changing mental health advice: ‘Run the dishwasher twice’ appeared first on Upworthy .

items.descriptionOriginal: There are a lot of personality tests out there, and we humans are endlessly fascinated by them. There are the ones popular in pop-psychology like Myers-Briggs and the Enneagram. There are highly clinical and academic models like the HEXACO and the MMPI. One of the most widely used and respected personality tests in academic and scientific circles is the Big Five, or OCEAN model. It scores people based on five traits: Openness, Conscientiousness, Extraversion, Agreeableness, and Neuroticism. It doesn’t group people into concrete buckets with snappy names, like “The Innovator,” but your collective scores in the five areas it measures come together to tell a story about you. Personalities can be complex. Photo credit: Canva But some people’s results don’t fit neatly into a story. It’s rare, but fewer than 10% of people have unusual results that don’t fit within the usual personality maps. Scientific research uncovers personality mutants A 2018 study in Frontiers in Psychology , by Jüri Allik, Martina Hřebíčková, and Anu Realo of the University of Tartu, the University of Warwick, and the Czech Academy of Sciences, tested more than 4,000 participants from the Czech Republic and Estonia. Each person completed a personality inventory and was also scored based on someone who knew them well in order to get the most accurate and realistic data. What the researchers realized was that a handful of personality traits, while all scored individually, are typically related: “When people describe their own or somebody else’s personality, many of the descriptors typically go hand-in-hand with each other. For instance, people who are often angry also experience many other negative emotions. Similarly, individuals who have vivid imaginations are regularly more open to trying new food and entertaining new ideas and values. And those who are motivated to achieve are usually also self-disciplined and methodical.” Most people have personality profiles that make logical sense. People who are highly Extraverted are usually Open to trying new things. People who are highly Neurotic tend to be less Extraverted. But the researchers also discovered some fascinating outliers in their data. Fewer than one out of every 10 participants had a personality trait map that just… didn’t fit. For the purposes of their study, the researchers used the term “personality mutants.” The 3 types of personality outliers Not only did roughly 5% to 10% of the people studied not fit neatly into the usual pattern of personality traits, the data showed that there were three specific personality combos that accounted for most of the “mutants.” They had multiple traits that didn’t seem to go naturally together, or had only one of a pair of traits that are almost always found in the same person. The clusters, sadly, did not receive a cool, grabby nickname like “mutants.” The first cluster, called H1, saw people who scored high in “Straightforwardness” also score low in “Trust.” These are straight-shooters who are usually frank and sincere, but don’t trust that others are returning the favor. These traits don’t usually go together in this combination. Most people who are highly honest and frank project that worldview onto others and trust easily. But some are more skeptical, and use their acute understanding of what honesty sounds like to easily sniff out people who are being deceptive. The H2 cluster features people who are highly Conscientious, that is, disciplined, organized, and responsible, and who score high in Aesthetics, meaning they place a lot of value in their style and visual tastes. However, this cluster of people scores low in other areas of Openness. They are stubborn and extremely resistant to trying new things or changing their mind. Interestingly, this cluster also featured people who were highly Straightforward but distrustful, just like cluster H1. The third cluster, H3, is a fascinating one: These folks score low on Fantasy, Aesthetics, and Emotional Sensitivity. But they’re highly open to trying new things, exploring new ideas, and challenging conventional beliefs; even their own. They’re a cerebral bunch. Not big on imagination, art, or style. Deep thinkers who are more head than heart. It’s an unusual and rare combination. Even more fascinatingly, this group showed a different trust pattern than the other two: H3s were highly Trusting of others but lower in Modesty. The “mutant” personalities discovered in the research are not inherently good or bad. They simply exist as outliers, and the researchers cite about one in 3,000 people being born with an extra finger or toe as a parallel. It’s the normal elements, just configured a little differently. Human personality is hard to classify It goes to show that even the most scientifically validated personality tests can’t perfectly capture the full spectrum of human individuality. Any test that claims all people fit into one of a handful of rigid “types” is missing the forest for the trees. The researchers put it best, and beautifully: “Personality facets are more like Lego, which can be assembled into different configurations. In addition to the customary assembly of elements, several infrequent compositions of the same elements can emerge.” If you’ve ever felt like you weren’t quite like everyone else, like the personality tests could never quite peg you perfectly, well, you were probably right. This article originally appeared in June. It has been updated. The post 1 in 10 people have such unusual personality trait combinations that researchers call them ‘mutants’ appeared first on Upworthy .

items.descriptionOriginal: ndia burns millions of tonnes of paddy straw every year. But what if this agricultural waste could grow mushrooms instead? At ICAR-National Rice Research Institute in Cuttack, scientists are helping farmers explore mushroom cultivation using paddy straw. Fungi break down tough plant fibres, allowing farmers to turn straw into growing beds for paddy straw mushrooms. According to a 2022 ICAR study, cultivating 4,000 mushroom beds annually could generate ₹3 lakh in net income, with leftover material potentially adding another ₹1.36 lakh through vermicomposting. But this isn’t a magic fix for stubble burning. These mushrooms need temperatures of 30–35°C, while poor-quality spawn, contamination, limited markets and food-safety risks remain serious challenges. Scientists estimate this method could handle only 8–12% of a region’s straw burden. Mushroom farming won’t end stubble burning on its own.
