items.descriptionOriginal: Scientists have long used chemogenetics to study brains in the lab. A pilot trial for seizures is its first leap into medicine. Flashing lights. Buzzing noises. A sudden wave of fear. For some people with epilepsy, these sensations herald an oncoming seizure. Drugs can keep some seizures at bay, but over 30 percent of patients don’t respond to them, a statistic that hasn’t budged in decades. Frequent, uncontrolled seizures rob people of a normal life. They can’t drive or swim alone. Some struggle to stay in school, hold down jobs, or maintain relationships. And despite growing public awareness, stigma lingers. For people with severe drug-resistant epilepsy, surgery is an option. If the seizures are associated with a local brain region, doctors can remove the tissue. It’s a drastic operation, but it isn’t rare. In 2024, over 2,000 patients elected to undergo the procedure. Depending on the brain region removed, surgery can control seizures in nearly 70 percent of patients, but they risk losing memory, language, and other cognitive abilities. A new gene therapy could offer an alternative. In a clinical trial , three men who had lived with epilepsy for at least a decade saw monthly seizures drop over 90 percent. One remained seizure-free for a year. In the trial, the team shuttled a gene into a small patch of the hippocampus, the source of their seizures. The gene produces a kind of protein “dimmer switch” in neurons. Normally silent, the protein springs into action when activated by an FDA-approved drug, allowing scientists to dial down the region’s electrical activity rather than shutting it off completely—something that’s not possible with current treatments. The technology, called chemogenetics, has been a staple of animal research in neuroscience. The findings, though early, suggest it could finally make the leap into human medicine. “It certainly has caused a lot of excitement in the field,” said Dimitri Kullmann at University College London to Chemical & Engineering News , who was not involved in the study. Chemical Romance Intricate webs of neurons underlie every brain function. Our ability to feel, move, remember, and reason all stem from electrical and chemical signals that wire brain cells into circuits. It’s a delicate balance. Some neurons release chemicals that fire up their neighbors; others dampen them. In epilepsy, this goes awry. The causes are plenty. Genetic mutations can disrupt how neurons develop or function. Brain injuries, tumors, stroke, and infections can also fuel the condition. In some frustrating cases, the culprit remains unknown. Rebalancing these circuits could tame runaway seizures. Most antiseizure drugs prevent neurons from firing too rapidly or boosting inhibitory chemical signals. But medication is a Band-Aid, not a cure. Because the drugs flood the whole brain, they can trigger fatigue, dizziness, mood swings, and sometimes more serious side effects , including liver or heart problems. Dampening electrical activity at the source could be a better bet. Around two decades ago, an emerging technology called chemogenetics first amazed neuroscientists with its precise control of single neurons. The technology relies on two parts: gene therapy and a drug. First, an engineered virus delivers a gene encoding a designer receptor into targeted neurons. The receptor is silent until a specific drug activates it. By adjusting the drug’s dose, scientists can fine tune the activity of modified neurons. Rather than simply flicking neurons on or off, the approach is flexible and targeted. Chemogenetics soon caught the attention of epilepsy researchers. In 2019, a team at Ghent University in Belgium tested the method in mice with seizures originating in the hippocampus. They delivered a designer receptor called hMADi to the region. A single dose of clozapine, an FDA-approved antipsychotic, controlled seizures for at least 15 hours. With repeated treatment, seizures nearly vanished. A subsequent study in monkeys also dramatically slashed seizures. Given these encouraging findings, some researchers were ready to take the next step. “I think scientists like me felt like, ‘Why haven’t we tried it in humans yet?’” said study author Minmin Luo at the Chinese Institute for Brain Research. Restoring Balance The trial enrolled three men under 40 diagnosed with epilepsy for 10 to 25 years. All had tried at least two antiseizure medications without success. Brain scans traced their seizures to a scarred hippocampus on one side of the brain. The same structure on the other side remained healthy. Despite their long history of epilepsy, none showed notable signs of cognitive troubles. Similar to previous work, the team delivered a gene encoding the hMADi receptor into the damaged region of each patient’s hippocampus in a series of three shots. A dye mixed with the therapy confirmed it reached nearly the entire region in two patients and spread slightly beyond it in the third. The infusion took roughly two hours. Two weeks later, the men began taking clozapine pills every eight hours. After five months, their average monthly seizure count had dropped from roughly four to nearly zero. Brain recordings also showed far fewer epilepsy-related electrical spikes, and their damaged hippocampuses increased metabolism, though levels remained below those in the region’s healthy counterpart. The benefits lasted. In check-ups throughout the following year, two patients remained seizure-free. The third experienced two “breakthrough” seizures after an unexpected interruption in medication, but the seizures stopped once he restarted the drug regime. All three participants also reported improved quality of life. The study’s main goal, however, was to gauge safety. The viral carrier has a relatively established safety record, but high doses have been linked to severe immune reactions and even deaths . Delivering the therapy directly into brain tissue requires far smaller doses than when injected into the bloodstream and perhaps, counterintuitively, could be safer overall. Blood tests, brain scans, and other assessments find no major side effects. One patient experienced a temporary rise in liver enzymes, a sign of liver stress, but levels returned to normal without intervention. The team plans to expand the trial, but there are plenty of unsolved questions. All three men continued taking their existing antiseizure medications throughout the trial, making it difficult to isolate the treatment’s effects. For example, could clozapine have somehow synergized with those medications to reduce seizure counts? The study was also open-label, without a placebo control. And clozapine, when taken at high doses, carries risks of heart and other problems , though the doses given here were much lower than those used in psychiatric disorders. Whether chemogenetics can deliver lasting seizure relief in larger groups remains to be seen. But its debut in human medicine is a hopeful glimpse of what’s possible, not just for epilepsy, but potentially for addiction, mood disorders, and other neurological conditions involving unbalanced brain circuits too. “These findings offer initial proof of concept,” the team wrote. The post Novel Gene Therapy Nearly Erases ‘Drug Resistant’ Seizures appeared first on SingularityHub .

items.descriptionOriginal: Vithabai Narayangaonkar was nine months pregnant and in the middle of a Tamasha performance when her labour began. She slipped backstage, delivered her baby and cut the umbilical cord with a stone. Maharashtra's folk theatre world has told the story ever since, and it stands for a woman who gave her life to the stage and spent decades keeping the Tamasha tradition alive. The stage was her first classroom Vithabai grew up in Solapur district in a family that lived by the stage. Her father, Bhau Bapu Mang Narayangaonkar, ran a Tamasha troupe founded by her grandfather, Narayan Khude, and she grew up on Lavani, Gavlan and Bhedik, the songs and forms of Tamasha, Maharashtra's travelling folk theatre. Nine months pregnant, Vithabai slipped backstage, delivered her baby and returned to a life devoted to Tamasha. Photograph: ( Lokmat ) She followed the family trade from village to village, performing and refining her art . When the Marathi playwright Mama Varerkar saw her on stage, he was so mesmerised that he invited her to join his troupe, where she mastered techniques such as Angik, Vachik, Satvik and Abhinaya without formal drama training. Her daughter, the Tamasha artist Mangala Bansode, later recalled that Vithabai had danced since the age of 7, and that she pulled her own daughter out of school in class two to put her on the stage at 9, because the troupe needed more women. In families like theirs, song and dance were the first lessons, drilled in by parents through long hours of rehearsal, and the stage was the classroom. Such artists traditionally came from nomadic, lower-caste and Dalit communities. She won hearts, but couldn't make ends meet Fame did not guarantee food. The family had name and recognition but little money to buy a meal, and Vithabai's songs said as much . In a Lavani she sang in the 1960s, she asked the men in the audience to keep their own sense of shame, because she was dancing for her daily living and cared for nobody else's opinion. From village performances to national honours, Vithabai made Maharashtra's travelling folk theatre her lifelong stage. Photograph: ( Mid Day ) Fans began calling her Tamasha Samradni, or Tamasha Empress, and when the India-China war began she performed a special Tamasha at the North-East Frontier Agency border. The President of India honoured her twice, in 1957 and 1990. Even then, her work depended on contractors, who decided when a Tamasha opened or closed, and on audiences who set the terms of what artists performed. Mangala recalled dancing at a tamasha held under a tree, with no stage and the crowd pressing in, where she had to walk up to men to collect money and some pulled at her sari. Holding on to art even on the hardest days After the birth, the contractor stopped the Tamasha and the family was moved back into a dharmashala. Mangala remembered visiting her mother in hospital, where there was no food and no clothes for the newborn. When she asked the contractor for help, he told her nothing could be done until the Tamasha started again. Someone suggested pawning the harmonium for cash, but Mangala refused, calling the harmonium and ankle bells the family's wealth. She instead asked another troupe for ₹1,000 and agreed to dance for it every evening. With that money she bought food for everyone, mutton biryani for her mother and clothes for the baby. The hardship never fully lifted. Despite the honours, Vithabai and her family were never financially stable, and she died in 2002. 3 generations & a shared love for Tamasha In 2006, the Government of Maharashtra instituted the Vithabai Narayangaonkar Lifetime Achievement Award for artists working in Tamasha, the art she had dedicated much of her life to. The state has given grants to traditional folk arts, including Tamasha, Dashavatar and Shahiri, since 2008. When money ran short, her daughter protected the harmonium and ankle bells that kept their family's art alive. Photograph: ( News24 ) Mangala carried the stage forward, calling her mother her guru and saying she was famous because of her. By 2004, she was 55 and still dancing, a Tamasgir, or troupe leader, with around 150 people depending on her for their daily survival. She called Tamasha a public service rather than a business, and said she would keep performing as long as the public wanted her. Three generations of her family had performed in Tamasha, and her son took the stage at 7. Yet Mangala said audiences were thinning as remixes and orchestras drew crowds away, and she wanted the state to do more for its traditional artists. She had the fame a stage can give and little of the security it cannot. She left behind a harmonium her daughter refused to pawn, ankle bells that kept sounding through a daughter and a grandson, and an award in her name for those who keep Tamasha alive. Sources ' Shraddha Kapoor is playing a famous folk artist in Eetha. items.descriptionOriginal: Wind turbines are designed to last for 20–25 years. By that measure, turbines around the world are an elderly lot. In the US alone, 7,500 wind turbines are at least 20 years old . As these clean energy-generating behemoths approach the end of their lives , their green reputation gets tainted. That’s because their large blades end up in landfills. Made to withstand the elements, turbine blades are so durable that breaking them down to recycle them is also not easy. But researchers at Tsinghua University have found a straightforward way to breathe new life into wind turbine blades. Their method turns old blades into two valuable manufacturing materials that can improve the mechanical and thermal properties of new blades. This new approach cuts greenhouse gas emissions by 83–92% compared to present-day recycling technique. The results can be found in the journal Chem Circularity . Wind turbine blades are made of tiny glass fibers in a resin that is made of chains that are linked closely. The fibers are difficult to separate from the resin for recycling. Existing recycling methods require rely on breaking down the resin with heat or chemical solvents. Besides consuming a lot of energy and producing chemical waste, these processes weaken the fibers and results in low-value materials. The Tsinghua team ground blade waste into powder and mixed it with carbon black. Then they place the mixture between electrodes and blast it with short intense pulses of electricity, using a technique called Flash Joule Heating. Therein lies a massive opportunity to decarbonize the grid. At these blistering temperatures, carbon reacts with silica to form silicon carbide, which is a tough, heat-resistant compound. Carbon atoms also reorganize into a one atom-thick lattice with a honeycomb structure, called graphene. Graphene, a material whose discoverers garnered the Nobel Prize, is known for its strength and ability to conduct heat and electricity. The process converted close to 60% of the mixture into a silicon carbide–graphene composite made up of 34% silicon carbide and 66% graphene. The researchers then added this composite to fresh epoxy resin for making new blades. Just 0.3% by weight of the additive made the new resin stiffer and stronger, which should increase lifetime of new blades. The researchers’ calculations also show that at commercial scale the new blade recycling approach could turn a profit of about $80 per ton of material because the recovered silicon carbide and graphene are valuable. Heat and chemical-based recycling methods, by comparison, cost $460 per ton and $1,800 per ton respectively, they say. “Many emerging waste streams, including aerospace composites, automotive lightweight structures, electronic encapsulants, and fiber-reinforced construction materials, share similar challenges,” the team writes in the paper. Their approach hints at a way to deal with those waste streams. The team is now working on ways to scale up their process. Source: Hao Bi et al. items.descriptionOriginal: Every year, thousands of mothers and newborns in India are lost during labour and the 24 hours that follow, even though 9 in 10 births now happen in health facilities. What if early warning signs never went unnoticed? A Mumbai-based startup born at IIT Bombay is putting AI-powered fetal and labour monitoring into the hands of frontline health workers and hospitals. Strapped on the mother, the devices send real-time data to a smartphone, flag risks like fetal distress and PPH early, and cut documentation time for nurses by up to 50%, so they can focus on care. Innovation like this proves that quality maternal care shouldn’t depend on where a woman lives. If you have a working, tech-led solution, share your innovation with us. items.descriptionOriginal: "Uruvaai arivil olirvaai Kanna! Uyirin amudhaai pozhivaai Kanna!" Shine within my consciousness, O Kanna; pour forth as the nectar of my life. In Subramania Bharati's poetry, the imagery of devotion and love often reaches beyond the immediate moment. More than a century after his words were written, one of his compositions has found a new musical life — this time, on a global stage. But when the Grammy nominations were being announced on 16 November, the man behind that contemporary interpretation was nowhere near a television screen. Back from a project in Sri Lanka, Devan Ekambaram could not bring himself to watch the nominations unfold. He went instead to a temple. "I was too nervous to watch," he recalls. At 6.47 pm IST, his phone lit up. A friend in Los Angeles sent him a message: "Congratulations!" His phone soon filled with 80 or 90 similar messages. "I realised what had happened and immediately broke down crying," he says. Released independently in August 2026, Varuvaaiy became the first Tamil song nominated for a Grammy. The song that had brought him to this moment was Varuvaaiy , an independent Tamil recording he composed and produced with vocalist Subhiksha Rangarajan, known as Susha. It had been nominated for Best Global Music Performance at the 69th Grammy Awards, becoming the first Tamil song to receive a Grammy nomination. For Ekambaram, the moment carried a childhood dream: watching Michael Jackson win a Grammy for Thriller and hearing presenter Whoopi Goldberg urge young viewers to hold on to their dreams. It was also a milestone reached without a family music legacy. "I come from a family of doctors and engineers. Nobody is in the art field, and I had to embark on this journey all alone," he says. A childhood tuned to music Growing up in New Jersey, often one of the few Indian children in his neighbourhood, Ekambaram found it difficult to fit in. Music became a source of confidence . His mother introduced him to different genres, while programmes such as American Bandstand and Solid Gold showed him performers building careers around music. He began playing guitar between the seventh and tenth grades, then joined the school choir and marching band. He learnt to listen for harmonies and how musical parts fitted together, and began recording at home. "I knew my weakness, but I found my strength," he says. He developed his musical identity through choir, harmony and arranging. Growing up in New Jersey, Devan Ekambaram found his first musical inspiration through school choirs, guitars and American television. The Grammys entered his imagination around this time. "I remember watching Michael Jackson win for Thriller , and hearing presenter Whoopi Goldberg urge young viewers to hold on to their dreams, come what may. And that became my dream," he says. At 19 or 20, while studying electrical engineering at the University of Illinois, he explored music opportunities during a college break in India. He eventually left engineering and moved to Chennai at 21. "I just quit my engineering degree in the US and came here with no support and no direction. It was the scariest thing because I never saw anyone do this growing up," he says. Building a life in music — and finding the right voice Ekambaram's move to Chennai gradually opened doors. His 1998 album Kamban Oru Kannile , made with S P Charan, caught A R Rahman's attention and led to work on Kadhalar Dhinam . He made his playback debut with "Oh Maria" in 1999 and went on to sing on more than 500 film soundtracks, while also working as a composer, voice artist, and vocal arranger. He had contributed to Grammy-winning projects such as Winds of Samsara (2015) and Divine Tides (2022). But this time, he wanted to create something that was unmistakably his own: an independent album reimagining the poetry of Subramania Bharati through contemporary arrangements. For the first single, he had a particular voice in mind. Ekambaram had met Subhiksha Rangarajan, known as Susha, back in 2007, when they appeared on the television programme Coffee with Anu . He had wanted to collaborate with her ever since, but the opportunity never quite came together. When he began working on the Bharati project, he reached out to her again. Years after meeting vocalist Susha in 2007, Ekambaram brought her into his independent project celebrating Subramania Bharati's poetry. Photograph: ( Instagram/@sushasings ) In June 2026, Susha arrived at his home studio with her mother, Lakshmi Rangarajan. The composition they were about to record was one Lakshmi had taught her, set to a tune by L Krishnan that was already around 40 to 50 years old. What followed was an unusually quick coming together of ideas . Ekambaram asked Susha to sing, and the recording took shape over the next two to three hours. For him, her voice brought together the musical sensibilities the song needed. Trained in Carnatic music and having studied jazz at the University of Toronto, Susha could move between the classical foundation of the composition and the contemporary sound he wanted to create. She had also been building her own independent music career, including through NEXA Music, an initiative by A R Rahman and Clinton Cerejo that selected her among 24 artistes in 2019. "Without her singing, nobody would have listened to the song," Ekambaram says. Giving an old poem a new sound He wanted to rebuild the traditional arrangement while retaining the melody's character. "I just gave it a makeover," he says. "I looked at it thinking, how I would want to hear this?" He wanted to make the form inviting to a new generation of listeners unfamiliar with Carnatic music without flattening its identity. Set in raga Desh, the arrangement brings Carnatic phrasing together with piano, slide guitar, acoustic guitar, bass and tabla. Ekambaram played keyboards and produced the track. It features pianist Anil Srinivasan, slide guitarist Prakash Sontakke, guitarist Naveen Samson, bassist Joseph John and tabla player Sarvajit Krishna Mohan. Roshan Sebastian mixed and mastered it. The collaboration was largely remote: Susha recorded at Ekambaram's home studio, while the instrumentalists sent their parts from elsewhere. "I coordinated the musicians and worked with Sebastian on the final mix. The result was a three-minute-and-26-second recording released independently on 12 August 2026," he says. Susha's Carnatic training and jazz influences shaped Varuvaaiy, a contemporary interpretation of a century-old Tamil composition. Susha's contribution was central to the sound he had imagined. "Without her singing, nobody would have listened to the song," Ekambaram says. Her Carnatic training, jazz studies at the University of Toronto and contemporary sensibility shaped the recording. In 2019, she was among 24 artistes selected for NEXA Music, an initiative by A R Rahman and Clinton Cerejo. Her debut album, Love Language , arrived in August 2026. Written more than a century ago, the poem's exact date is unknown, though it is believed to date from Bharati's years in Pondicherry. Its imagery calls for a force to enter human thought and dispel darkness, and has been read as a metaphor for resisting oppression and colonial rule. That purpose appealed to Ekambaram. Rather than create a new song with contemporary lyrics, he wanted to bring a poet whose words shaped Tamil public life to younger listeners. "I thought this had a purpose," he says. He hoped a fresh musical arrangement would allow his children's generation to encounter Bharati's language without feeling distanced by it. A release against the clock Getting the single out in time required a difficult decision. Ekambaram says labels he approached were hesitant because the underlying work was in the public domain, and the permissions process threatened to delay the release. "With the Grammy submission deadline approaching, I chose to release the track independently and complete the distribution myself. But I never imagined how well it would work," he recalls. Rooted in raga Desh, the recording blends Carnatic nuances with jazz influences, guitars, piano and tabla. He had submitted work before and contributed to Grammy-winning projects, but this time concentrated on Varuvaaiy , preparing its streaming links for the Best Global Music Performance category. The category had 526 submissions, he says, and seeing the names on the ballot made a nomination feel far from certain. On nomination morning, the song had around 300 YouTube views, according to Ekambaram. As the news spread, the count rose to about 35,000. Messages of appreciation came from musicians including Scott Hoying of Pentatonix and Chandrika Tandon. What comes after the nomination The recognition arrived as Ekambaram questioned what came next. He had considered continuing in Chennai or returning to the United States if work did not move forward. He wanted to build a body of work listeners could associate with him, not a film or star. He worried that short-lived online trends left less room for songs that stay with people. The February 2027 Grammy ceremony will see Varuvaaiy compete alongside recordings by internationally acclaimed musicians. "The nomination has renewed my resolve to make independent music, compose and experiment rather than rely only on past successes. To think that I almost gave up and left for L. A., but we never know when opportunities will come. Today, I'm glad I continued on the path," he says. Ekambaram credits mentors including Madhav Das at Magnus Sound, choir director Ruth Lane McIntyre and the high-school teacher who encouraged him to sing. He wishes they could have witnessed the announcement. The larger Bharati album is now the next step. Ekambaram says it will contain 10 to 12 contemporary interpretations, with the tracks already taking shape and around two months of work remaining at the time of the interview. He is also waiting for a bilingual Tamil-Telugu film for which he composed the music to reach audiences. The ceremony is scheduled for February 2027 in Los Angeles, where Varuvaaiy will compete alongside recordings by Ang lique Kidjo, Rosal a, Shakira and Burna Boy. Winning would be wonderful, he says, but the nomination has already given him something deeply valuable. For Ekambaram, the nomination is already a milestone: bringing Tamil poetry and music to a global audience. "I don't care whether I win the category or not," he says. "I've been a catalyst in placing Tamil music on the global map. That is my win." More than a century after Bharati wrote the poem, its words have travelled into a new musical language: first through a melody passed down across generations, then through a contemporary arrangement shaped by musicians working across genres and distances. Now, listeners far beyond Tamil-speaking communities are being invited to hear it, too, today. That, perhaps, is the lasting possibility of Varuvaaiy . A poem written in another time has not been left behind in it. It has been given another voice, another audience and another chance to be understood. And somewhere, a listener encountering Bharati for the first time may follow the song back to the words that began it all.

items.descriptionOriginal: A car brakes suddenly as a two-wheeler slips into the gap ahead. An auto-rickshaw swerves to avoid a bus, while another vehicle edges into the next lane. On Indian roads, where cars, buses, three-wheelers and two-wheelers often share limited space, traffic can change its rhythm in seconds. For urban planners and traffic engineers, understanding this movement is no easy task. Many conventional traffic models assume that vehicles follow lanes and maintain relatively predictable speeds. But Indian roads rarely offer such orderly conditions. Researchers at the Indian Institute of Technology (IIT) Guwahati are working to bridge this gap. By combining drone footage, automated vehicle tracking and machine learning, they have developed mathematical models that better account for the unpredictable ways vehicles move on Indian roads. Tracking nearly nine million vehicle positions Led by Professor Akhilesh Kumar Maurya from the Department of Civil Engineering, the research team studied traffic on an eight-lane divided highway on the outskirts of Delhi. Using drones equipped with high-resolution cameras, they recorded around five hours of daytime traffic footage in 4K resolution. The videos were then processed using DataFromSky, an automated software that extracts vehicle movements from aerial footage. Led by Professor Akhilesh Kumar Maurya, the IIT Guwahati research could help improve traffic simulations, highway planning and congestion management in India. Photograph: (IIT Guwahati) The result was a dataset of 36,818 vehicles and 8,938,920 vehicle-position data points, captured at 10 frames per second. Researchers categorised the vehicles into six groups: two-wheelers, three-wheelers, cars, buses, heavy commercial vehicles and light commercial vehicles. This gave them a detailed picture of how different vehicles moved, how closely they followed one another and how their speeds changed as traffic became denser. Explaining why India-specific data is necessary, Prof Maurya says, "Traffic conditions in India are different from those in many countries where existing traffic models have been developed. We need traffic data that represents the diversity and characteristics of Indian roads." Drone-based data collection provides an opportunity to observe a large number of vehicles and their movements over a road section at high spatial and temporal resolution. Teaching traffic models to account for unpredictability One interesting finding was that the distance vehicles maintained from one another changed with traffic density. On relatively empty roads, vehicles kept larger gaps. As traffic increased, these gaps became smaller. However, when congestion became severe, the spacing patterns changed again. This variability is important because two vehicles travelling under seemingly similar traffic conditions may not necessarily move at the same speed. Using automated vehicle tracking and machine learning, the researchers mapped 36,818 vehicles and nearly nine million vehicle-position data points. Photograph: ( iStock ) To understand these differences, the researchers tested six mathematical traffic models, including established approaches such as Greenshields and Underwood. They also trained two machine learning models: Artificial Neural Networks (ANN) and Random Forest (RF). But perhaps the most interesting part was their development of stochastic fundamental diagrams. In simple terms, conventional traffic models generally estimate one speed for a given traffic density. Stochastic models go a step further by accounting for the range of speeds that vehicles may actually travel at under those conditions. This allows the models to represent the randomness of Indian traffic more realistically, rather than smoothing over the differences between individual vehicles. From better predictions to smarter road planning The researchers found that the Underwood model performed most consistently among the mathematical models tested, achieving an R² value of 0.86. The two machine learning models achieved approximately 0.83. The research could have practical applications in assessing highway capacity, designing intersections, estimating road speeds, and improving traffic simulations. The data could also help researchers calibrate car-following models, which study how drivers adjust their distance and speed in relation to vehicles ahead. Prof. Maurya explains, "Reliable traffic management begins with models that represent how traffic actually behaves on Indian roads. The high-resolution trajectory data generated through drones allows us to capture interactions among different vehicle types and the large variability that conventional traffic models often overlook." Such India-specific models can support more realistic traffic simulation, better road and intersection design, congestion management, capacity assessment, and the development of intelligent traffic-management systems suited to Indian conditions. Unlike conventional traffic models, the stochastic models developed by the team account for variations in vehicle speeds and distances, even under similar traffic conditions. Photograph: ( Adobe Stock ) For anyone who has spent time on an Indian road, the challenge of predicting traffic is easy to understand. A car slows down, a two-wheeler slips into a narrow gap, an auto-rickshaw changes lanes, and the movement of hundreds of vehicles can shift in seconds. By capturing these interactions in detail, the IIT Guwahati team hopes to make traffic models better reflect what commuters experience every day. The research is a step towards understanding not just how many vehicles use a road, but how they move around one another. And that understanding could eventually help make the daily journey a little more predictable, whether someone is driving to work, taking a bus to school or navigating a crowded intersection.

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Trust and Climate-Smart Agriculture Scaling Depend More on Neighbors Than Institutions, Study Finds Reading Time: 3 minutes A study of 514 Central American farmers found that trust and climate-smart agriculture scaling are closely linked, with relationships with neighbors mattering more than trust in outside organizations. Trust and climate-smart agriculture scaling have long been treated as separate concerns, one social, one technical. New research published in Agricultural Systems directly challenges that separation, showing that farmer-to-farmer relationships shape whether climate innovations spread at all, regardless of how well-designed they are on paper. Researchers from the Alliance of Bioversity International and CIAT, the University of Copenhagen, and the Gates Foundation analyzed data from 514 smallholder farmers participating in Climate-Smart Villages, known locally as Territorios Sostenibles Adaptados al Clima, across Guatemala and Honduras. The study examined how different dimensions of social capital influence knowledge sharing about climate-smart practices, and what that process reveals about the earliest stages of responsible scaling. The findings reframe how funders and policymakers should evaluate trust and the scaling of climate-smart agriculture. Success is traditionally measured only after an innovation has already reached large numbers of adopters. This study instead focuses on an earlier moment: when farmers first share experiences, discuss new practices, raise questions, and learn from one another, long before adoption becomes visible at any meaningful scale. Trust among farmers emerged as the single most consistent factor enabling knowledge sharing. When farmers trust one another, they are much more likely to share experiences, discuss new practices, and learn from each other’s successes and failures. Close relationships among farmers further strengthen these learning networks, making it easier for knowledge and hands-on experience to circulate freely within a community rather than remaining isolated within individual households. Perhaps the study’s most striking finding for trust and scaling climate-smart agriculture is the role of mutual support. Researchers found that support between farmers becomes especially critical in communities where trust remains low. In these lower-trust environments, guidance, collaboration, and the exchange of practical experience help sustain knowledge flows that trust alone would otherwise fail to carry. Mutual support effectively functions as a backup mechanism, compensating for weaker social bonds that might otherwise block information sharing entirely. Trust and climate-smart agriculture scaling depend heavily on mutual support in low-trust communities, where researchers found that guidance and collaboration between farmers help sustain the flow of knowledge that institutional trust alone fails to provide. Photo by Frank Meriño on Pexels. By contrast, the research found that trust in formal organizations, whether government agencies, NGOs, or research institutions, carried notably less influence than trust built directly among farmers themselves. This distinction matters enormously for how development programs are typically designed, since many climate-smart agriculture initiatives invest heavily in institutional credibility and extension services while underinvesting in the peer networks that this study identifies as more decisive. Researchers also found a positive association between adopting climate-smart practices and knowledge sharing, reinforcing that these two processes reinforce each other rather than operating independently. A farmer observing a neighbor successfully implementing a drought-coping technique, discussing the results, adapting that practice to their own land’s specific conditions, and later sharing their experience with others exemplifies the kind of organic circulation of trust and climate-smart agriculture scaling research seeks to capture and understand. These findings carry direct implications for how governments, development organizations, and innovation programs design their interventions. The evidence suggests development organizations need to place social dynamics at the center of scaling strategies rather than treating community relationships as secondary to technical training and resource distribution. Programs that invest in building trust and facilitating informal peer networks, rather than relying solely on top-down institutional messaging, appear better positioned to achieve the kind of local ownership that sustains results over time. Trust and climate-smart agriculture scaling research also supports what the study authors describe as a responsible scaling approach, one that anticipates and manages unintended consequences before they emerge rather than addressing problems only after widespread adoption has already occurred. Understanding how knowledge circulates among farmers before adoption becomes visible allows program designers to build strategies that are more inclusive, more context-sensitive, and more attuned to the specific social fabric of the communities they aim to serve. As agrifood systems worldwide face mounting pressure to accelerate climate adaptation, this research corrects purely technical approaches to scaling innovation. The impact of any climate-smart agricultural practice depends not only on its scientific merit, but equally on farmers’ capacity to share knowledge, learn collaboratively, and build the relationships of trust that let that knowledge travel organically through a community, often well before any formal program measures success. The post Trust and Climate-Smart Agriculture Scaling Depend More on Neighbors Than Institutions, Study Finds appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: This story was originally published by Grist . Sign up for Grist’s weekly newsletter here . Doing the laundry has grown easier and more efficient over the years, yet two things have always remained the same: A washing machine needs water, and a dryer needs heat. Technology designed to clean aerospace parts reimagines the process by ditching both of those in favor of an unlikely substitute: carbon dioxide, the very gas we’re trying so hard to contain. Under pressure, CO2 becomes a low-viscosity liquid capable of penetrating fabrics and carrying away oils and grime. When depressurized, it reverts to a gas, leaving clothes clean and dry. No wastewater. No dryer. Beyond its novelty, the idea could clean up a resource-intensive chore. The average family runs roughly 300 loads a year, consuming thousands of gallons of water. And more than 80 percent of U.S. households own a dryer, with one study putting the annual CO2 emissions from machine drying alone at 27 million metric tons . Tersus Solutions’ industrial CO2 washers use high pressure to turn carbon dioxide into a liquid that can clean fabrics without water. The machines’ bulky pressure chambers, pumps, pipes and compressors illustrate the challenge appliance makers face in trying to shrink the technology for household use. Courtesy of Teresus Solutions Long confined to industrial operations, liquid-CO2 cleaning is getting a second look from appliance giants LG and Samsung — this time for the home. Still, shrinking a technology built around bulky, high-pressure machinery to fit both a laundry room and household budget is a tall order. No less challenging is doing so without washing away the environmental gains that make waterless, dryerless laundry so enticing in the first place. Just getting this far has taken decades. Hughes Aircraft developed the process in 1990 to remove grease and other contaminants from electronic components. Electrolux later pursued it as a safer alternative to solvent-based dry cleaning, though cost, complexity, and bulky equipment kept it from catching on. In 2009, Colorado-based Tersus Solutions began refining the technology and has since carved out a niche cleaning outdoor apparel and equipment, as well as firefighter gear contaminated with hazardous residues. Its machines offer a glimpse of what CO2 cleaning can do and why squeezing it into a household appliance is no simple feat. Weighed down by negative news? Enter your email below to receive our smart, uplifting newsletters. Or click here to choose exactly which ones you want [contact-form-7] Tersus CEO Peter Whitcomb describes the machines as “futuristic front-loading washers,” though the company’s two models dwarf those found in a typical laundromat. Each occupies a roughly 10-foot cube, with the larger unit handling up to 85 pounds of laundry, or a dozen sleeping bags. Behind a thick, submarine-like hatch, a rotating drum sits inside a pressurized chamber amid a maze of pipes, pumps and compressors. Despite the complexity, what happens inside is relatively simple. Carbon dioxide turns from gas to liquid at 900 pounds per square inch of pressure — roughly one-third of what’s inside a full scuba tank . As it circulates, filters trap the grime, which accumulates as a thick purplish sludge for disposal. When the 45-minute cycle ends, the pressure drops and liquid returns to gas, instantly drying the load. More than 90 percent of the CO2 is recaptured for the next run; the rest escapes in a smoky wisp. The process is particularly effective on firefighter gear, with tests showing an average of more than 95 percent removal of contaminants such as PAHs, potentially harmful compounds found in smoke and soot. Water-soluble stains from sweat and food can be trickier, said Chris Robbins, Tersus’ chief technology officer, occasionally requiring pretreatment — “think Tide pen, but for CO2” — or conventional washing. For most loads, however, the process eliminates water and additives alike. “We’re not using detergent, we don’t use heat,” Whitcomb said. Tersus estimates its larger machines save roughly 300 gallons of water per load compared with conventional washing. There is another potential upside, as well: By eliminating wastewater and trapping shed fibers for disposal, the process could further reduce microplastic contamination from laundry. The energy equation, however, is more complicated. A California Energy Commission demonstration with the U.S. Navy found the method used about 15 percent less energy than smaller commercial washers and dryers, yet about as much as larger industrial combinations. Tersus has found comparable performance, said Robbins. While CO2 cleaning avoids thermal drying — typically the most energy-intensive part of conventional laundry — removing impurities from the carbon dioxide for reuse requires significant power. The company is exploring more efficient ways of heating and cooling the gas, Robbins said. As for the CO2, Tersus gets it from a nearby ethanol plant, where it’s a byproduct of fermentation. That minimizes transportation needs, although purifying and liquefying it require additional energy — further complicating the calculation of the technology’s overall carbon footprint. Then there’s the question of scale: Could all that machinery — enough to fill a small bedroom — be shrunk into a household appliance? LG and Samsung are working on that. Recent patents from the companies, both of which declined to comment, tackle distinct challenges: removing stains resistant to CO2 cleaning and reducing the pressure required to make the tech work. LG’s design uses detergents and other additives to help remove water-soluble stains. Although the patent doesn’t specify a formula, a recent study found that adding isopropyl alcohol and water improved liquid carbon dioxide’s ability to remove sugars, salts and other compounds. Samsung, meanwhile, proposes combining CO2 with other solvents to bring operating pressures down to a fraction of those used in industrial machines. That could make home models more compact, though some of the mixtures include PFAS , raising questions about environmental trade-offs. Smaller, however, doesn’t necessarily mean simpler. Separating and recovering those added solvents could require still more equipment, said Eckhard Groll, head of mechanical engineering at Purdue University and an expert in CO2 refrigeration. “There’s no question” that a home version is technically feasible, he said, “but it may be very costly, the technology.” Even if the machines become affordable, the environmental benefits may not carry over, said Rainer Stamminger, a household appliance efficiency researcher at the University of Bonn. With households running just a few loads a week, pressurizing and recovering carbon dioxide could be “very inefficient just for one wash” compared to industrial machines that run continuously. The economics may be especially challenging in the U.S., where electricity is relatively cheap. Groll pointed to heat pump dryers, which use about half the energy of conventional electric models. Popular in Europe, they made up 75 percent of new dryer sales in 2020, helped by higher electricity prices that helped ease the sticker shock; meanwhile, American sales still lag . CO2 washers could as well if their efficiency comes with a hefty upfront premium. Whitcomb sees greater opportunities in commercial dry cleaning, apartment buildings and institutions, where higher volumes could justify the equipment costs — and keep the machines running often enough to take advantage of their scale. With a new facility in Calgary expanding its Colorado operations, Tersus now works with more than 40 brands and retailers, offering repairs, restoration and resale services that “complement the cleaning” to extend garment life and keep products in circulation, Whitcomb said. Wait, you're not a member yet? Join the Reasons to be Cheerful community by supporting our nonprofit publication and giving what you can. Join Cancel anytime Even if engineers can make a home CO2 washer affordable and efficient, they would still have to convince people to buy one. The early market for water-efficient front-load washers offers a precedent: Energy and water savings attracted some consumers, while upfront costs deterred others. Performance and convenience mattered, too, said Gwendolyn Hustvedt, a textiles and consumer sciences professor at Texas State University who studied the trend. The technology may have one big selling point, however: The clothes come out dry. Beyond saving time and hassle, skipping what Hustvedt called “cooking your clothes in a box” could help garments last longer by reducing shrinkage and wear from heat and tumbling. Whether consumers would pay a premium for those benefits is another question. Home CO2 washers still have a long way to go before they break up the familiar washer-dryer combo. But if engineers can make the physics work economically — and environmentally — at household scale, the next big thing in laundry might be one less appliance. This article originally appeared in Grist at https://grist.org/science/carbon-dioxide-is-a-climate-problem-it-might-also-be-a-laundry-solution/ . Grist is a nonprofit, independent media organization dedicated to reporting on climate change. items.descriptionOriginal: Garry oak trees, home for bluebirds nested in cavities, were tended by First Nations for millennia. Without their care, 95 percent of the Garry oak ecosystem was lost to agriculture, pesticides, and urban development. Their homes gone, bluebirds left, and were declared extinct on Vancouver Island and the southern Gulf Islands. “Garry oak trees are a great source of insects,” said Jacquie Taylor, coordinator for the Cowichan Bring Back the Bluebirds Project. “They have a real biodiversity of their own, things that live in the bark and on the trees.” Saving them would help save the bluebirds. Canadians and Americans worked together, along with a military base, a slew of permits, thousands of volunteer hours, private property owners, Cowichan Tribes, and lots and lots of tiny, wriggling mealworms to help the bluebirds return. “But most noticeable is the sound: a gentle musical chortling so cheerful and soothing that it immediately banishes all thought of the ills of the world.”

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Watershed Restoration in Ethiopia Reaches First Major Milestone Reading Time: 3 minutes Watershed restoration in Ethiopia reached a new milestone as 1,000 community members planted 152,333 seedlings across four degraded micro-watersheds in the Tana Subbasin. Watershed restoration in Ethiopia reached a new milestone in July, with more than 1,000 community members planting over 150,000 tree seedlings across four degraded micro-watersheds . The effort marks ProTana’s first major field campaign, a five-year project led by the World Resources Institute and partners. Nearly half of the volunteers were women. ProTana focuses on the Tana Subbasin in Ethiopia’s Amhara Region, home to Lake Tana, the country’s largest lake and the source of the Blue Nile. The lake and its surrounding watersheds supply water for millions of people across the region. Decades of deforestation, overgrazing, and soil erosion have steadily degraded the land feeding into it. Lake Tana’s importance reaches well beyond Ethiopia’s borders. Water flowing out of the lake eventually joins the Blue Nile, which supplies a significant share of the water reaching Sudan and Egypt downstream. Keeping the watersheds that feed the lake healthy therefore affects water security across the wider Nile basin, not just the communities living closest to it. The World Resources Institute (WRI) is implementing the project alongside WaterAid Ethiopia and ORDA Ethiopia, focusing on three districts: North Mecha, Farta, and Dera. Selecting which specific watersheds to restore took months of consultation with local officials and community leaders. Criteria included erosion severity, the importance of water supply, and each community’s willingness to participate. The four selected micro-watersheds span more than 2,100 hectares combined. During July’s planting campaign, workers and volunteers put in over 152,000 seedlings, split between private agroforestry plots and communal or institutional land. Planting took place at the start of Ethiopia’s main rainy season to give seedlings the best chance of survival. Community turnout exceeded expectations, with more than 1,000 people taking part directly. Many children and young people also attended, watched the planting process, and learned why restoring the land matters for their future water security. Organizers see early engagement as key to building long-term support, since restoration work without community buy-in rarely survives past its first planting season. Watershed restoration in Ethiopia drew more than 1,000 community participants, with children and young people watching and learning alongside adults, as organizers bet that early engagement is the only way to build the long-term community buy-in that keeps restoration work alive past its first planting season. Photo by Khedir Dawed, courtesy of World Resources Institute . This campaign builds on an earlier three-year pilot in the Minzir 01 micro-watershed, part of the same broader area. That pilot showed measurable improvements in local water supply alongside benefits for nearby crop farming. ProTana now aims to apply those same lessons across a much larger area. Tree planting represents only the first phase of watershed restoration in Ethiopia under this project. Future work will include soil and water conservation measures such as terracing, check dams, and soil bunds. Regenerative agricultural practices are also planned to help households manage land more sustainably over the long term. A WRI program specialist working on the project described success as depending heavily on strong local leadership and coordination between partners. He noted that when communities see real benefits firsthand, they tend to stay far more committed to protecting restored land afterward, rather than treating conservation as an outside obligation imposed on them. According to the World Resources Institute, watershed restoration in Ethiopia fits into a broader strategy addressing water risk, climate resilience, and sustainable water governance across the country. The organization continues to monitor seedling survival through the rainy season to track how well the new plantings take hold. If ProTana’s larger rollout matches the results seen in its earlier pilot, this round of watershed restoration in Ethiopia could improve water availability and livelihoods for thousands of households in the Tana Subbasin. Much of that outcome will depend on how well new seedlings survive and how consistently local institutions keep up conservation work after the initial planting rush ends. For now, the scale of community turnout offers an early, encouraging sign that residents are ready to stay involved for the long haul. The post Watershed Restoration in Ethiopia Reaches First Major Milestone appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: Once known as the Garden City for its tree-lined avenues, blooming parks and pleasant weather, Bengaluru is now facing a growing question: How can a rapidly expanding city make room for nature while preparing for heavier rains, water shortages and rising temperatures? Now, a neighbourhood-level climate planning exercise across five wards aims to address some of these concerns through better drainage, rainwater management and urban greening. The Greater Bengaluru Authority (GBA) has prepared ward-level Climate Action Plans for five pilot wards across the city, identifying environmental challenges and proposing interventions suited to the conditions of each neighbourhood. The initiative is now awaiting budgetary approval from the respective city corporations before implementation can begin. The five wards selected for the pilot are Shantinagar in Central Bengaluru, Jakkur in the North, Begur in the South, Vijinapura in the East and Nalwadi Krishnaraja Wadiyar ward in the West. Developed under the GBA's Climate Action Cell, the plans aim to take climate planning beyond city-wide recommendations and identify what individual neighbourhoods need. The assessments cover energy and buildings, transportation, solid waste management, urban planning, greenery and biodiversity, water management, wastewater and stormwater management, and disaster preparedness. According to The New Indian Express, the plans were prepared following sector-wise assessments and consultations with residents, experts and other stakeholders. The exercise recognises that climate-related challenges are not uniform across Bengaluru. While some localities experience recurring flooding, others face water scarcity, declining green cover, rising temperatures or inadequate waste management. Why Bengaluru needs neighbourhood-level climate planning The city's contrasting water challenges illustrate why localised planning matters. Bengaluru experiences heavy surface runoff during the monsoon, even as several neighbourhoods face groundwater depletion and water shortages during summer. A March 18, 2026 report by Mongabay-India, which examined the ward-level planning exercise, highlighted how geography influences flood vulnerability. For instance, Shantinagar, a densely populated urban ward, lies in a downstream valley zone. Hydrological assessments by WELL Labs and Bengaluru's Climate Action Cell found that floodwater can originate beyond the ward's boundaries, making flooding a problem that cannot always be addressed through isolated drainage work within one locality. The five-ward pilot is intended to provide a model for extending climate action planning to other neighbourhoods under the GBA. Photograph: (Bengaluru Climate Action Cell-via Mongabay) Anam Husain, programme associate for Urban Water at WELL Labs, told Mongabay-India that nature-based interventions such as rain gardens, bioswales, permeable surfaces and small retention systems can help slow down rainwater runoff and improve groundwater infiltration. These interventions offer ways to manage excess rainwater closer to where it falls, while also reducing pressure on conventional drainage infrastructure. Rainwater harvesting and groundwater recharge are particularly relevant in a city where water scarcity and monsoon runoff exist side by side. Alongside improving stormwater management, wastewater reuse and stormwater reuse can contribute to longer-term water security. Bringing green infrastructure into urban planning Urban greening is another important component of Bengaluru's climate planning exercise. In neighbourhoods experiencing rising temperatures, the GBA is considering measures such as increasing green cover, using heat-reflective cool paints and establishing cool shelters. These interventions can help address the urban heat island effect , in which built-up areas with extensive concrete surfaces and limited vegetation retain more heat than surrounding areas. Bengaluru's existing Climate Action and Resilience Plan also identifies nature-based solutions as an important part of urban development. View this post on Instagram A post shared by ಬೆಂಗಳೂರು ದಕ್ಷಿಣ ನಗರ ಪಾಲಿಕೆ (Bengaluru South City Corporation) (@bscc.gba) Its sectoral recommendations include restoring the city's blue-green networks, increasing tree canopy and expanding green and permeable surfaces to help reduce flood and heat-related risks. The plan sets targets to increase the city's tree canopy by 10% from its baseline by 2030 and 20% by 2040. It also proposes increasing green cover and permeable surfaces to 40% of the city's area by 2040. From climate plans to neighbourhood-level action Public participation has also been part of the planning process. Just recently, The Better India documented how Bengaluru residents are taking small, collective steps to care for their city's shared spaces . From removing 110 kg of plastic waste around Madiwala Lake during a 75-minute plogging drive to watering hundreds of saplings at Vengaiah Lake through the Bhagiratha initiative, the report highlighted how citizen participation can complement urban conservation efforts. Read the report. Other efforts include residents in Balagere, Panathur and Varthur clearing accumulated roadside dust, and volunteers working with civic authorities to restore neglected footpaths and public spaces. The Greater Bengaluru Authority's proposed Climate Action Plans across five wards take this approach further by seeking to integrate local environmental needs into formal urban planning. The five-ward pilot is intended to provide a model for extending climate action planning to other neighbourhoods under the GBA. For Bengaluru, the next step will be translating these local assessments into funded projects that improve drainage, strengthen water management and expand green infrastructure. The effectiveness of the exercise will ultimately depend on how consistently these proposals are implemented and monitored at the neighbourhood level. Sources: 'GBA goes micro local with ward-level climate plans' : By Express News Service, Published on 4 November 2026 'Ward-level plans bring climate action closer to communities' : By Mahima Jain, Published on 18 March 2026

items.descriptionOriginal: Scientists have discovered a rare inherited mutation in the CDK12 gene linked to aggressive prostate cancer, with all five identified carriers developing metastatic disease between ages 44 and 62. The finding could lead to expanded genetic testing, helping families uncover hidden cancer risks and potentially detect the disease while it is still treatable.

items.description: ΑΠΟ ΤΗΝ OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM Οι συγκεντρώσεις των PFOS και PFOA, των δύο πιο τοξικών για πάντα χημικών ουσιών, έχουν μειωθεί κατά 30 τοις εκατό και 29 τοις εκατό στα ποτάμια της Αγγλίας τα τελευταία 10 χρόνια, σύμφωνα με νέα στοιχεία της Υπηρεσίας Περιβάλλοντος (EA). Στα ψάρια του γλυκού νερού, τα επίπεδα μειώνονται κατά 49%. Ο οργανισμός αποδίδει την πτώση σε περιορισμό…
items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM Concentrations of PFOS and PFOA, the two most toxic forever chemicals , have fallen by 30 percent and 29 percent in England’s rivers over the past 10 years, according to new figures from the Environment Agency (EA). In freshwater fish , levels are down 49 percent. The agency attributes the decline to restrictions that removed both compounds from most products, which makes the data one of the clearer measures yet of what a chemical ban does to a river system over time. Two forever chemicals, two bans, one decade of data PFOS and PFOA PFAS, short for per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances, were first developed in the U.S. in the 1930s. Manufacturers adopted them for their resistance to oil, water, and heat, and they ended up in nonstick pans, firefighting foam, and electrical components. The same chemical stability means they take a very long time to break down, which earned them the label forever chemicals. PFOS and PFOA were among the earliest compounds in the family. About 20 years ago, researchers began linking them to tissue damage in animals and to higher rates of certain serious illnesses in people, including testicular cancer . The UK all but banned PFOS in 2010 and PFOA in 2020. Results from the latest Environment Agency figures The new data, published by the EA this month, covers 10 years of monitoring. Both chemicals declined by nearly a third in river water, while the near-halving in fish points to less of the compounds moving up the food chain. Dr. David Megson, a reader in environmental forensics at Manchester Metropolitan University, welcomed the trend. “It’s brilliant to see how far we have come in the last 10 years,” he said. Lower concentrations, same total load Where forever chemicals go after a ban The EA report attaches a significant caveat to its own numbers. Because PFOS and PFOA break down so slowly, the total quantity in the environment has likely not changed much. Concentrations in rivers have dropped because the chemicals have been diluted and carried downstream into the sea. A ban stops new inputs, but it does not remove what is already circulating. Very few methods can destroy PFAS permanently. High-temperature incineration is one of them, and England currently has only two facilities suited to the job. Making polluters pay Megson sees the monitoring record as a starting point for accountability. “There is a lot to do, and this report provides an essential foundation to support investigations to make the polluters pay for any damage they have caused,” he said. Regulating PFAS as a group 15,000 compounds, 200 in common use PFOS and PFOA are two of an estimated 15,000 PFAS, of which around 200 are in frequent use. The EA said that “uncertainty remains regarding the toxicity of many PFAS” and that its findings reinforce the case for regulating the chemicals as a class instead of one at a time. The chemicals industry has long resisted a group approach, arguing that evidence of toxicity for most other PFAS is limited or absent and that some have essential applications, including in life-saving medical equipment. Wider monitoring The agency now tests regularly for 60 additional PFAS to map contamination across England, and the government announced earlier this month that it will begin measuring forever chemicals in people’s bodies. Taken together with the river data, those programs will show whether the pattern seen with PFOS and PFOA holds for other compounds once restrictions arrive: a slow but steady fall in water and wildlife, with the legacy load still to be dealt with downstream. Did this solution stand out? Share it with a friend or support our mission by becoming an Emissary . The post Bans cut two forever chemicals by 30 percent in England’s rivers first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News .

items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM It’s 6 p.m. on a Friday, and the dinner you booked two weeks ago is in an hour. Back then it sounded like the perfect plan. But now your couch has never looked softer, your sweatpants feel like a hug, and your thumb is hovering over a message that starts with “So sorry, something came up…” Nothing came up, of course. You just don’t want to go anymore, and you can’t quite explain why. If that sounds familiar, you have plenty of company. According to the Survey Center on American Life , 55 percent of Gen Z adults say they feel relief when plans fall through. In the U.K., research from the Institute of Practitioners in Advertising found that 68 percent of people under 34 have bailed on plans, and one in 10 do it “very often.” There’s a name for that late-afternoon dread, and once you can name it, it gets a lot easier to put your shoes on anyway. What anticipatory anxiety feels like The doorway as a dividing line Mindy DeSeta , a licensed mental health counselor, calls it anticipatory anxiety. “It’s the stress we feel before something happens,” she says. Part of the pull comes from home itself, which is familiar and predictable in a way a crowded restaurant isn’t. “Walking through the doorway is the visual trigger that separates your safe space from the unknown,” DeSeta said. It’s the same jittery feeling you might have had before a school recital or a big presentation at work, just pointed at something that’s supposed to be fun. Why the dread rarely matches the night Think back to the last time you went out despite wanting to cancel. Chances are, an hour in, you were laughing at something and had forgotten all about the couch. DeSeta has seen that pattern again and again. “In most cases, the anticipation anxiety is often worse than the event itself. Don’t allow the jitters to deter you!” she said. What canceling plans costs your friends When everyone bails, everyone feels it Canceling feels harmless in the moment, and sometimes it’s the right call. But when it becomes a habit for a whole generation, someone is always on the other end of that text. Rachel Schleider, a 23-year-old social strategist said her birthday has become a source of stress for exactly this reason. “I literally dread making plans for my birthday every year because I know people are going to cancel the day before,” she said. She thinks the culture around flaking has swung too far. “We’ve kind of taken it too far and now people are way too comfortable bowing out,” Schleider said. How to manage anticipatory anxiety before a plan Name it, then don’t negotiate with it DeSeta’s first suggestion is to call the feeling what it is. Once you recognize the dread as anticipatory anxiety, you can remind yourself that the feeling isn’t an instruction. Feeling uneasy about going is a different thing from having a reason not to go. Breathe, and look at what the nerves are telling you A few slow, deep breaths can take the edge off the physical side of it, the tight chest and the restless hands. It also helps to flip the meaning of the nerves around. Feeling jittery about seeing someone usually means the plan matters to you, which is a reason to show up instead of a reason to stay home. Set an alarm and let the routine carry you DeSeta’s most practical trick happens before the dread has a chance to build: set an alarm for when you need to start getting ready, and when it goes off, get in the shower and get dressed without debating it. By the time your hair is dry, you’re most of the way out the door. None of this means you should drag yourself out when you’re sick or running on empty. Rest is a valid reason to cancel. But if the only thing standing between you and your friends is that familiar pre-plan heaviness, it might help to picture the walk home afterward, a little tired and full and glad you went, and let that version of the evening make the decision for you. There’s a name for that feeling first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News .

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Types of Cycling Explained for Eco Riders and Race Followers Reading Time: 4 minutes From Daily Rides to Pro Races, Cycling Comes In Many Forms. Here’s a Simple Guide to Each One What Do You Mean by Cycling? Everyday Riding for a Greener Life The cost of gas and vehicle repairs and maintenance has many people looking at cycling as an alternative way to get around, but what do you mean by cycling exactly? Depending on where you’re cycling and your purpose for doing the activity, there are different types of cycling available for you. Some people are just looking to get places on main streets, while others are more adventurous and want to explore with off-road cycling. There are many different types of cycling , so let’s take a closer look at what the best might be for you. The Best Bicycle for Beginners So you think you want to give cycling a try. But what is the best bicycle for beginners ? As we already talked about, it really depends on the type of cycling you’re wanting to get into. There are many different types of cycling, and your equipment needs to fit the type that you are doing. Anyone who bikes regularly knows that each has its own needs, so your equipment needs to match where and how you’re going to be cycling. Different Types of Cycling: Road, Track, Mountain and More So what are the different types of cycling? There are many, as the sport has few limits on how you decide to approach it. For getting places and more relaxing rides, there is road cycling. This occurs – as the name implies – on roads, so there isn’t much terrain to worry about. The bike for road cycling is more sleek and aerodynamic, allowing for smoother rides on the smoother terrain that is being used. This leads to track cycling, where speed is more of a concern. The cycle and the attire of the cyclist are made for less wind resistance and greater speeds. Mountain biking comes with less predictable terrain, so the cycle itself must have more of a suspension system and wider tires to help the cyclist deal with the different obstacles that come up. There is less of a need for being aerodynamic with the cycle and the attire, since this type of cycling is more focused on getting through off-road trails. Another of the types of cycling is gravel cycling, which is a bit of a cross between mountain biking and road cycling. As you might guess, this type is on gravel trails, which brings fewer obstacles and a bit more stability on trails than mountain biking. The type of bike for this is a cross between mountain biking and road cycling, with wider tires but less suspension. A growing form of cycling is e-biking, which can be applied to almost any form of cycling. This is not a motorcycle or moped, as the cyclist still has to be doing work. The motor and battery on an e-bike assist when needed to make for longer rides and easier times for cyclists when they face obstacles like a steep climb. There are also racing forms of cycling, whether on streets like the Tour de France or over ramps and jumps in BMX racing. Types of Bicycle Racing in the Olympics When it comes to racing, the top venue for cycling is the Olympics. There are five different disciplines that are held in the Summer Olympic Games. Road cycling is done on outdoor courses with a mass-start road race. Also on outdoor courses is mountain bike racing, with rougher natural terrain, steep climbs, and obstacles. One of the more popular types of bicycle racing at the Olympics is track cycling, which is held on a banked oval track using fixed-gear bicycles with no brakes. There are multiple different events within this form of cycling, including team pursuit and sprints. There are two types of BMX racing in the Olympics as well. BMX racing is held on dirt tracks with as many as eight cyclists running the course filled with jumps and banked turns at a time. There is also BMX freestyle, which is a judged competition as riders perform tricks in a one-minute run on a park course. Bicycle Racing Categories Every Fan Should Know One of the most popular bicycle racing categories , or sporting events, in the world is the Tour de France, which is a stage race over multiple days that tests a cyclist’s endurance and strategy. Cyclists have stages that they complete each day, with the Tour de France having 21 stages over three weeks. It has made stars out of past winners like Greg LeMond and Lance Armstrong, and is also a big betting event for fans. Speaking of betting, you can see BetUS Sportsbook odds to win the 2027 Tour de France. There is also a form of racing called criteriums, which are shorter races in both distance and time but are just as spectator- and betting-friendly. These are often on street courses like auto racing, with the cyclists going around a track and past spectators. You can also find road races that are held over street courses for longer distances. These can be held with a mass start (everyone all at once), or in individual time trials where cyclists start in staggered intervals. FAQs What are the different types of cycling? There are many different types of cycling, from road cycling, mountain biking, gravel cycling, BMX cycling, e-biking, and track cycling. Which type of cycle is best for racing? The type of cycle needed for racing depends on the type of racing being done. Track or road cycling is different from off-road or BMX racing. Each type of racing requires a different kind of bicycle. How is a gravel bike different from a mountain bike? A gravel bike is made to be a combination of a mountain bike and a road bike, so it has the look of a road bike but the features of a mountain bike as well. They have wider tires and a more relaxed frame to give more versatility than a straight mountain bike. items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News PET Cans vs Aluminium Cans: What Producers Should Know About Recyclability and Lightweighting Reading Time: 2 minutes PET Cans vs Aluminium Cans: What Producers Should Know About Recyclability and Lightweighting Understanding Beverage Container Evolution The beverage packaging industry continually seeks materials that balance structural integrity, consumer appeal, and environmental responsibility. Producers must evaluate various packaging formats to meet shifting regulatory demands and sustainability targets. Two prominent contenders in modern production lines are the traditional metal cylinder and the transparent polymer vessel. Understanding their distinct characteristics regarding material recovery and mass reduction helps brand owners make informed decisions for their product portfolios. The Mechanics of Lightweighting Lightweighting remains a primary strategy for reducing transport emissions and material consumption. Aluminium packaging has historically achieved significant mass reduction through advanced wall-ironing techniques, resulting in thin, rigid walls that withstand internal pressure. On the other hand, the PET can offers unique advantages in mass optimization because polymer distribution can be precisely controlled during the stretch blow molding process. This allows manufacturers to tailor wall thickness to specific product requirements, whether packaging still water or carbonated beverages. Recycling Infrastructure and Material Recovery End-of-life processing heavily influences the overall sustainability footprint of any packaging format. Metal recycling systems are globally mature, allowing aluminium to be melted down repeatedly without losing its core mechanical properties. Polymer recovery has also advanced significantly, with dedicated sorting facilities capable of processing clear and colored containers efficiently. Both materials fit into circular economy models, though the specific infrastructure varies by geographic region. Key Production Considerations When selecting between these two packaging formats, producers must analyze several operational factors: Filling line compatibility and conversion costs for existing equipment Barrier properties required to protect product shelf life against oxygen and light Consumer perception of touch, transparency, and tactile experience Supply chain resilience and raw material price volatility Balancing Sustainability Goals Ultimately, the choice between metal and polymer containers depends on specific brand priorities and distribution models. While metal provides permanent recyclability, polymers offer design versatility and complete product visibility. By carefully assessing lightweighting potential and local recovery streams, producers can optimize their packaging strategy for long-term operational success.
