items.descriptionOriginal: When people coined the proverb that “mighty oaks from little acorns grow”, they certainly weren’t thinking of Lyme disease. But literal acorns—not poetic metaphors—turn out to play a surprisingly big role in the spread of this mighty tick-borne illness, according to a recent paper in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences . A surge in acorns one year can translate into a boom two years later in the population of ticks that transmit the disease to people. This discovery illustrates the ways in which a web of tiny, interconnected things—acorns, mice, microbes—can have big and unexpected consequences for people. It also shows that it can take decades of scientific research to decipher the head-scratching complexity of ecosystems. The results are “helping us to inform management of tick-borne disease risk,” said Shannon LaDeau, one of the paper’s authors and an ecologist with the Cary Institute of Ecosystem Studies in New York State’s Hudson River Valley. LaDeau and colleague Richard Ostfeld oversee a Lyme-related research program at the institute that stretches back more than 30 years, just a few decades after the disease was first identified. Over that time, scientists have turned plots of New York forestland into an outdoor Lyme laboratory. They’ve assembled mountains of data tracking the ups and downs of a huge range of elements: temperature, rainfall, oak seedlings, mouse populations, tick numbers, infection rates, you name it. The results have repeatedly surprised scientists, defying expectations about the disease. It’s been known since the 1980s that the disease is caused by the bacteria Borrelia burgdorferi. The bite of an infected deer tick transmits the bacterium to people, causing flu-like symptoms that can escalate to chronic fatigue, memory loss, depression and even brain swelling and cardiac problems. More than 450,000 cases are reported in the U.S. each year, plus more than 200,000 in Europe. Despite the tick’s association with deer, the Cary Institute work didn’t bear out initial suspicions that more white-tailed deer translated into more dangers for people. The researchers found no correlation between deer numbers and the abundance of tick nymphs—the life stage when they most commonly transmit the disease to people. Lyme Disease: Prescribed fire Instead, the researchers uncovered evidence of a cascade of cause and effect between oak trees, white-footed mice and ticks. Acorns from red oak trees at the study sites are a primary food source for the mice. The year after a big acorn harvest, the mouse population boomed, the scientists found. The mice, in turn, are a prime feeding target for larval ticks which go on to become nymphs the following year. A big year for mice translated into a roughly 40% increase in abundance of tick nymphs the next year. All this thanks to a bumper crop in acorns two years earlier. While acorns aren’t abundant everywhere that the disease occurs, fluctuations in other crucial mouse food, such as seeds, could have the same effect, the scientists wrote. While it took years to tease apart these dynamics, researchers were still puzzled by other patterns. A surge in mice meant more ticks—and therefore a greater risk of people getting infected. But it didn’t translate into a higher percentage of the ticks themselves carrying the disease, the data showed. “It kept me up at night,” Ostfeld said of the result. “It meant that my understanding of how the system works was incomplete or wrong.” An apparent answer emerged when the researchers looked not just at the mouse population, but at a variety of small mammals. The long-term study plots were located in relatively intact forest that supported a range of other warm-blooded critters, such as skunks, squirrels and opossums. Many of these creatures are less prone to getting infected when a tick feeds on them, which also means they are less likely to spread the bacteria to other ticks. As a consequence, the percentage of infected ticks was driven not just by the number of mice but the population of a range of creatures. By contrast, in nearby places where forests had been broken into pieces by human intrusion , the diversity of small mammals was smaller. In those spots, where ticks had fewer options, higher mouse numbers did translate into more infected ticks. So in addition to small things like acorns, add two very big things that shape people’s risk of encountering Lyme disease: loss of habitat and of biodiversity. Ostfeld, et. al. “ The ecology of Lyme disease: Long-term data, surprises, and a synthesis .” Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences , Aug. 17, 2026. Image:© Theclarkester | Dreamstime.com

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News The Students Giving Tennis a Second Serve Reading Time: 4 minutes A student-run nonprofit born in Flower Mound, Texas, now keeps used tennis balls out of landfills in 16 states. A single tennis ball weighs about two ounces. That is easy to overlook, because nobody throws away just one. Since 2024, BallBack , a student-led nonprofit based in Flower Mound, Texas, has recycled or repurposed more than 160,000 of them. At roughly 58 grams apiece, that is about 9.3 metric tons of rubber and felt, a little over 20,000 pounds. Every one of those balls was headed for the trash. According to RecycleBalls, a tennis ball takes roughly 400 years to break down, slowly shedding microplastics into the surrounding soil. Curbside recycling programs do not accept them. The national picture is larger still. The United States discards an estimated 125 million tennis balls each year, or about 340,000 a day. By comparison, 160,000 balls is less than half a day of the country’s tennis ball waste. What makes BallBack interesting is not only its total so far, but how quickly a model built by high school students is spreading, and how easily it can be copied by anyone with a court, a school, and a car. BallBack began with Prem Kamasani, a varsity tennis player at Flower Mound High School. After practice one evening, he watched his coach getting ready to throw out roughly 400 used balls. He asked whether he could take them instead. “I noticed hundreds of balls going to the trash every week, and no one was doing anything about it,” Kamasani says on BallBack’s website. The balls went home with him. Some went to animal shelters as toys, and others ended up under school chairs. He then began calling local tennis centers to ask whether they had balls to give away as well. Most did. The collection outgrew his family’s garage, then several garages, and teammates joined in. A Lead4Change grant helped turn the school project into a national organization, spreading to over 310 members in 2026. The funding covered prepaid shipping, so courts anywhere in the country could send in their balls at no cost. Partnerships spread across Dallas–Fort Worth, from public facilities such as Kiest and Samuell Grand tennis centers to SMU’s college tennis program and the Flower Mound Animal Shelter. BallBack’s process is deliberately simple. A chapter leader places a free, branded collection bin at a partner facility, such as a tennis center, club, school, or homeowners’ association. Players drop off dead balls after practice instead of tossing them in the trash. Nobody on site has to sort or clean anything. Leaders monitor fill levels and stop by once or twice a month before anything overflows. Recycling bins at Samuell Grand Tennis Center in Dallas, one of BallBack’s partner facilities, let players drop off used tennis balls instead of throwing them away. Photo courtesy of BallBack . Sorting comes next, and it reflects the organization’s priorities. Balls that still bounce are never shredded. They go back into play through youth tennis programs and school teams that cannot afford new equipment, as well as other repurposing partners. Others go to dog shelters as enrichment toys, or to senior living communities, where they serve as walker feet. BallBack boxes only the balls with no play left in them, labels them with prepaid UPS shipping, and sends them to RecycleBalls or the USTA, BallBack’s national recycling partners. There, they separate the rubber and felt and grind them into crumb rubber that becomes new tennis court surfaces, playground padding, and footing for equestrian arenas. Through RecycleBalls and USTA, BallBack’s shipments help feed a North American collection network of roughly 10,000 locations. BallBack now runs with a national team of students recruited from across the country, each responsible for a distinct part of the work. The media team shapes how BallBack tells its story, from pickup-day footage to chapter spotlights. The marketing team carries that story to new schools, players, and facilities. The onboarding team brings each new chapter leader up to speed with step-by-step guides, so a student in Seattle or Fort Lauderdale can complete a first pickup within a week of signing up. Leaders trade questions and progress in a shared online community. This structure lets the network grow without relying on any one person. BallBack now counts 31 student chapter leaders across 16 states, more than 310 members, and over 55 partner facilities. Chapters operate in New York City, Philadelphia, Chicago, Portland, Seattle, Minneapolis, Folsom, and Green Bay, among other cities. In Manhattan, one senior ships roughly 750 balls a month. In Falls Church, Virginia, chapter leader Surya Arivumani has already recycled more than 1,200. BallBack is set up so that taking part does not depend on where you live. High school sophomores, juniors, and rising seniors in any U.S. city without an existing chapter can apply to start one at their local school. The commitment is one or two pickup trips a month, an hour or two each, for at least four months. Costs are close to zero, and leaders unlock $60 in credit after their first shipment. New chapter leaders are accepted every quarter. Tennis facilities near an existing chapter can list themselves as operating partners and receive free bins, pickups, and shipping. Facilities elsewhere can join as affiliate partners and ship their own boxes for free using prepaid FedEx labels. Individuals with a bag of old balls in the garage can also request a free shipping label, pack a box, and drop it off at FedEx. In Dallas–Fort Worth, anyone with 100 or more balls can arrange a free pickup. BallBack’s next milestone is a world record for the most tennis balls recycled in a single week. The plan is a coordinated national recycling week in spring of 2027. Chapter leaders, members, and partner facilities nationwide would collect, sort, and ship tennis balls at the same time. The effort is still being organized, as BallBack has yet to choose an adjudicator to set the rules for counting and verifying the balls. Whatever the final tally, the week is designed to do what no single chapter can: show what happens when hundreds of courts in dozens of cities choose to recycle at once. Long before BallBack, Kamasani’s father sent him to gather old balls from behind their neighborhood courts instead of buying new ones. Today, Kamasani mentors student leaders he’s never met in cities he’s never visited, who are doing the same thing on a national scale. In BallBack’s latest milestone update, he wrote that the 160,000 mark showed what “a bin by the fence and a student with a car” can accomplish. Students interested in starting a chapter, facilities that want to host a bin, and players with balls to donate can find details at ballback.org . The post The Students Giving Tennis a Second Serve appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Japanese Scientists Design a Plant-Based Plastic that can Become Fertilizer Reading Time: 3 minutes Researchers at Chiba University have developed a flexible, plant-based plastic that can be turned into crop fertilizer after use. Plant-based plastic often ends up in the same places as ordinary plastic, from landfills to incinerators. A research team in Japan wants to give it a more useful ending. What if a used plastic film could help grow the next crop? Associate Professor Daisuke Aoki of Chiba University led the study . Colleagues from the University of Tokyo and Tohoku University joined the work. They published their results in the journal Scientific Reports in August 2026. The need for new ideas is growing. Global plastic use reached 460 million metric tons in 2019, according to the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development. If current trends continue, it could climb to 1.2 billion metric tons by 2060. Recycling and waste-to-energy plants are struggling to keep pace with this growth. Aoki’s team took a different route by designing a plastic with its end-of-life already planned. The material starts with isosorbide, a nontoxic compound made from glucose. Glucose is a simple sugar that can come from plant starch, such as corn. Chemists link isosorbide units into a clear, hard plastic called poly(isosorbide carbonate). In 2021, Aoki and his students showed that warm ammonia water breaks down this plastic. The process splits it back into isosorbide and urea. Urea is one of the world’s most widely used nitrogen fertilizers. Aoki compared the goal to the Haber-Bosch process, which turned nitrogen from the air into fertilizer a century ago. His team hoped to turn plastic waste into food in a similar way. Their conversion also needed no costly metal catalysts. One problem remained. The original plastic was hard and brittle, stretching only about 4% before it snapped. That limited it to a narrow range of rigid products. Most plastics are softened with additives called plasticizers. Common ones, such as phthalates, do not break down into anything useful. Some also raise health concerns. The Chiba team designed a plasticizer for its plant-based plastic from the same building block. It has an isosorbide core linked to two short triethylene glycol chains, a common industrial chemical. Like the plastic, it breaks apart when treated with ammonia. With the new plasticizer, the material stretched about 45% before breaking, more than ten times as far as before. It also began to soften at about 40 degrees Celsius instead of 161 degrees, a sign of greater flexibility. Unlike a phthalate blend, the new mix stayed clear and uniform at every mixing ratio. The phthalate version turned cloudy, indicating its ingredients had separated. The team also made a longer-chain version of the plasticizer that stretched the plastic even further. It could be made at yields above 80%, versus under 25% for the first version. That makes it more practical to produce at scale. Converting the used plastic is simple. The team heated it in ammonia water at 90 degrees Celsius for 24 hours. The solid plastic dissolved completely into a clear liquid. That liquid held most of the original building blocks. The team recovered about 98% of the isosorbide, 78% of the possible urea, and 90% of the glycol. Some carbon escaped as carbon dioxide, and better conditions could raise the urea yield. Next came the most important test. The researchers used the liquid as fertilizer without any purification. They tried it on a common lab plant and on komatsuna, a leafy green often called Japanese mustard spinach. Over 36 days in a greenhouse, komatsuna grown with the recycled product matched plants fed commercial urea. Both groups grew far better than plants given no nitrogen. In the lab, the product performed at least as well as urea alone. Komatsuna grown with fertilizer from recycled plant-based plastic matched plants fed commercial urea. Photo courtesy of Scientific Reports . The authors are clear about the limits. Their plant-based plastic is not biodegradable, so it only becomes fertilizer after chemical treatment. Its strength is also not yet high enough for demanding uses. Other questions remain open. The team has not yet tested whether the plasticizer leaks out over time. They also have not measured the full energy cost and environmental footprint of the conversion process. Even so, the researchers see clear uses ahead. This plant-based plastic could be used for agricultural mulch films, seedling pots, shopping bags, and packaging. Farms could then turn used films and pots into fertilizer on site. Aoki believes plastics are at a turning point. He hopes people will one day see plastic waste as a valuable resource for growing food rather than trash. If that happens, plant-based plastic could complete a full circle. Plant-based material would return to the soil to feed new plants. The post Japanese Scientists Design a Plant-Based Plastic that can Become Fertilizer appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: Welcome back to our weekly behind-the-scenes glimpse at what’s getting our team talking. Tell us what you’ve been reading at info@reasonstobecheerful.world and we just might feature it here. Get smart Over the last decade, the rise of smartphones across the U.S. has coincided with a significant drop in kids’ performance at school. Now, as the New York Times reports in a story shared by Executive Editor Will Doig, a new study has found that school phone bans are leading to modest improvements. Published this week by the Center for Education Policy Research at Harvard, the study included 3.3 million students in third through tenth grade, comparing the math and reading test scores of students at schools with and without strict phone bans. Though the gains seen at the schools with phone bans were modest, they suggest that gradual improvement is underway. Will says: As a parent, there are so many reasons I’m in favor of banning phones at school, academics being just one of them. Still, it’s great to see data showing proof of concept on that aspect. Mapping roots In other phone-related news, there’s now an app that can help you find remarkable old trees. According to a Guardian article shared by Editorial Director Rebecca Worby, Ancient Trees offers a curated map of notable trees. “I thought it was quite a niche, geeky thing,” the app’s creator, Hidde Burgmans, told the Guardian, “but apparently more people are interested in ancient trees than I thought.” Becca says: On the one hand, using an app takes away the serendipity of just happening into a notable tree. On the other hand, I do like the idea of people detouring to see cool trees . What else we’re reading Minnesota announces ‘effective end’ to veteran homelessness, achieving decades-long goal — shared by Contributing Editor Michaela Haas from KSTP Free tool helps young men to take responsibility for sexual harm — shared by Contributing Editor Geetanjali Krishna from Positive News ‘Music is the most powerful way of connecting to what’s happening’: can this album change your mind about the climate crisis? — shared by Michaela Haas from the Guardian In other news… Turns out people love moss! Our Instagram video about how moss is taking over cities has really taken off. To learn more about all the cool things moss can do, read Michaela Haas’s great story. The post What We’re Reading: Phone Bans Are Improving Kids’ Test Scores appeared first on Reasons to be Cheerful .

Αυτό που την έφερε πίσω ήταν μια φράση από έναν μέντορα: μείνετε πιστή σε αυτό που πραγματικά ακούτε από μέσα. Αυτή η γραμμή την ακολουθεί σε κάθε δωμάτιο από τότε. Μεγάλωσε σε ένα…
items.descriptionOriginal: At fourteen, Shakhzoda Saidova slipped away from a conference table with the UN General Assembly and UNICEF in Tajikistan — too nervous, too convinced she didn't belong. What brought her back was a single sentence from a mentor: stay true to what you're actually hearing from inside. That line has followed her into every room since. She grew up in a country where her mother — who finished school with perfect marks and won a law scholarship — was forbidden by her husband's family from ever practicing as a lawyer. Watching that buried ambition became Shakhzoda's compass. Now studying in Romania, she is building SafeVoice: a disarmingly simple website listing real lawyers and crisis shelter numbers for women in Tajikistan facing domestic violence, because she knows what it costs a woman with three children and one free minute to find a page of dead links. She speaks five languages and is already being criticized for living in Europe at nineteen instead of being married. What's striking is the image of her mother, smiling serenely at those who disapprove — "Yes, I allowed that; yes, she's my daughter" — after accepting her daughter's diploma while the teenager boarded a flight towards a future she herself was never allowed to choose.

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Mycelium Leather at Mass-Production Scale Moves Closer to Reality Reading Time: 3 minutes Finnish researchers found a way to make mycelium leather at mass-production scale using papermaking methods. Mycelium leather at mass-production scale may be within reach, according to new research from VTT Technical Research Center of Finland. The team made leather-like sheets using a continuous process rather than slow-growing trays. The study appeared in ACS Applied Bio Materials in July 2026. Mycelium is the underground network of fibers below mushroom caps. Researchers see it as a promising animal-free material for bags, shoes, and clothing. The hard part has been making enough of it. Most mycelium materials grow in trays. Fungi spread across the tray until the fibers knit into one solid sheet. That works for small batches but cannot support mycelium leather at mass-production scale. The VTT team took a different path. They grew a fungus called Trichoderma reesei using submerged fermentation. That means the fungus grows in a nutrient-rich liquid inside a bioreactor. A bioreactor is a tank with controlled growing conditions. The result is a wet mycelium pulp. The researchers washed the pulp and mixed it with sorbitol and cellulose. Sorbitol is a sugar-based softener that keeps the sheet from becoming brittle. Cellulose is a plant fiber that adds strength. The formulas used nanofibrillated cellulose, which is cellulose broken into extremely fine fibers. Sorbitol acts as a plasticizer, an additive that makes materials more flexible. Together, they shape how the finished sheet feels and performs. The team then spread the mix into thin sheets and dried them. The result is a nonwoven fabric, meaning the fibers are bonded together rather than woven or knitted. The researchers could handle, cut, and sew it much like a regular textile. Strength matters for any leather substitute. Tests showed tensile strength of 11 to 19 megapascals (MPa), depending on how the mycelium was pretreated. That number measures how much pulling force a material handles before it breaks. The sheets also stretched about 9% to 10% before fracturing. That flexibility matters for products like bags and shoes, which bend and flex every day. Scale was the real test. The team adapted a roller system similar to those used in paper manufacturing. It produced continuous sheets about 8 inches wide and 26 feet long. That is roughly the width of a letter-size page and the length of a large moving truck. The team used a roll-to-roll pilot line and a wet-casting process. Wet casting means spreading liquid pulp into a thin layer that dries into a sheet. It is still a pilot run. But it shows that mycelium leather at mass-production scale can move past small lab samples. Researchers in Finland used liquid fermentation and a roller line to bring mycelium leather at mass-production scale closer to reality. Photo by Cottonbro Studio on Pexels. Using familiar equipment could matter as much as the material itself. Manufacturers might not need to build entirely new production lines from scratch. That could lower the cost and risk of trying a new material. Co-author Manuel Arias-Barrantes said the work solves a major bottleneck in large-scale, affordable production. He noted that scalable options remain limited today. The pulp approach also gives researchers more control over the final material. They can adjust its properties, add color and texture, or layer it onto cotton fabric. The recipe is easy to change, opening the door to different products. The researchers sewed a prototype accessory bag from black-dyed mycelium fabric. It shows the material can take color and hold stitching. That is a practical first step toward real products. Why does this matter for shoppers? Many vegan leathers are made from petroleum-based plastics that are difficult to recycle. Animal leather also has environmental costs, including livestock and chemical processing. Géza Szilvay of VTT said the process uses renewable feedstocks and mild conditions. It involves no livestock and no chemically intensive steps. He believes the concept could become a viable alternative to non-renewable synthetic leathers, and scaling mycelium leather to mass production is central to that goal. Researchers describe the finished fabric as compostable. That could give it an advantage over plastic-based options at the end of a product’s life. It also supports a wider shift toward materials made from renewable sources. See also: Converting Kombucha to Green Textiles for Sustainable Fashion Questions remain. Mycelium materials still need further development to meet the demands of tough, everyday uses. Long-term durability and cost at factory volume will need testing. Mycelium is not the only plant-based option under study. Brands are also exploring leathers made from cactus and pineapple leaves. Several clothing companies already use pineapple leaf material in garments. Still, the study offers a clear path forward. A handbag grown in a tank and dried on a roller line no longer sounds far-fetched. If later tests hold up, mycelium leather at mass-production scale could give brands a renewable option made with familiar equipment. The post Mycelium Leather at Mass-Production Scale Moves Closer to Reality appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: This year’s Nature Photographer of the Year competition received 27,108 entries from photographers in more than 96 countries — and the overall winner, announced Nov. 14, stands out in more ways than one. Titled “The One That Left and the One That Stayed,” Hannu Ahonen’s shot of a water lily leaf beside a mirror-image frozen replica is stunning in its own right, but it’s also a “rare” example of a plant photo winning the annual contest, according to the chair of the judging panel, Theo Bosboom. “It is not often that a photograph of a plant is crowned the overall winner of a major photography competition, but the jury could not overlook this fascinating image by Hannu Ahonen,” Bosboom said in a press release shared with Nice News. “First and foremost, the photograph captures a unique situation: a water lily leaf with an almost perfect black-and-white replica of it lying next to it in the water.” He continued, “It takes a moment for the viewer to realize what has happened here: A thin layer of ice that had formed on the leaf has been blown away by the wind. The shapes in the sheet of ice are delicate; even the veins of the water lily leaf are clearly recognizable. Because the water lily and the sheet of ice are still touching, a sense of connection emerges; you realize that they belong together, like yin and yang.” In addition to being named overall winner, the Finnish photographer took the top spot in the Plants and Fungi category. Scroll on to see the other category winners and read commentary from the judging panel on each one. Birds: “Painting From the End of the World” by Lucas Mugnier-Lavorel (France) Lucas Mugnier-Lavorel / NPOTY 2026 “Environmental portraits of wildlife can make us feel closer to the animals despite being farther away from them, when done right. This image of a Magellanic woodpecker in its gorgeous habitat was a perfect example. It stood out from thousands of submissions because of its understated sense of place, beauty, simplicity, and timing. Diagonal lines formed by several trees guide the eyes to discover the bird — expertly framed against the backdrop and placed off-center — while encouraging exploration of the forest and the Patagonian landscape beyond it. Overall, it was a very successful reminder of how the portrayal of nature in its literal state can still be the most powerful of photographic expressions.” – Jury member Steffen Foerster Mammals: “Play Misty” by Paul Goldstein (U.K.) Paul Goldstein / NPOTY 2026 “Quiet images can be easy to overlook in the fiercely competitive mammal category, one of the largest in NPOTY. This ethereal image of a giraffe peeking out of the mist revealed its strengths gradually. Initially a little disorienting, it offered just enough of a visual puzzle to keep the viewer engaged until the image resolved. The soft pastel colors create a soothing atmosphere, while the image’s simplicity and quiet emotion ultimately made it stand out among the category’s strongest contenders.” – Jury member Steffen Foerster Other Animals: “The Pitcher’s Micro Kingdom” by Marcus Kuan (Singapore) Marcus Kuan / NPOTY 2026 “The lighting, colors, and unexpected gathering of species immediately caught our attention. Kuan beautifully captured a world where crustaceans, amphibians, and carnivorous plants cross paths. As judges, we were drawn to the possibilities unfolding within this single frame. Could the pitchers be digesting invertebrates? Might the frog be exploring a potential egg-laying site, while the crab continues its daily search for food among the plants? The image invites us to imagine the separate lives of these organisms, briefly brought together. The carefully balanced composition, beautifully controlled lighting, and rich greens and reds against the dark nighttime background make this a striking photograph.” – Jury member Louis Guillot Landscape: “In the Circle of Vultures Around the Falls” by J Fritz Rumpf (U.S.) J Fritz Rumpf / NPOTY 2026 “What immediately caught our attention was the incredible light and atmosphere in this photo. The longer we looked, the more fascinating it became. There is so much to discover: the last light of day illuminating the mist rising from Iguazú Falls, the silhouettes of trees and rocks, the birds circling above, the sunlight streaming through an opening in the rock at the center, and the subtle waterfall on the left. The interplay of light and shadow transforms the immense power of the waterfalls into something intimate and almost dreamlike. A beautiful example of how an iconic natural wonder can be captured in a truly extraordinary way.” – Jury member Ilse Koks Underwater: “Beneath Aquatic Constellations” by Matt Pérez (U.S.) Matt Pérez / NPOTY 2026 “Pérez’s photograph immediately drew us in. As a jury, we wanted to linger over it, exploring the details and wondering what we were seeing. Newt egg masses decorate the submerged branches like baubles on a Christmas tree, framing the scene and guiding our eyes towards the pond turtle with its piercing yellow eyes.The scene feels almost otherworldly, busy with intricate details yet still peaceful to look at — an impressive balance to capture in a single photograph. Its beautiful composition, striking lighting, and balance of rich detail and serene feel made this photo stand out to the jury. Matt Pérez also deserves credit for stepping back from the turtles’ courtship behavior to capture this wider view of a male pond turtle within an extraordinary habitat.” – Jury member Louis Guillot Nature Art: “Peach Blossoms in the Snow” by Xuzhong Liu (China) Xuzhong Liu / NPOTY 2026 “This photograph has everything that can make a drone shot interesting and fascinating. First and foremost, there are beautiful shapes and subtle colors, but there is also a sense of alienation. What am I actually looking at, and what is the scale of the landscape in the photograph? The image was taken in September in a wetland area in China, but it reminded the photographer himself of peach blossoms he had previously photographed during a spring trip to Tibet. A good abstract photograph like this also leaves plenty of room for the viewer to decide for themselves what they see in it. This makes it the perfect winner of the nature art category.” – Judging panel chair Theo Bosboom Human and Nature: “Evolution” by Petr Bambousek (Czechia) Petr Bambousek / NPOTY 2026 “The winning image stood out for its striking depiction of the impact human activity has on local wildlife. The sleeping Malayan sun bear inside a garbage incinerator creates a powerful visual contrast, showing how habitat loss and human waste increasingly force wild animals into close contact with human environments. The image is both unexpected and unsettling, capturing a broader story of how wildlife is forced to adapt as its natural surroundings are altered and destroyed.” – Jury member Lana Tannir Black and White: “Storm on the Sea” by László Tóth (Hungary) László Tóth / NPOTY 2026 “This photo really stood out to us. At first, we were not quite sure what we were looking at. It sparked some wonderful discussions among the jury and made us look even closer. The black-and-white contrast, dark diagonal lines, and striking patterns create a fascinating abstract composition. It looks like a storm at sea, but in reality, it is a thin layer of snow shaped by strong winds on a frozen lake, captured from above.” – Jury member Ilse Koks Animal Portraits: “A Seal’s Worst Nightmare” by Audun Rikardsen (Norway) Audun Rikardsen / NPOTY 2026 “Just when we thought we had seen about every kind of polar bear image there is, along comes this shot taken from inside a hole in the ice looking up at the bear. Once you realize what is happening, you start thinking about how this shot could possibly have been taken. Then it dawns on you that it seems almost impossible, no matter how. Showing something never seen before is a pretty effective method of captivating an audience, and one that carried this image all the way to the top. With oceans warming and ice melting, the ‘What’s going on down there?’ look gives the image a deeper layer of meaning that I appreciate. Right now humanity is looking back up at the bear and shrugging its collective shoulders in pretense. For how much longer?” – Jury member Steffen Foerster Nature of “De Lage Landen”: “Fairies” by Enikő Kálovics (Hungary) Enikő Kálovics / NPOTY 2026 “The winning image stood out for its ability to transform a familiar landscape into something dreamlike and unexpected. The combination of the tiny lacewings, the autumn forest, and the purplish night sky creates a delicate, atmospheric interpretation of the nature of ‘De Lage Landen.’ The thoughtful use of double exposure adds another layer to the image, capturing not just the insects themselves, but also the sense of wonder and atmosphere of their natural habitat.” – Jury member Lana Tannir Fred Hazelhoff Award, Portfolio: “Eagle Owls in the City” by Simone Baumeister (Germany) Simone Baumeister / NPOTY 2026 “In the portfolio category, the bar is set considerably higher for participating photographers than in the individual categories. Whilst a single fantastic photograph is sufficient there, in the portfolio category you need a whole series of outstanding images that not only complement one another but also fit together well in terms of style and theme. Simone Baumeister has succeeded brilliantly in this with her portfolio on eagle owls in the city. It is clear that she has put a great deal of time into creating the series: She has managed to capture all sorts of special moments with her camera, and the series showcases a wide range of situations, locations, and atmospheres. In doing so, she offers a unique glimpse into the world of a bird that is making a comeback in Germany and which, despite its size, often goes unnoticed by the people around it. Or, as the photographer herself puts it, her images make the invisible visible. And that is one of the great strengths of (nature) photography!” – Judging panel chair Theo Bosboom Youth Photographer of the Year: “Tree of Life” by Parham Pourahmad (U.S.) Parham Pourahmad / NPOTY 2026 “In ‘Tree of Life,’ Pourahmad captured a striking scene that could comfortably hold its own in the adult categories. Black and white was an excellent choice, defining the coyote’s silhouette and revealing the majestic oak’s intricate network of branches. Even within this wider scene, the coyote’s downward gaze is clear. Pourahmad explained that it was searching for rodent prey, a small detail that brings the photograph to life. The image combines a beautiful portrait of the animal’s habitat with an intimate glimpse of its hunting behavior.” – Jury member Louis Guillot

items.title: Η μείωση του αριθμού των αστέγων στις ΗΠΑ σημειώνει την πιο απότομη πτώση του ενός έτους της τελευταίας δεκαετίας
items.titleOriginal: US homelessness decline hits its steepest one-year drop in a decade
items.description: ΑΠΟ ΤΗΝ ΚΑΘΗΜΕΡΙΝΗ ΣΥΝΤΑΚΤΙΚΗ ΟΜΑΔΑ ΟΠΤΙΜΙΣΤΩΝ Οι άστεγοι στις Ηνωμένες Πολιτείες μειώθηκαν κατά περισσότερο από έξι τοις εκατό το 2025, η πιο απότομη μείωση των αστέγων σε διάστημα ενός έτους σε περισσότερο από μια δεκαετία, η οποία οδηγεί σε περίπου 49.000 λιγότερους ανθρώπους χωρίς στέγη. Ήταν η δεύτερη συνεχόμενη ετήσια πτώση μετά από μια μικρότερη πτώση το 2024 και σπάει μια σειρά αυξήσεων που είχε…
items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM Homelessness in the United States fell by more than six percent in 2025, the steepest one-year homelessness decline in more than a decade, which works out to roughly 49,000 fewer people without housing. It was the second straight annual drop after a smaller dip in 2024, and it breaks a run of increases that had pushed the homeless population to record levels. The numbers come from the annual count conducted in communities nationwide. The Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) announced the results ahead of its detailed report, and a separate analysis of the same count , commissioned by the National Alliance to End Homelessness, found a similar decline. However, the two part ways on the question of why. Where the homelessness decline showed up Veterans and the long view The clearest long-term gains are among veterans. Homelessness among U.S. veterans dropped more than seven percent last year and is down nearly 60 percent since 2010. Ann Oliva, CEO of the alliance, ties that record to programs that move people off the street and into housing without preconditions. “Investments in programs like that are much closer to the scale of need for veterans than for any other population experiencing homelessness,” she said. Four big cities and two disaster zones A large share of the drop is concentrated in a handful of places. New York, Chicago, Boston and Denver all saw large numbers of asylum seekers arrive at their shelters during the Biden administration, and according to Devon Kurtz, public safety policy director at the Cicero Institute, a think tank aligned with the administration on homelessness policy, those cities now account for about half of the most recent decline. “That’s also the four cities that have driven half of the drop most recently,” he said. Kurtz also pointed to San Francisco, which is moving toward more sober-living housing that prohibits drugs and alcohol. Numbers also fell in western North Carolina and Hawaii, both hit by major weather disasters. When HUD and other agencies arrive to help displaced residents, people who were already unhoused often receive assistance they had not been getting before. Rents easing in some markets Oliva described the decline as broad and likely the result of several forces at once, including softer rental markets in parts of the country. Rents remain high, but they have come down from their pandemic peaks, which could slow the number of people losing housing for the first time. Competing explanations for falling homelessness The administration credits enforcement and recovery HUD Secretary Scott Turner attributed the decline to the administration’s broader agenda. HUD also cited stepped-up enforcement against encampments following the 2024 Supreme Court ruling that allowed cities to ban sleeping and camping in public places. The administration argues that the long-standing federal approach of placing people in permanent housing first and offering voluntary treatment afterward has failed, and it blames that approach for the rise in homelessness during the pandemic. Requiring residents to stay drug-free, it says, helps more people reach recovery. HUD wants to redirect several billion dollars in homelessness funding toward short-term housing paired with mandatory addiction and mental health treatment, a plan courts have blocked so far. Advocates credit housing programs The alliance reads the same data differently. “It’s good news that more people are getting housed, and that the programs that are funded by Congress are working,” Oliva said. She argued that housing-first programs were a major driver of the decline, particularly for veterans , and said the analysis her group commissioned found that cities with camping bans performed worse than the national average. Critics of drug-free housing requirements add that relapse is common, and that such rules can push people back onto the street when it happens. The work still ahead Chronic homelessness moved the other way Both analyses agree that nearly 700,000 people in the U.S. are still living in shelters or on the streets, well above pre-pandemic levels. One group also bucked the trend: people who have been homeless for a long time saw a small increase last year, even as most other groups declined. Oliva said this population, which is more likely to live with mental illness and addiction , needs more permanent housing, while the administration is pushing for treatment-linked short-term options. With HUD’s funding overhaul still tied up in court, the next annual count will show whether the homelessness decline holds, and how far either approach can reach the people who have been without a home the longest. items.title: Η April Surac κατασκεύασε το NeuraSensa ώστε η τέχνη να προσαρμόζεται στους ανθρώπους που το χρησιμοποιούν
items.titleOriginal: April Surac built NeuraSensa so art adapts to the people using it
items.description: ΑΠΟ ΤΗΝ ΚΑΘΗΜΕΡΙΝΗ ΣΥΝΤΑΚΤΙΚΗ ΟΜΑΔΑ OPTIMIST Αυτό το άρθρο είναι μέρος της σειράς Local Changemakers 2026 του The Optimist Daily, δίνοντας έμφαση στους δημιουργούς αλλαγής 30 ετών και κάτω. Οι περισσότεροι δημόσιοι χώροι είναι κατασκευασμένοι για έναν μέσο επισκέπτη που δεν υπάρχει. Ο φωτισμός, ο θόρυβος, οι υφές κάτω από τα πόδια και ο ρυθμός ενός δωματίου προϋποθέτουν ένα συγκεκριμένο είδος σώματος και εγκεφάλου, και ούτως ή άλλως…
items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM This article is part of The Optimist Daily’s Local Changemakers 2026 series, spotlighting changemakers 30 and under. Most public spaces are built for an average visitor who doesn’t exist. The lighting, the noise, the textures underfoot, and the pace of a room all assume a certain kind of body and brain, and anyone who takes in the world differently is left to manage on their own. April Surac, a Florida teenager and the founder of NeuraSensa , has spent the past two years making the opposite: art that changes in response to whoever is standing in front of it. How NeuraSensa began in a furniture workshop Textures, materials and a younger sister April grew up in her family’s furniture workshop, where she learned early that materials follow their own logic and that a texture one person finds soothing can be unbearable to someone else. She also grew up with a younger sister who has autism , and that taught her something before she had words for it: the designed world fits some nervous systems far better than others. Paul Moore, who nominated April for this series and has followed the project since the beginning, sees both influences running through everything she makes. “April is one of those students whose work has grown directly out of something deeply personal to her,” he said. April founded NeuraSensa in June 2024, and she has summed up its guiding idea in a single sentence: “I believe design should adapt to people, not the other way around.” NeuraSensa’s responsive textile installations Art that reacts to touch, motion, light and sound The installations layer fabric with embedded sensors, so surfaces shift under a visitor’s hand and the light and sound in the room change as people move through it. For someone whose senses register the world at a different intensity, a space that responds instead of making fixed demands can decide whether they stay or leave. NeuraSensa designs this work for autistic people and others with sensory or cognitive differences, including people living with dementia. The installations have reached more than 15,000 people through gallery exhibitions and community events, with shows at SOBO Windermere Art Gallery and CityArts Orlando. NeuraSensa has also run workshops with organizations such as United Cerebral Palsy of Central Florida and the Brevard Achievement Center , where participants work hands-on with April’s sensory-friendly pieces. Sensory kits for homes, classrooms and hospitals Outside the gallery, NeuraSensa’s Sponsor-a-Kit program has distributed more than 250 therapeutic kits to families, educators, hospitals and disability-serving organizations, putting sensory support tools into places that rarely have them. April also organized a community drive that delivered more than $3,000 worth of tactile toys to Nemours Children’s Hospital in Orlando. Much of this runs on her own resources. She funds NeuraSensa through personal savings, grants, and fundraising, and Moore has watched how much that asks of her. “I have seen firsthand how much of her own time, savings, grant funding and effort she puts into making each project possible,” he said. A young changemaker’s growing recognition The Barron Prize and a TEDx stage In 2025, April was one of 15 top winners of the Gloria Barron Prize for Young Heroes , each of whom receives $10,000 toward their work or education. That same year, she was named a Daily Point of Light honoree by the Points of Light organization, and she has since been nominated for the KidsRights international award and published research through Figshare. According to Moore, she gave a TED-Ed Talk in October titled “ What’s Next: Designing Technology for Every Nervous System ,” which he said she developed with mentorship from a Nobel laureate in neuroscience. “I’ve loved seeing her share each stage of that journey with me, and watching an idea close to her heart grow into work that has now supported thousands of people in our community,” Moore wrote. Sensory-inclusive design beyond compliance From retrofits to spaces built for everyone For a long time, making public space accessible meant meeting minimum requirements after a building or exhibit was already finished. The conversation around neurodivergence in art and public life has moved toward design justice, the principle that spaces should be planned from the start for the full range of human experience instead of patched later for people who fall outside a narrow norm. NeuraSensa sits where art practice and disability advocacy overlap, and April has not waited for museums or city planners to adopt that principle before acting on it. The next phase reaches well past Central Florida. April is developing commissions for galleries in New York City, Los Angeles and London, along with textile-based systems for large installations and wearable sensory tools, designs she is moving toward patent protection. Moore says he is “incredibly proud of how she keeps learning, expanding the project and finding new ways to use her talents in service of others,” and the scale of what she’s attempting suggests the lesson from her family’s workshop has traveled a long way: a room can be built to meet the person who walks into it, wherever that room turns out to be. You can follow her work on NeuraSensa’s Instagram . Did this solution stand out? Share it with a friend or support our mission by becoming an Emissary . items.title: Feel-Good τηλεοπτικά αγαπημένα: 30 σειρές ροής που θα φωτίσουν την ημέρα σας
items.titleOriginal: Feel-Good TV Favorites: 30 Streaming Shows That’ll Brighten Your Day
items.description: Ποια είναι η συνταγή για μια καλή τηλεοπτική εκπομπή; Για κάποιους, είναι ένας συνδυασμός ρομαντισμού και χιούμορ. Για άλλους, είναι μια νοσταλγική ιστορία με συγγενείς χαρακτήρες. Και μερικές φορές συμβαίνει ακριβώς το αντίθετο: ριάλιτι απόδρασης που σε μεταφέρει κάπου μακριά. Ευτυχώς, οι ενθουσιώδεις ιστορίες όλων των ειδών είναι διαθέσιμες για ροή όλες τις ώρες της ημέρας (και της νύχτας).…
items.descriptionOriginal: What’s the recipe for a feel-good TV show? For some, it’s a mix of romance and humor. For others, it’s a nostalgic storyline with relatable characters. And sometimes it’s just the opposite: escapism reality TV that transports you somewhere far away. Luckily, uplifting stories of all kinds are available to stream at all hours of the day (and night). From comedies and coming-of-age-stories to heartwarming reality series, these shows can help you feel a little better about the world. So, make yourself a cup of tea and cozy up on the couch — a heartwarming streaming session awaits! A Man on the Inside | Netflix This is perhaps the most wholesome whodunit you’ll ever watch. In Season One, retired professor Charles (Ted Danson) goes undercover at a retirement community to investigate the theft of a family heirloom. The next season, he takes on a new case at a college campus where he meets Mona, played by Danson’s real-life wife of over 30 years, Mary Steenburgen. We’re excited to see what’s in store for Season Three, which, alas, will be this endearing tale’s final chapter . Abbott Elementary | Hulu This hilarious mockumentary series follows teachers (and an outrageous principal) at a Philadelphia public school who go above and beyond to help their students succeed, despite the hurdles the faculty encounters both in and out of the classroom. Fun fact: Abbott Elementary is named after Joyce Abbott , a real sixth-grade teacher who taught creator and star Quinta Brunson at Andrew Hamilton School in Philadelphia. All Creatures Great and Small | PBS and Prime Video All Creatures Great and Small is based on author and veterinarian James Herriot’s beloved memoirs about his years treating animals in rural Yorkshire beginning in the 1930s. The British series is so peaceful that all six seasons feel like taking a breath of fresh air (the seventh premieres in the U.S. in January 2027). Black-ish | Hulu This Emmy-winning comedy is heartwarming, family-centered, and will keep you laughing. Follow the beloved Johnsons for eight seasons as they navigate highs, lows, and life changes together. Choir | Disney+ Meet the inspiring kids who make up the Detroit Youth Choir (of America’s Got Talent fame ) in this moving Disney+ docuseries. Over six episodes, you’ll find yourself cheering on all of the talented singers as they pursue their dreams and prepare for “the performance of a lifetime”: taking the stage at Carnegie Hall in New York City. Derry Girls | Netflix Witty and wonderful, Derry Girls is a British teen sitcom that follows a tight-knit group of friends during “ The Troubles ” in Ireland. It’s a beautiful example of the power of embracing humor amid hardships, without glossing over truths. English Teacher | Hulu English Teacher is another warmhearted, witty comedy set in the classroom, and often the faculty lounge and principal’s office as well. You’ll follow a group of offbeat high school teachers in Austin, Texas, as they navigate everything from a chaotic camping trip to AI-powered trash cans. The show boasts a rating of 94% on Rotten Tomatoes, and our only complaint is that the episodes, which run just over 20 minutes, aren’t longer — because the characters are endlessly fun to be around. Extraordinary Attorney Woo | Netflix South Korean series Extraordinary Attorney Woo follows a young lawyer who is on the autism spectrum as she navigates everyday interactions in her unique and authentic way. The show, which is dubbed in English, has a 93% audience score on Rotten Tomatoes and was the most-viewed title on Netflix for a week . Gilmore Girls | Hulu For a dose of mother-daughter love, Gilmore Girls offers seven seasons (and a four-part reunion series) of feel-good content. The young mom and her teenage daughter — played by Lauren Graham and Alexis Bledel, respectively — talk fast, drink a lot of coffee, and lean on each other through family drama, job changes, and romantic ups and downs. Hart of Dixie | HBO Max If you’re a fan of Gilmore Girls , this wholesome show will be right up your alley. Rachel Bilson stars as Zoe Hart, a doctor from New York City who inherits half of a family practice in the small, fictional town of Bluebell, Alabama: a perfectly cozy community where neighbors support each other, get tangled up in romance, and attend many a quirky festival. Home for Christmas | Netflix The first season of this Norwegian show follows Johanne, a 30-year-old single nurse, as she gives herself 24 days to find a boyfriend to bring home for Christmas. Three seasons later, the show (always set during the holidays) remains full of tender moments about navigating romance, independence, and family expectations. Is It Cake? | Netflix The premise is super simple and super silly: Contestants bake elaborate cakes that look like everyday items, including purses, paintings, and rubber ducks. The desserts are then placed next to the real objects they resemble, and guest judges have to guess which one is the cake. It’s fun to play along, though it’s delightfully tricky! Love on the Spectrum U.S. | Netflix There are plenty of reality shows about finding love, but Love on the Spectrum stands out — not only because its stars are neurodivergent but also because it possesses a warmth and hopefulness that make you truly root for the cast as they seek meaningful relationships. The U.S. version is a spinoff of the Australian series , and both are available to stream on Netflix. North of North | Netflix If you need a reminder that good things can come during uncertain times, this show fits the bill. Set in the tiny, fictional Arctic community of Ice Cove, North of North follows a young Inuk mother as she embarks on a new chapter after leaving her marriage. Viewers follow along with her highs and lows as she tries to get a handle on dating and building a career, while breaking down traditional gender expectations. Psych | Prime Video and Peacock Watch a quick-witted and perceptive police consultant (played by James Roday Rodriguez) solve cases using the power of observation — and the help of his reluctant BFF (played by Dulé Hill). The eight-season show combines comedy, drama, and detective work, all the while highlighting the infectious friendship between the two main characters. Tip: Keep an eye out for pineapples ! Queer Eye | Netflix The “Fab Five” gives emotional makeovers to ordinary folks across the country. But they don’t focus on appearance alone: The team explores the powerful connection between how we look, how we treat ourselves, and how we interact with the world — a reminder we can all use. Schitt’s Creek | Hulu Riches-to-rags is the premise of Schitt’s Creek : a series about a wealthy family who loses all their money and moves into a motel in a (very) small town. Laugh-out-loud moments, endearing friendships, and perfectly quotable one-liners earned this rewatchable, lighthearted show an Emmy for outstanding comedy in 2020. Shrinking | Apple TV On paper, Shrinking doesn’t sound particularly feel-good — it follows a father (played by Jason Segel) navigating parenthood and his career as a therapist following his wife’s sudden death. However, the show portrays grief through a lens that’s undeniably uplifting. It’s impossible not to fall in love with the nosy neighbors and hilarious coworkers, especially Paul, the lovably gruff mentor played by Harrison Ford (who earned his first Emmy nomination for the role at age 83). Sister, Sister | Paramount Plus A ’90s classic, Sister, Sister — starring twins Tia and Tamera Mowry — is still a joy to watch decades after it originally aired. Equally heart-filling and funny, the six-season series captures the magic of sisterhood and the positive impact of supportive family units. Somebody Feed Phil | Netflix There are many foodie travel shows out there, but this one has Phil Rosenthal. The creator of Everybody Loves Raymond supplies just the right amount of wholesome dad jokes as he tries local cuisine in Kyoto, Copenhagen, and Cape Town, among dozens of other cities around the world. All eight seasons are packed with enticing eats and conversations, but we’re partial to the first two, which include scenes of Rosenthal video chatting with his mom and dad before they passed away in 2019 and 2021, respectively. Somebody Somewhere | Prime Video Described as “a totally platonic love story” by HBO, Somebody Somewhere is about two coworkers (played by Bridget Everett and Jeff Hiller) who become dear friends. Audiences watch as they develop the sweetest bond that’s filled with lots of laughs and good vibes. “I hope that people come away with ‘never give up on yourself,’ because a lot of people do,” said Everett. St. Denis Medical | Peacock and Netflix Think of this as a hospital-centered version of The Office (another comfort TV favorite). This sitcom chronicles the day-to-day lives of nurses and surgeons as they navigate wacky medical scenarios and even wackier workplace dynamics. But we’d be remiss not to mention that there’s plenty of heart among the staff, who lean on each other as they care for patients. Stick | Apple TV A love letter to golf, Stick follows a former pro golfer seeking redemption by mentoring a teen prodigy who has his own complicated relationship with the game. The soun d track is stacked with hits, and you’ll never listen to “Cecilia” by Simon & Garfunkel the same way again. Survivor | Netflix (Select Seasons) and Paramount Plus (All Seasons) A show that just keeps on giving, Survivor has delivered over 50 seasons of real-life drama about “castaways” competing for a prize of $1 million. While the concept has remained mostly the same for more than two decades, every season delivers new personalities and social dynamics. Ted Lasso | Apple TV The epitome of comfort TV, Ted Lasso centers on an American football coach (Jason Sudeikis) who is hired to manage a British soccer team. Even if you’re not a sports fan, this four-season series is so charming and rich with wholesome humor that makes it a feel-good favorite for everyone. Tex Mex Motors | Netflix Watch old junkyard cars from Mexico get radically restored in Texas, thanks to a talented team of experts on Tex Mex Motors . While the car transformations are fun to watch (and very impressive), the restoration pros are the real stars of the show. The Dog House | HBO Max and Hulu ​If you haven’t watched The Dog House yet, you’re in for a treat. The unscripted show follows staff at a British animal rescue charity as they match pups with new pet parents. It’s a joy watching people light up when they fall in love with their new best friend — and of course, seeing the pups fall in love with their new best friends, too. The Durrells in Corfu | PBS and Prime Video The Durrells in Corfu is a British series based on memoirs about a family who left England for Greece in the 1930s. Not only is the story full of wit and heart, but it’s also set in the dreamiest of settings. And after you watch the show’s four seasons, we recommend checking out this documentary about the real Durrells . The Great British Baking Show | Netflix Of all the comfort shows streaming lately, The Great British Baking Show (titled The Great British Bake Off in the U.K.) takes the cake — pun intended. Each week, contestants bake all kinds of mouthwatering treats in hopes of making it to the finale, where one talented baker earns the coveted cake stand and is crowned winner. But unlike so many other competition shows that can feel cutthroat, the judges offer kind, constructive feedback, and the contestants often help one another finish their creations. You can stream most seasons on Netflix, including the most recent with new judge Nigella Lawson, a star addition as far as the Nice News team is concerned. Younger | Netflix In Younger , Liza, a 40-year-old mom (played by Sutton Foster), pretends to be in her 20s to land an entry-level assistant job at a publishing house in New York alongside Kelsey (played by Hilary Duff). A love triangle, book deals, and many stories of female friendship ensue over seven seasons of lighthearted TV. Highly recommend for fans of Lizzie McGuire . A version of this article was originally published in July 2023.

items.descriptionOriginal: In the last couple of decades, many companies have reduced the heft of plastic bottles , cardboard boxes, paper envelopes, and other packaging materials, a strategy known as lightweighting. At first glance, this seems like a win-win: less material means lower costs and a lighter burden on the environment. But the approach may also backfire, a new study suggests. Researchers found that people are more likely to throw lightweight packaging away, and less likely to recycle it, compared to more substantial packaging materials. “Even well-intended sustainability practices can have unexpected negative consequences,” the researchers write. First, the researchers set out to determine the scope of the problem. A small pilot study at a university campus event and a larger week-long audit of trash and recycling bins on campus showed that lighter-weight recyclable plastic beverage containers were more likely to end up in the trash compared to more substantial plastic cups and bottles. “Once low-density packaging gets into consumers’ hands, it produces more waste, as consumers are more likely to improperly trash low-density versus high-density recyclable packaging,” the researchers write. Investigating causal relationships, the researchers concocted a laboratory study in which participants were asked to assess the properties of a piece of paper—either flimsy newsprint or sturdy cardstock—which they were instructed to dispose of at the end of the experiment. As expected, participants rated the thinner paper as lower quality than the thicker paper and were more likely to throw it in the trash at the end of the experiment—although a statistical analysis people get from recycling has a downside More details about the nuances of people’s thought processes emerged from an online experiment in which participants imagined receiving a takeout meal in either a thin paper bakery bag or a thick paper grocery bag. “Where would you put this bag?” they were asked. The participants then rated the quality of the bag, assessed its value, and indicated their level of discomfort about putting the bag in the garbage. “Ultimately, we find that consumers are more apt to throw low-density packaging in the trash because it is perceived as being more disposable (i.e., lower in value and associated with lesser feelings of waste aversion),” the researchers write. So far, so hopeless, given the human foibles and imperfect decision-making. But the solution could be a relatively simple one, according to the new work. In both an online study and a small field trial, the researchers found evidence that including a message on lightweight packaging—for example, “You may be done with this envelope, but it still has value”—increased the likelihood that the material would make it to the recycling bin. “Prompting consumers to reconsider the value of low-density packaging can curtail this unintended wastefulness,” the researchers write. Issuing such prompts is in companies’ own best interests, the researchers point out. In addition to lightweighting, many firms aim to increase the proportion of recycled material in their packaging. And where is that recycled material going to come from if consumers have thrown the previous iteration of that packaging in the trash? Source: Loomer L. and S.C. Whitley . “ Through thick and thin? items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Geography, Not Technology, Holds Back Reusing Retired EV Batteries for Climate Gains Reading Time: 3 minutes Moving old batteries between Chinese provinces could unlock 6 billion tons of emissions savings by 2050, a key to reusing retired EV batteries for climate gains, according to a study. Reusing retired EV batteries for climate gains begins with a simple fact. An electric vehicle (EV) battery usually leaves the car when its capacity drops to about 80%. That leftover capacity can still store solar and wind power for years. In China, the problem is location. Most batteries retire in wealthy eastern provinces, where EV ownership is highest. The wind and solar farms that need storage sit mainly in the west. Much of the batteries’ value is already slipping away. In 2022 alone, about 465,000 tons of retired batteries in China went to waste locally. Researchers at Fudan University in Shanghai have now measured the cost of this mismatch. Their August 2026 study finds it strands about 6 billion tons of carbon savings through 2050. That is roughly a full year of US greenhouse gas emissions. The team published its findings in Environmental Science and Ecotechnology. Its province-by-province model tracks where batteries retire, where they could be reused, and what each option costs. China, the world’s largest EV market, offers a critical test case. Retired batteries can take three main paths. Metallurgical recycling, the most common route, breaks batteries down to recover metals. Direct recycling restores battery materials without breaking down their chemical structure. This keeps more of the value built into the original battery. Storage reuse gives whole batteries a second job. Those last two options deliver far more value. Scenarios that favor storage or direct recycling produced three to five times the cost savings of metallurgical recycling. They also cut emissions by one to three times as much. The study maps the storage mismatch in detail. By 2050, Inner Mongolia alone could be short about 340 gigawatt-hours of storage batteries. Meanwhile, Guangdong and Shandong could each have surpluses of more than 220 gigawatt-hours. Direct recycling needs batteries in manufacturing regions with specialized factories. Under that scenario, Guangdong and Fujian each face shortfalls of thousands of gigawatt-hours. Other provinces would hold surpluses. The gap will widen as eastern EV sales rise and western wind and solar farms expand. In a storage-focused scenario, a 0-to-1 measure of regional imbalance rises from 0.6 in 2035 to 0.7 in 2050. Left alone, this mismatch undercuts the climate gains of reusing retired EV batteries. Without moving batteries between provinces, 50 to 87% of the possible cost savings disappear. Up to 53% of the possible emissions cuts are lost as well. Moving the batteries is cheap by comparison. In the direct recycling scenario, transporting every 100 yuan saved would cost only about 2.3 yuan. Transport emissions would offset just 0.01 to 0.03% of the climate gains. A Fudan University study finds that moving batteries between provinces is central to reusing retired EV batteries for climate gains in China. Photo by Nico Kusuma Jaya on Pexels. Safe handling is essential to reusing retired EV batteries for climate gains. Retired batteries can leak, deform, or catch fire in transit, and they cannot be stacked like ordinary freight. Specialized transport vehicles exist but remain scarce in China. Paperwork adds another hurdle. Because retired batteries count as hazardous materials, both the sending and receiving provinces must approve each transfer. The researchers call for a streamlined national transport network to cut these delays. Those barriers have side effects. Limited transport and processing capacity pushes many batteries into illegal channels. The authors urge stronger penalties for unlicensed recyclers and subsidies for proper disposal. The study’s best scenario gradually shifts away from metallurgical recycling after 2030. By 2050, direct recycling would handle about 56% of collected batteries, and storage would handle about 24%. It would save about 6.1 billion tons of emissions and nearly 4 trillion yuan, about USD 550 billion. Reuse and recycling work together in this plan. Batteries used for storage typically return to recycling within about six years, once capacity falls to 40 to 50%. Each battery can serve cars, then the power grid, and then supply materials for new batteries. The researchers argue that planning, not technology, is the main barrier. Early, coordinated investment in transport and treatment sites could turn spatial barriers into climate and economic gains. Waiting risks locking companies into lower-value metallurgical recycling. China is not alone in this challenge. Europe and the United States face similar splits between where people drive EVs and where renewable power is produced. The authors suggest their model could support reusing retired EV batteries for climate gains there too. The findings come from modeling, so real results will depend on investment, safety rules, and market demand. Building treatment capacity in the right places will also take time. As EV adoption grows, the number of retiring batteries will only rise. Reusing retired EV batteries for climate gains will depend less on new inventions than on trucks, permits, and planning. Getting old batteries to the right place may be one of the simplest climate wins available. The post Geography, Not Technology, Holds Back Reusing Retired EV Batteries for Climate Gains appeared first on Happy Eco News .
